10335-children-s-rights-a-book-of-nurser:
Kate Douglas Wiggin published this book of nursery logic in 1892, gathering talks first given to societies concerned with training children. Three essays by her sister Nora A. Smith join Wiggin's own pieces. The tone is informal, witty, and serious about children as persons, not as small adults.

Essays treat the rights of the child, plays, playthings, reading, stories, and the kindergarten's link to social reform and public schools. Wiggin asks how adults should govern children with love and reason. Readers get a warm, early plea for respect, play, and good books in childhood.
10549-a-romance-of-the-republic:
Lydia Maria Child published this novel in 1867, dedicating it to the parents of Colonel Robert Gould Shaw, early friends of freedom and equal rights. Child, a leading abolitionist, sets the tale in New Orleans, where Mr. Royal meets young Alfred King, son of an old friend, outside his counting house. The Crescent City frames a story of race, love, and republican ideals.

Royal boasts of his daughters as the best sight in town, and Alfred, eager to resemble his father in character, enters a world of slavery, family secrets, and moral choice. Child writes with passion and reforming zeal. Readers get a powerful, abolitionist romance of the American republic.
11374-fun-and-frolic:
Edited by E. T. Roe and profusely illustrated, Fun and Frolic gathers poems and stories for children, opening with Grandmother's Chair. in which an old woman knits and sings by firelight, patiently awaiting reunion in heaven with husband, daughters, and sons. A second piece, How Grandma Surprised Elsie, follows four-year-old Elsie Dean to her first party, Dollie Blossom's fifth birthday. The tone throughout is gentle and domestic.

The collection belongs to the illustrated gift-book tradition for young readers, where verse and short prose alternate. Its subjects are home, holidays, and kindness. For modern readers, it offers a nostalgic sample of what American children read for fun before radio and film.
11573-the-crater-or-vulcan-s-peak-a-tale:
J Fenimore Cooper's 1863 tale, The Crater, opens with a preface. Readers ask why geographies never mention the Reef or Rancocus Island. They ask the same of Vulcan's Peak and the Crater. Cooper admits the places are unknown to geographers, then tells their story anyway.

Mark, the hero, builds a schooner called the Friend Abraham White. Expert American axemen cut the frame for the ship. Heaton brought cart and wagon wheels, which help haul keel timber down to a cove. The novel follows a castaway settlement, its building, its laws, and its fate. It follows the Robinson Crusoe pattern closely.
12088-composition-rhetoric:
Stratton D. Brooks and Marietta Hubbard published this school textbook in 1905 with the American Book Company. Brooks was superintendent of schools in Boston, Hubbard taught English in Illinois, and the book aims to make school writing feel less like a chore.

Part one starts from ideas pupils already have, from experience, imagination, and reading, then moves to purpose, whole compositions, letters, and poetry. Part two teaches description, narration, exposition, and argument, with exercises, grammar review, figures of speech, and synonym lists. Sample passages from writers like Madame de Stael model each form. The book shows Progressive-era faith that clear writing grows from interest and practice, not from rules alone.
1212-love-and-freindship-sic:
Jane Austen, still in her teens, wrote these sharp little tales and letters mocking the sentimental novels of her day. Heroines faint, run off, steal, and marry on a whim, all in high-flown prose that Austen punctures with jokes. The title itself keeps Austen's youthful misspelling.

The pieces show the future novelist already at work: clear eyes, brisk wit, and a taste for exposing folly. They are short, funny, and very young, and they delight readers who know Pride and Prejudice and want to see where Austen began. The pieces are short, funny, and very young, and they delight Austen's readers.
12528-a-voyage-round-the-world-volume-i-:
James Holman, a blind traveller and Fellow of the Royal Society, published this first volume of a voyage round the world in 1834. It covers travels in Africa, Asia, Australasia and America from 1827 to 1832, with an advertisement promising four volumes, each complete in itself, forming a consecutive series.

Holman, who travelled by ear, touch and talk, records ports, peoples, customs and landscapes with unusual care. An Akenside verse fronts the book, praising knowledge and truth above sound and taste. The volume stands as a remarkable feat of travel writing, a blind man's circumnavigation told in clear, observant prose.
12638-public-lands-and-agrarian-laws-of-:
Andrew Stephenson's Johns Hopkins study, ninth series, numbers seven and eight, published in 1891, traces public lands and agrarian laws of the Roman Republic. Stephenson, professor at Wesleyan, aims to follow domain lands from earliest times to the empire, sketching the origin and growth of private property in land.

Expansion of the ager publicus by conquest, and its absorption by sale, gift and settlement, form the argument, under Freeman's motto that history is past politics and politics present history. The study is academic, concise and source-based. It remains a useful introduction to Roman land law, and to the agrarian struggles that shaped republican politics.
12776-dave-darrin-at-vera-cruz-fighting-:
Hancock brings Dave Darrin back as a young naval officer during the American landing at Vera Cruz, Mexico. Aboard ship and ashore, Dave and Dan Dalzell face snipers, street fighting, and a traitor working against his own service. Rescues of trapped American families give the action its human stakes.

Dave must also handle orders he doubts and a rival officer out to trip him, so courage alone will not carry the day. The book mixes sea duty, small-unit fighting, and detective work in the author's brisk style. Young readers get a stirring, if old-fashioned, tale of duty under fire in 1914.
12953-sketches-of-western-north-carolina:
C. L. Hunter's 1877 Sketches of Western North Carolina gather history and biography of the Revolutionary period in Mecklenburg, Rowan, Lincoln, and adjoining counties. Much of the information, the title promises, had never before been published. The dedication speaks to descendants of patriots and to young men seeking lessons in wisdom and endurance.

A heroine's tale stands out. A woman finds Captain Joseph Graham cut down by British cavalry near Sugar Creek Church and dresses his ball and sabre wounds. She carries him four miles on her own pony to his mother. She later won a pension at eighty-six. The book is a rich local history of the Carolina backcountry.
13292-the-romantic:
May Sinclair's 1920 Romantic has two books, Charlotte Redhead and John Roden Conway. It opens with Charlotte turning at the end of a platform, conscious of a big tweed-suited man squaring and swelling in dignity beside her. Its epigraph holds that every kind and beautiful thing on earth has been made so by some cruelty. Sinclair writes modernist fiction with psychological depth.

John calls war the most romantic thing that ever happened, a gamble where nothing matters, even being killed or mutilated. His father calls it false romance, and makes pots of money selling motors. Later, Charlotte lifts a wounded Flamand onto her shoulder, dulls her pain with effort, and lowers him gently back to his stretcher. The novel is a powerful study of war, love, and illusion.
13831-evolution-of-the-japanese-social-a:
Sidney L. Gulick, a missionary scholar in Japan, wrote this study of Japanese social and psychic growth. He traces how Japanese society, art, memory, and imitation developed over time. Diagrams illustrate his arguments about brain size, social unity, and aesthetic growth. Gulick compares East and West without claiming one superior.

Chapters treat architecture, art, and the psychology of imitation. He argues that social life shapes mind more than biology alone. The book grew from missionary writing, but its tone stays calm and scholarly. Readers interested in Japan, psychology, or social theory will find it thoughtful. It also records Western views of Japan in the early 1900s.
14025-mount-music:
Somerville and Martin Ross set this 1920 Irish novel in a great house during years of political strain. Christian, the spirited younger sister, clashes with her elder brother and finds an ally in Larry, an impatient painter who loves her frankness. Around them, priests, visitors, and neighbors argue over religion, land, and loyalty. A hotel reading party, a Protestant Sunday service, and a piano player who crosses lines all stir talk.

Big-house life carries the story. Billiard rooms, gardens, hill walks, and long afternoons of callers give the novel its texture, while Irish politics press at the edges. Christian grows older in feeling than Larry, and their bond deepens through quarrels about art and duty. Readers of the authors' earlier Irish tales will know the humor and the sharp ear for speech. Newcomers meet a household where affection and division live under one roof.
150-the-republic:
Plato's longest dialogue asks what justice is, in a soul and in a city. The Republic, in Benjamin Jowett's classic translation, stages Socrates in debate with friends about the just life. The talk builds an ideal city as a mirror for the human mind.

Guardians, poets, and philosopher-kings take their places in the argument, along with the cave, the divided line, and the myth of Er. Plato weighs democracy, tyranny, and the rule of reason with equal force. Readers still argue over whether his city is a model or a warning. The dialogue anchors Western political thought.
1546-sonnets-on-sundry-notes-of-music:
Sonnets to Sundry Notes of Music is a short Elizabethan sequence, printed with Shakespeare's name, telling in sonnet form a tale of love, rivalry. A lording's daughter torn between a master and a gallant English knight. The poems move between narrative and lyric, with combat of love set against combat of swords.

Only a handful of sonnets survive in this form, and their authorship is debated, as with much of the Shakespeare Apocrypha. Their charm lies in their story and their music. The booklet is a curiosity for Shakespeare lovers, a glimpse of how his name travelled beyond the plays.
15506-philip-winwood-a-sketch-of-the-dom:
Robert Neilson Stephens published this historical novel in Boston in 1900, with L. C. Page, illustrated by E. W. D. Hamilton. It presents itself as the domestic history of Captain Philip Winwood in the War of Independence. The tale covers 1763 to 1786 in New York and London. Its supposed writer is Herbert Russell, his enemy in war, a lieutenant in the Loyalist forces.

Chapters follow Philip's arrival in New York, the Faringfields, rivals in love, enemies in war, and a flight by sea with a duel by moonlight. Winwood declines a promotion, visits his wife, and meets old friends in the dark. Stephens, whose Philip Winwood reached a fiftieth thousand, writes adventure with a domestic heart: war seen through households, friendships, and a rivalry that outlasts the fighting.
15689-gascoyne-the-sandal-wood-trader-a-:
A boys' adventure tale by R. M. Ballantyne, set among the Pacific islands in the days of the sandal-wood trade. Gascoyne, a trader with a rough past, sails a schooner through island waters where missions, chiefs, and rival traders meet. Ballantyne, a veteran of such tales, packs the book with action and moral choice. A. L. Burt Company issued it in New York for young readers.

Early chapters bring a fiery mate named Bumpus, a missionary, and a pastor's household bracing for war. Suspicions, surprises, and fights follow as Gascoyne's past catches up with him. The story praises courage, loyalty, and fair dealing with island peoples, while keeping its pace brisk. For modern readers it offers both a rousing yarn and a window on how Victorians pictured the Pacific.
15770-germany-the-next-republic:
A wartime argument by Carl W. Ackerman, issued in New York by George H. Doran Company in 1917. Ackerman, an American journalist, holds that lasting peace needs a German republic. While the Kaiser and his generals rule, he warns, the world will face the same terror it bore in war. The title states his battle cry for America and its allies.

Ackerman traces German rule, war aims, and the hopes of reformers inside Germany. He weighs what a republic would change for Europe and for America, and what it would cost to win one. The tone is urgent and plain, aimed at citizens following a distant war. As history, the book captures American war aims before the armistice, and the faith that free rule could end old empires.
16595-charles-dickens-and-music:
James T. Lightwood, author of Hymn-Tunes and Their Story, studies Dickens and music in this 1912 volume, fronted by Tom Pinch at the organ. Chapters treat Dickens as a musician, instrumental combinations, flute, organ, and guitar, church music, and songs and singers. Lists of songs, instruments, characters, and music founded on Dickens close the book.

Lightwood writes with affection for both Dickens and music, tracking every tune and instrument in the novels. The book suits Dickens lovers who want to hear his world. It shows how much of Victorian life sang, played, and hummed through his pages.
16686-verses-for-children-and-songs-for-:
Juliana Horatia Ewing wrote this book of verses for children and songs for music, issued by the Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge in London. Pieces run from The Burial of the Linnet and Master Fritz through garden tales, doll songs, and nursery rhymes to a soldier's children and an elf adventure. Music and verse sit side by side.

Ewing writes for young ears: short lines, plain words, and scenes from home, garden, and play. Dolls wash, birds nest, boys build, and girls hold tea parties in her pages. The book still works for reading aloud to small children, and it shows Victorian taste in children's verse at its most gentle and homely.
16866-the-eclipse-of-faith-or-a-visit-to:
This fifth edition of The Eclipse of Faith, issued by Crosby, Nichols in Boston in 1854, stages a visit to a religious skeptic. The American preface warns that the book does not aim to answer every new objection from criticism and philosophy, nor to remove all doubts about Christian revelation. It is ascribed to Henry Rogers, known for Edinburgh Review papers on reason and faith.

The book works by dialogue: a skeptic presses doubts, and a believer answers within a narrow, set design. Its force lies in fair, sharp talk rather than in proof. Readers keen on Victorian faith debates will find a clear, readable sample of how believers met doubt in print, without claiming more than the book intends.
17604-amusing-trial-in-which-a-yankee-la:
Published at the office of the Youth's Cabinet in New York in 1841, this verse tale tells of an amusing trial in which a Yankee lawyer renders a just verdict. The poem opens in a time when, as it puts it, no one thought it sin to hold a person bought as a slave. A Yankee lawyer long kept an enslaved man with whom he shared meals and Sabbath days. The trial that follows turns on the lawyer's wit.

Readers get a short, humorous American verse tale, with period views of slavery that modern readers will find troubling. The book suits readers of early American humour and of the Youth's Cabinet's didactic style. Its interest today lies partly in what it reveals about 1841 attitudes.
17615-in-search-of-the-okapi-a-story-of-:
Ernest Glanville, author of The Diamond Seekers and Tales from the Veld, published this Central African adventure in Chicago in 1904 with A. C. McClurg and Company, with pictures by William Rainey. The hunt for the okapi, the forest animal then newly known to science, gives the book its quest. Chapters open with the hunter, a novel craft, and a canoe adrift.

The story of Muata, trouble brewing, a flight, and the thousand islands follow, with bulls and wild dogs, a lion's charge, a night in the reeds, a trap, and man-eaters ahead. Readers get a boys' adventure of the Congo forest, brisk and full of incident. Glanville's tale suits readers of African adventure fiction.
17803-laxd-la-saga-translated-from-the-i:
Muriel A. C. Press turned the Laxdaela Saga into English in 1899, printed in London by J. M. Dent. The saga tells of the folk of Laxardal in Iceland, from Ketill Flatnose in the 800s through his sons, Unn the Deep-Minded, and the proud house of Olaf the Peacock.

Chapters trace voyages from Norway, land claims, weddings, feuds, ghosts, drownings, and the building of Herdholt. The tale is full of strong women, crafty men, and hard fate, told in the spare saga voice. It stands as one of the great Icelandic family sagas, and Press's version keeps its clear, stern music.
17955-the-trials-of-the-soldier-s-wife-a:
Alex. St. Clair Abrams wrote The Trials of the Soldier's Wife in Atlanta in 1864, calling the Civil War the second American revolution. The book was entered at the Confederate court in Georgia, and its author warns in an appendix that the text holds many errors.

The tale opens in New Orleans, the Crescent City on the Mississippi, as a husband leaves for war and his wife faces want, fear, and lonely days. Abrams writes from the Southern side, with pride in refined Creole life and scorn for the foe. It is a wartime novel of the home front, best read as a period voice, not as fair history.
18284-for-every-music-lover-a-series-of-:
Aubertine Woodward Moore published this series of practical essays on music in 1902. Her preface argues that music belongs to all people, not only to a privileged class, and that teachers and ministers of the art should serve that wider public. The essays then take up the origin and function of music, blunders in music study, and the place of song in human life.

Portraits of Mozart, Brahms, Liszt, Paganini, Jenny Lind, Corelli, and Saint-Saens mark the range of her examples. Moore draws on myth, church ritual, folk song, and the views of writers from Plato to Wagner. A reader gets plain guidance for listening with more care, and for treating music as a common good rather than a closed art.
19676-shakespeare-and-music:
Edward W. Naylor wrote this study of Shakespeare and music, published in London in the late eighteen hundreds with examples from sixteenth and seventeenth century music. It cites plays act by act to show how songs, dances, and instruments shaped the stage.

Tavern music gets a vivid note: a man could hardly dine without itinerant players following him, singing or playing for a fee, while Falstaff and his crew enjoyed the custom. Naylor's book remains a standard guide to music in Shakespeare's world. Naylor traces one quoted song, Richard Edwards' When griping grief, through Shakespeare's variations on it.
19880-voice-production-in-singing-and-sp:
Voice Production in Singing and Speaking rests, its title says, on scientific principles. Wesley Mills, a physiologist, wrote it. Its illustrations contrast healthy and diseased throats for singers. One plate shows a larynx pale with tuberculosis. A weakened muscle leaves the vocal band slack on one side. The voice turns uncertain and harsh as a result. Such images impress the normal by contrast, Mills explains.

Voice teachers of the era craved anatomy to replace guesswork. Laryngoscope pictures brought the singing throat into view. Mills treats breath, cords, and resonance as one machine. Singers and speakers both get exercises from the science. The book marks elocution's turn toward the laboratory. Its plates remain striking medical documents.
20571-woman-s-work-in-music:
Arthur Elson's Woman's Work in Music, published in 1903, surveys what women had done in music and compares it with the work of men. Elson was a music critic, and he writes with a critic's store of examples. The question of women composers was much argued in his day.

He notes a curious fact about the Church of Rome. The church admits no women to a share in its services, yet it has made a woman, Saint Cecilia, the patron saint of music. The religions of the ancient world paid women even more homage in this art. Elson builds his case from such history.
21072-the-pirate-island-a-story-of-the-s:
A gale on the Essex coast opens Harry Collingwood's South Pacific tale. Rescuers pull an orphan boy from a sinking ship, and a fisherman adopts him. Years later, young people sail for Australia aboard the Galatea. Fire breaks out on the return voyage, and all aboard take to the boats.

Their rescuers turn out to be pirates, who carry them to an island base full of captured ships. Learning that one prisoner has built his own fast yacht, the pirate captain orders a new fast ship built. The captives also find a reef of gold, then flee in the new ship as an earthquake and eruption kill their pursuers.
21084-jokes-for-all-occasions-selected-a:
Jokes for All Occasions was published in New York by Edward J. Clode in 1921 and 1922. An unnamed speaker, billed as one of America's foremost public speakers, selected it. After-dinner speakers were its market. The jokes are sorted by topic so a speaker can find one fast.

The opening section covers absentmindedness. It starts with a man who grabs a woman's umbrella on a street car. He meets her again that day, carrying eight repaired umbrellas of his own. Other tales mock inventors, clergymen, and forgetful husbands. The humour is gentle, dated, and built for retelling aloud at banquets and club nights.
21456-the-cruise-of-the-dainty-or-roving:
Two brothers endure a flat calm at the start of W. H. G. Kingston's The Cruise of the Dainty. Their ship roves the Pacific, where many islanders had good cause to hate Europeans. Traders had lured folk aboard, shut them below, and sold them as slaves in Peru.

On deck, mates set hands to mats, rope yarns, knots, and splices in the heat. The Dainty meets wary islands, bad weather, and worse crews on other ships. Kingston keeps the book short, but he packs it with the ways of Pacific voyaging. Honest dealing, he shows, is rare and precious in those seas.
21457-the-cruise-of-the-mary-rose-or-her:
Kingston's The Cruise of the Mary Rose wears the dress of a boys' sea story, but its heart lies elsewhere. Much of the book treats the work of Christian missions in the Pacific. A thin plot links long extracts from reports by mission staff and naval officers.

Those reports tell of island life, new churches, and the hardships of the work. Kingston, a devout man, writes here with extra zeal for the cause. He does not hide the ugly customs the missions fought against. Readers who care for mission history will find rich, first-hand matter, gathered from men who saw it.
21542-spirit-and-music:
H. Ernest Hunt argues that music is a spiritual art in Spirit and Music, published in 1922. Hunt lectured on psychology at London schools for music teachers. His other books treat nerve control, self training, and the influence of thought.

He notes that, strictly, no sound exists until the brain renders the ear's message. Chapters treat the spirit of music, its place in life, and the conditions of inspiration. The interpreter, the teacher, and the soul of song each get a chapter. Hunt closes on pure music and the purpose of art, in a thoughtful Edwardian key.
21552-masterman-ready-or-the-wreck-of-th:
Captain Marryat wrote Masterman Ready, or the Wreck of the Pacific, in 1841 for young readers. A captain watches the helm with care as his ship runs before a heavy gale. He sings a low sea song while he studies the sky.

Ready, the old seaman of the title, guides a wrecked family on a Pacific island. The book was Marryat's nineteenth, and its plainer style suits its child audience. Storm, wreck, and the slow building of a home fill the tale. Generations of children learned seamanship and grit from Ready's steady, knowing hands.
21714-the-red-eric:
Captain Dunning, owner of a South Sea whale ship, bursts with color from the first page of this Ballantyne novel. His whiskers are red, his coat is blue, and his waistcoat is yellow. He is abrupt in speech but kind at heart, and his eyes twinkle more often than they flash. The Red Eric is his ship, and her crew fills out the tale.

Whaling in the South Seas means long months of work, danger, and strange sights far from home. Ballantyne keeps the captain's good humor at the center of the story. Around him he builds a crew's life at sea: storms, whales, ports, and the bonds that hold sailors together.
22252-rollo-on-the-atlantic:
Jacob Abbott sent his most famous boy travelling in Rollo on the Atlantic. Rollo, about twelve years old, makes the voyage to Europe under extraordinary circumstances. He goes alone, or rather with no one appointed to take care of him. A kind uncle and fellow passengers must fill the gap on the long crossing.

Abbott fills the steamship days with lessons on ships, the sea, ports, and manners. Rollo asks the questions young readers would ask, and grown-ups answer them patiently. The Rollo books taught geography and conduct to millions of American children. This volume opens the European tour that carried Rollo through England, France, Switzerland, and Holland.
22815-the-philippine-islands-a-political:
Spanish rule comes under sharp attack in The Philippine Islands, a wide survey of the islands' politics, land, peoples, and trade. The writer charges Spain with chasing new dominion like a mania while neglecting roads, schools, and commerce at home in the colony. Money spent on fruitless expeditions, he argues, could have built wealth many times over.

Around that argument sits a full portrait of the archipelago. Geography, native customs, government, and resources each get their turn, giving readers of the era a single volume for a distant place. The book matters now as evidence of how the islands were described to English-speaking readers, praise, blame, and bias included. It should be read with that slant in mind.
23162-no-great-magic:
Fritz Leiber checks the callboard in No Great Magic. The dresser puts the question quietly to Siddy. Which play tonight, Anderson's Elizabeth or Shakespeare's Macbeth? The callboard says Macbeth, yet Miss Nefer is preparing Elizabeth. She has just sent him to fetch the red wig.

A dresser who has served every great stage magician of history narrates Leiber's tale, and theatre itself becomes the spell. Costumes, wigs, and two plays competing for one night carry an argument about where magic really lives. Leiber loved actors, swords, and cats in roughly that order, and his backstage knowledge glows here. The story is a connoisseur's piece, greasepaint over genuine wonder, by a writer who never separated the two.
23260-the-two-whalers-or-adventures-in-t:
The Two Whalers, or Adventures in the Pacific is a sea adventure tale. Its warmest moment is a reunion. A sailor gives his name as Bill, then grips the narrator's hand and wrings it till it nearly comes off, half laughing and half crying with pleasure.

He is sure he has found his brother Jack. At once the questions pour out: how are father and mother, Susan and Jane, Mary and Dick, and little Tommy? The scene sets family feeling at the heart of whaling adventure. Readers get the Pacific whaling world of ships, ports, and chance meetings between men long lost to home.
23745-aladdin-co-a-romance-of-yankee-mag:
Herbert Quick published Aladdin and Co. in 1904, calling it a romance of Yankee magic. Its hero, Jim, discovers his coral island, reaches an atoll, and is inducted into a cave and enlisted in an enterprise that carries him from the South Seas to Wall Street. The magic here is American: money, railroads, and deals, worked with Aladdin's boldness.

Chapters follow Jim abroad under the Jolly Roger and the dedication of Lynhurst Park. Then come the burdens of wealth falling on its holders, and affairs of the heart considered in relation to dollars and cents. Laura and Clifford go away, Mr. Trescott departs, and events resume their usual course. Quick's fable asks what a poor man does when fortune hands him a lamp.
24588-the-natural-history-of-chocolate-b:
Published in the eighteenth century, this treatise gives a distinct and particular account of the cocoa tree, its growth and culture, and the preparation, properties, and medicinal virtues of its fruit. Its author sets out to correct the errors of earlier writers on chocolate, and to explain the best way of making it.

Chapters describe the tree, its fruit, and the many uncommon medicines and uses claimed for chocolate, with notes on its history from the Americas to Europe. The spelling is old and inconsistent, as in the original. Readers get a curious, learned, and appetising piece of food history, from a time when chocolate was still a medicine as much as a treat.
24821-diamond-dyke-the-lone-farm-on-the-:
George Manville Fenn set this boys' adventure on a lone ostrich farm in the dry South African veldt. Two young Britons, helped by a local married couple and a wise dog, face lions, drought, and thin stores. When the elder brother falls ill of African fever, sixteen-year-old Dyke must ride six or seven days to the nearest honest storekeeper.

A flash flood delays his return, and on his way home he finds neighbors ready to seize the stock. Dyke nurses his brother back to health, and a visit from the old German storekeeper brings a discovery that could change the brothers' fortunes for good. Fenn tells a gripping tale of pluck and hard work on the frontier.
25009-the-world-s-greatest-books-volume-:
Volume fourteen of The World's Greatest Books, jointly edited by Arthur Mee and J. A. Hammerton and published by Wm. H. Wise, continues philosophy and adds economics. Its contents run from Hegel's Philosophy of History and Hume's moral and political essays through Kant's two Critiques, Lewes's history of philosophy, Locke on human understanding, and Montaigne's essays. Plato's Apology and Republic, Schopenhauer's World as Will and Idea, Seneca on Benefits, and Spencer on education, biology, and sociology complete the survey.

A passage from Spencer's Education argues that the laws of life hold throughout organic creation. It compares two boys: one made happy by mastering interesting subjects, the other facing cold looks, threats, and punishment, and loathing for his studies. Success benefits temper and mind, failure injures both, showing the mind's power over the body. The volume serves as a compact library of great thought.
25681-the-quadrupeds-pic-nic:
This 1840 verse tale in rhyming couplets, The Quadrupeds' Pic Nic, was published in London by William Pickering. Its advertisement calls the poem a humble imitation of Mrs. Dorset's Peacock at Home, admitting even that imitation lacks originality, since quadrupeds already enjoyed an Elephants' Ball and a Lions' Masquerade.

Grasshoppers' feasts excited the spleen of birds and beasts, and peacock and turkey flew into a passion at insects pretending to fashion. The poet, thinking it hard that beasts go unsung, gives quadrupeds their own picnic in rhyming couplets, a light animal satire for children and their parents. The author signs the advertisement F. B. C.
26206-pandemic:
J. F. Bone's science-fiction story opens in a disordered laboratory, where Dr. Walter Kramer studies a plague called Thurston's Disease. Kramer explains the name with grim humour: Thurston found the disease and died of it first. For public use, the staff call it virus pneumonic plague, a better term than advertising a killer's name.

A new assistant joins Kramer at the Institute, tidies his lab, and frees him to think while she runs blood slides and stains. The tale's motto argues that people rarely do useless things widely and steadily, so some custom may hold a hidden reason. The story pairs plague research with a puzzle about human habits that refuse to die.
26279-on-singing-and-music:
This 1885 essay from Philadelphia Friends states the Quaker testimony against singing and music in worship. It was read from the minutes of the Meeting for Sufferings at the Yearly Meeting held in late Fourth Month, 1885, and Friends ordered it printed for information and warning. Joseph Walton signed the minutes as clerk.

The essay holds that true worship is spiritual, not outward, and it quotes Christ's words that the Spirit quickens while the flesh profits nothing. George Fox and his fellow workers, it says, saw that outward forms led believers back into dependence on rites. Singing for amusement, it warns, pleases carnal ears rather than a holy God. The tract preserves a plain Quaker voice on worship.
27434-doctor-jones-picnic:
S. E. Chapman, M.D., published this romance in San Francisco with the Whitaker and Ray Company in 1898. Chapman admits he offers it with trepidation, since he has broached fearlessly the deep things of God. Its scope grew upon his hands day by day until he could not stop short of the Millennium.

Chapman says Dr. Jones's marvelous cures rest on cases from practice, and one object of the work is to stimulate scientific study of the law of cure that guided the doctor's choice of remedy. Silver Cloud and her achievements, and air currents in the upper deep, also figure. The book mixes romance, healing, and prophecy in a bold, old California manner.
27578-two-years-with-the-natives-in-the-:
Dr. Felix Speiser wrote this account of two years among the peoples of the western Pacific, with forty illustrations from photographs and a map. His chapters move from Nouméa and Port Vila through Maei, Tongoa, Epi, and Malekula, to life on a plantation in the Segond Channel.

Speiser then treats recruiting, Vao, Port Olry and a sing-sing, and Santo, with its pygmies, its pigs, and its peak. Ambrym, Pentecoste, Aoba, the Banks Islands, Tanna, and the Santa Cruz Islands follow. Illustrations show taro fields, looms, dancing grounds, gamals, and chiefs' houses. The book is a detailed ethnographic travel account of its period.
28451-i-like-martian-music:
Charles E. Fritch's short story I Like Martian Music pictures Mars as an old, finite culture of music and colour. Longtree, a Martian musician, sits before his hole in the sandy red hills, trying to finish a brief symphony. His skin changes colour with his feelings: yellow for pride, green for disappointment, and orange for happiness.

His friend Channeljumper, striding on long thin legs, urges him to play what he has written, but Longtree cannot find the final note. It must sum up the whole symphony, and it may sound alien. Fritch's story is a gentle fantasy about art, friendship, and the search for one perfect note on another world.
28696-symbolic-logic:
Lewis Carroll's Symbolic Logic, part 1, elementary, in its fourth edition, teaches reasoning by diagram. Carroll opens with a worked syllogism about a sea-serpent story: the tale always sets him yawning, and he never yawns except at what is totally devoid of interest. Diagrams combine the premises, and the conclusion follows: the story is totally devoid of interest.

The fourth edition revises classification and propositions, treating the whole universe as a class and recasting propositions of existence. Carroll promises advanced and transcendental parts to come, with hypotheticals, dilemmas, triliteral propositions, and curiosa logica. Readers get logic as a game, exact and playful at once.
29499-the-paper-moneys-of-europe-their-m:
Francis W. Hirst's 1922 book, printed by Houghton Mifflin of Boston and New York, treats the paper moneys of Europe and their moral and economic significance. Delivered as Barbara Weinstock Lectures on the Morals of Trade at the University of California, it weighs what paper money does to trust, thrift, and honest dealing. Hirst opens by noting how much attention is given to the prehistoric history of mankind, while the morals of money go unexamined.

The book follows Europe's paper currencies through war and inflation, judging them as moral instruments, not mere counters. Its lessons speak to any age of easy money. Students of economic history will find a clear, principled study of money's power to build or to corrupt.
29744-kristy-s-rainy-day-picnic:
Olive Thorne Miller's Kristy's Rainy Day Picnic, printed in 1906 by Houghton, Mifflin of Boston and New York with pictures by Ethel N. Farnsworth, opens on a rainy day that spoils a picnic. Its chapters follow playing doctor and what came of it, a schoolgirl's joke, all night in the schoolhouse, and Molly's secret room. How mamma ran away, how Aunt Betty made her choice, and Nora's good luck follow.

Kristy learns, as another girl did, that disappointment comes sometimes from carelessness, not weather, and that fussing helps nothing. A picture shows the children playing that a wax doll is sick. Young readers will find a gentle, old-style book of rainy-day play and small lessons.
29860-a-great-man-a-frolic:
Arnold Bennett published A Great Man, subtitled A Frolic, in London in 1904. It opens on an evening in 1866, exactly eight hundred years after the Battle of Hastings. Above the Oxford Street shop he runs, Henry Knight, forty years old and a draper's manager, occupies his sitting room. He is proud of that room, which stands for an ideal achieved, and Bennett lets the reader feel that pride.

Twenty-nine chapters follow a life from birth and christening, through school, marrons glaces, and a school calamity, to fame, a lion in his lair, and Geraldine. A novelist in a box, press and public, and a rake's progress mark the later course. The book is a comic chronicle of talent, vanity, and London life, told with Bennett's dry, watchful wit.
30412-on-the-execution-of-music-and-prin:
M. Camille Saint-Saëns speaks On the Execution of Music, and Principally of Ancient Music. It was delivered at the Salon de la Pensée Française at the Panama-Pacific Exposition in San Francisco on June first, nineteen hundred and fifteen, done into English by Henry P. Bowie, and published by the Blair-Murdock Company in San Francisco in 1915. Until the thirteenth century, Saint-Saëns notes, music notation was an undecipherable scrawl.

Plain Song, or Plain Chant, then arrived in square and diamond-shaped notes, before graduals and introits were barred at all. Troubadour songs seem to use three-beat bars, accented on each bar's feeble note, though exclusive triple time is probably a mistaken theory. St. Isidore recommends high, sweet, and clear voices for introits, graduals, and offertories.
30487-confessions-of-a-neurasthenic:
William Taylor Marrs, M.D., writes Confessions of a Neurasthenic, copyrighted in 1908 and published in Philadelphia by F. A. Davis, with original illustrations. Marrs apologizes in advance, saying his life work made him especially observant, so nearly every incident and statement rests on actual experience, not whole cloth invention.

In this monograph, the neurasthenic carries a heavy burden, suffering in a measure vicariously for his whole class. Marrs uses one patient's story to show the strain, nerves, and fatigue that marked the diagnosis in his day. The book reads as a medical memoir, candid about suffering and about the limits of early nerve medicine.
30866-analysis-of-mr-mill-s-system-of-lo:
Held here is a detailed analysis of John Stuart Mill's System of Logic, Ratiocinative and Inductive, a work Mill issued in a sixth edition in two volumes. The front pages list Mill's other books, from Principles of Political Economy and On Liberty to Considerations on Representative Government and Utilitarianism. The analysis itself works through Mill's system step by step, rather than offering a short summary.

Its opening section argues for starting logic with an analysis of language, and later pages weigh connotative terms, laws, and fallacies in Mill's sense. Readers who study philosophy will find a careful Victorian guide to a large and influential book. It is best read beside Mill himself, since its value lies in unpacking arguments that Mill states in dense, formal prose.
31175-a-new-species-of-frog-genus-tomoda:
Robert G. Webb's 1962 paper names a new frog, Tomodactylus saxatilis, from thirteen specimens collected in Durango and Sinaloa, Mexico, in the summers of 1960 and 1961. The specimens went to the museums of the University of Kansas and Michigan State University. The species is described from a holotype taken eight miles west of El Palmito, Sinaloa, at about 6,100 feet in June 1961.

Its diagnosis lists truncate tips on the two outer fingers, a tympanum less than half the eye's diameter, and smooth belly skin. It also lists a marbled pattern on back and head and a whitish belly without dark marks. Published as volume 15, number 3 of the Kansas museum series, the paper is the formal record for this western Mexican frog.
31482-smeaton-and-lighthouses-a-popular-:
Smeaton and Lighthouses, a popular biography with a historical introduction and sequel, was published in London by John W. Parker in 1844, the year given as M.DCCC.XLIV. Its preface argues that biography should show the influence a person exerted on a pursuit and an age, not merely personal and trivial details. The book applies that rule to John Smeaton, the engineer, and to the lighthouses he built and improved.

Early chapters survey lighthouses from beacon fires and the Pharos of Alexandria to the Tour de Corduan, then turn to England's lights and Trinity House. The Eddystone chapters trace Winstanley's and Rudyerd's towers, their fates, and Smeaton's appointment to build anew. Readers of engineering history will find a clear Victorian life-and-works study.
31582-st-gregory-and-the-gregorian-music:
E. G. P. Wyatt's St. Gregory and the Gregorian Music was published for the Plainsong and Medieval Music Society in London in 1904. It is a short study of the pope and the chant that bears his name. Wyatt notes in his preface that the original conception of the little book was due to the Reverend W. H. Frere, whose help and advice were ungrudgingly given. Frere, Wyatt adds, is responsible only for the notes on the tropes and for the third and fourth portraits of St. Gregory, while the rest was compiled from other sources.

The book traces Gregory's life and the tradition of plainsong, the unaccompanied chant of the Western church. Wyatt's study remains useful as a clear, short guide to a pope, a chant, and the scholarship that joined them.
31799-sketch-of-a-new-esthetic-of-music:
Ferruccio Busoni's Sketch of a New Esthetic of Music, translated from German by Dr. Th. Baker and published in New York in 1911, gathers notes that Busoni says grew from convictions long held and slowly matured. Its epigraph asks what the seeker wants, and answers that he wants the unknown, beyond the end.

Busoni frames a problem of the first magnitude with apparent simplicity, while admitting that it cannot be solved for generations, if at all. Readers get a short, provocative essay by a composer-pianist arguing that music must reach past what is already known toward sounds and forms not yet imagined.
31992-titanic:
Filson Young's Titanic, published in London, is the account of the great liner's sinking by a writer already known for books on Columbus, on memory and description, on Velasquez, and on music. Young's other titles listed in the volume include Memory Harbour, Venus and Cupid, The Sands of Pleasure, When the Tide Turns, Ireland at the Cross Roads, and Mastersingers.

The Titanic book itself tells, with the immediacy of a contemporary, how the largest ship of her day struck an iceberg and was lost. It also tells what the disaster meant for the age that built her. Readers get an early and influential account of the sinking, written before the legend hardened into myth.
32329-guy-in-the-jungle-or-a-boy-s-adven:
William Murray Graydon's Guy in the Jungle, or A Boy's Adventure in the Wilds of Africa, published in Chicago by M. A. Donohue and Company with copyrights in 1890 and 1902, is a boys' African adventure by the author of Jungles and Traitors, In Barracks and Wigwam, and The Camp in the Snow. Its frontispiece shows the moment when the spear flashed in the torchlight. A prologue sets the scene far from Africa, in a foggy London November.

The city lies buried under a dank, yellow fog. Traffic is temporarily checked, foot passengers grope by street lamps, and link boys run before cabs and carriages with blazing torches. In the coffee-room of a Strand hotel, a young man stands by the window, light-haired, with a drooping golden mustache and a bronzed complexion telling of foreign lands and tropical suns. Readers get a boys' jungle tale, framed by London fog.
32447-the-thing-in-the-attic:
James Blish's tale, printed in If Worlds of Science Fiction in July 1954, follows Honath the Pursemaker, arch-doubter on the world Tellura. Honath and fellow doubters do not believe in the Giants, and for that unbelief they are cast into Hell, as the tale's sidenote puts it. When survival depends on unwavering faith in their own beliefs, they learn that Giants exist after all.

The Book of Laws, quoted at the opening, says Giants came from the far stars and found Tellura wanting. They made men live always in air and sunlight and starlight, to be reminded of them. Giants taught men speech, writing, weaving, and needful arts, then departed, promising return. Honath, hauled from nets before dawn and led through musky orchid gardens, must test doubt against a world built by beings he denied.
32715-a-history-of-the-third-french-repu:
C. H. C. Wright, professor of French at Harvard, writes the history of the Third French Republic, published by Houghton Mifflin in May 1916. He opens with Napoleon III and Bismarck, the two men chiefly answerable, each in his own way, for the republic born from the Franco-Prussian War and the Fourth of September.

Ten chapters follow the administrations in turn, from Thiers and Mac-Mahon through Grevy, Carnot, Casimir-Perier, Faure, Loubet, Fallieres, and Poincare. Along the way Wright weighs Jules Ferry's school laws and the Article 7 fight, the Dreyfus agitation, and Waldeck-Rousseau's long ministry, ending with the republic on the eve of war.
33109-arabian-wisdom-selections-and-tran:
John Wortabet's Arabian Wisdom, selections and translations from the Arabic in the Wisdom of the East series edited by L. Cranmer-Byng, appeared in a third impression from John Murray in London in 1916. Wortabet dedicates the book to his children. An appendix gives the first chapter of the Koran, in the name of God, abundant in mercy and compassion, with praise to God, Lord of the universe.

The selections that follow gather proverbs, sayings, and short pieces from Arabic literature, translated for English readers who wanted the wisdom of another tradition in brief, readable form. Wortabet, a physician and translator, keeps the pieces short and pointed. The book remains a gentle introduction to Arabic moral literature, useful for readers who like proverb collections and for students of how Eastern wisdom was presented in the West.
33324-k-k-k-sketches-humorous-and-didact:
James Melville Beard's K. K. K. Sketches, published in Philadelphia in 1877, treats the more important events of the Ku-Klux-Klan movement in the South, with humor and didactic purpose. Beard discusses the causes that gave rise to the Klan and the social and political issues that flowed from it, in sketches that mix story with argument. The book was entered for copyright in 1876.

The volume's interest today lies in its early, contemporary view of Reconstruction violence, told by a writer close to the events. Its tone, at once comic and moralizing, reflects its age's way of handling a dark subject. For students of Reconstruction, it is a revealing, if dated, source on how the Klan was seen soon after its rise.
33527-whales-dolphins-and-porpoises-of-t:
Stephen Leatherwood, David K. Caldwell, and Howard E. Winn prepared this NOAA technical report as a guide to identifying whales, dolphins, and porpoises of the western North Atlantic. Published in Seattle in August 1976 as Circular 396 of the National Marine Fisheries Service, it follows an earlier photographic guide to the cetaceans of the eastern North Pacific.

The guide helps readers recognize species encountered at sea, using descriptions and illustrations suited to field use rather than laboratory study. It covers the full range of whales, dolphins, and porpoises found in western Atlantic waters. Naturalists, sailors, and whale watchers will find it a practical reference, and historians of marine science will value it as a record of what was known about these animals in the 1970s.
34488-the-cruise-of-the-frolic:
The Cruise of the Frolic is a yachting novel by Kingston, framed as the true adventures of Barnaby Brine, a naval officer whose preface swears he meant to wound no one. Friends in the tale, he admits, thought themselves caricatured and talked of duels. The first chapter opens on a regatta morning at Cowes in the palmy days of the club.

Brine looks back on fleets of white ensigned yachts following their commodore, before steamers came to spoil the water. Kingston, the great boys' sea writer, mixes race, cruise, and comic mishap. The book keeps the shine of the early yachting world.
35145-paul-gosslett-s-confessions-in-lov:
Paul Gosslett's Confessions in Love, Law, and the Civil Service, by Charles James Lever, was printed at Boston in 1906. The first confession is headed My First Mission. Paul walks Green Park in low spirits when a friend slips an arm in his and asks if he knows Italian. A task is on offer for a few months. The son of a rich baronet, a Wiltshire member, has been seized by brigands in Calabria and held for a stiff price.

His father lies too ill to be told, and the Foreign Secretary, a friend of the house, will pay at once. The catch is cover: the state needs a man who can carry the cash and treat with the band, yet wear a public air. Paul takes the road south. Tale fans get Lever's blend of farce, state craft, and risk.
35157-handel-the-story-of-a-little-boy-w:
Handel is a life of the composer for children by Thomas Tapper, in the Child's Own Book of Great Musicians series. The Theodore Presser Company of Philadelphia published it. Its full subtitle calls Handel the little boy who practiced in an attic. The book came with cord and needle and directions for binding it.

The series list names Bach, Mozart, Beethoven, Wagner, and others, each with a volume of his own. Numbered pictures show scenes of Handel's life. Tapper tells how the boy, forbidden music at home, stole practice on a clavichord hidden in the attic. Such books were sold to piano teachers and parents across America.
3526-five-weeks-in-a-balloon-or-journeys:
Jules Verne sends three travelers across Africa by balloon in this early adventure novel, presented as from the notes of Dr Ferguson and translated by William Lackland. The balloon carries them over deserts, rivers, and mountains that European explorers had only partly mapped. Verne's preface praises the ingenuity of the plan and the travelers' tales that inspired it.

The journey mixes scientific talk about winds and altitude with escapes from storms, hostile peoples, and wild animals. Verne writes with the excitement of an age when maps still held blank spaces. The novel suits young readers and adults who enjoy classic adventure, and it launched Verne's career as a storyteller of travel and invention.
35566-history-of-the-postage-stamps-of-t:
History of the Postage Stamps of the United States of America is a work by John K Tiffany, issued at Saint Louis in eighteen eighty seven. Tiffany was president of the American Philatelic Association. A portrait of the author serves as frontispiece. The contents open with a preface and an introduction, then take up early local posts chapter by chapter.

Chapter one treats the city dispatch post of the United States. Later chapters handle the stamps of single cities in turn. Among them are Saint Louis, Brattleboro, New Haven, and Providence. Alexandria, Baltimore, and Millbury follow in the list. Stamped envelopes earn a chapter of their own. Tiffany held posts in philatelic societies abroad as well, his title page notes. The book is a founding text of American stamp study.
35721-shakespeare-and-music:
Shakespeare and Music, by Christopher Wilson, was published by the Stage office in London in 1922. A memoir of the author, reprinted from the Musical Times of April 1919, stands before the chapters; the frontispiece calls him the late Christopher Wilson.

Wilson was born at Melbourne in Derbyshire in 1874, of musical stock on both sides. The Times praised his master song of 1901, a setting of Come away, Death. It was all that such a song should be, the paper said, and as musicianly as a Mendelssohn scholar's work ought to be. Little of his work was printed, the memoir laments. The chapters then take the plays in order, from Antony and Cleopatra to The Winter's Tale, each on its music. Hamlet runs longest. A chapter on Shakespeare's songs and an index close the book.
35977-letters-of-abelard-and-heloise-to-:
Letters of Abelard and Heloise, printed at London in 1782, joins the famous love letters to a full account of the pair. John Hughes wrote the history of their lives, amours and misfortunes. Pope's poem of Eloisa to Abelard stands among the letters. This edition adds a mate to it: Madan's poem of Abelard to Eloisa.

Peter Abelard was born at Palais in Brittany, the son of Beranger, a wealthy gentleman. He gave his birthright to his younger brothers to follow philosophy and divinity. The letters were written long after the lovers' marriage and parting, when both lived under religion. Hughes finds in them a surprising mixture of devotion and tenderness, frailty and suffering, that still moves every reader.
36659-magic:
Ellis Stanyon wrote this handbook of magic tricks and how they work. Penn printed it in Philadelphia in 1910, first copyright 1901. Stanyon promises clear word on well known illusions and new ones. An introduction gives background before sleight of hand rules begin.

Tricks with coins, handkerchiefs, balls, and hats each take a chapter. Anti-spiritualistic tricks and after dinner tricks fill the mid book. Stage tricks, shadowgraphy, and the servante device close the survey. The wand chapter says a plain rod answers as well as ebony. A servante figure shows the hidden shelf device that helps coin work at the table.
37383-the-argentine-republic:
The Argentine Republic is a book about the country, offered by the Argentine Commission as a souvenir of the Panama Pacific Exposition at San Francisco in 1915. Horacio Anasagasti, the head of the commission, signs the offering. Its president was Gallardo, and its staff covered farming, schools, fine arts, and live stock.

An opening survey treats the country's physical features and its growth. The republic's rise, the text says, dates from May 25, 1810, when the people of Buenos Aires declared their independence and set up the United Provinces of the River Plate. From an obscure Spanish colony, Argentina grew into one of the great countries of the world, with progress and freedom as watchwords. A constitution followed on May 25, 1853, proclaimed at Santa Fe.
37715-mother-meg-or-the-story-of-dickie-:
Catharine Shaw tells a child's tale in Mother Meg, or The Story of Dickie's Attic, in a new edition from Shaw of London. Shaw wrote The Galled Farm, Alick's Hero, and Nellie Arundel, as the title page notes. The book stands in a gift line of neat, gilt edged tales for the young.

A front plate quotes a rough voice from page 109. Well, you can have him, the voice says, but the girl will take on if I say yes. The line hints at a hard choice over a child's fate. Shaw's tales for boys and girls mix home scenes, faith, and kind hearts. Young readers get a tale built round Dickie and the attic that bears his name.
38086-the-social-evolution-of-the-argent:
The Social Evolution of the Argentine Republic is a study by Ernesto Quesada, reprinted from The Annals in May 1911. Quesada served as Attorney-General of the Argentine Republic and taught at the universities of Buenos Ayres and La Plata. The piece appeared as number 636 in the line of the American Academy of Political and Social Science, priced at twenty-five cents.

Quesada writes as both a scholar and a servant of the state he studies. His theme is the growth of Argentine society over time: how the young republic changed as it grew. The reprint placed his account before American readers at a moment when trade and ties between the two Americas were much in debate.
38448-modern-magic:
Modern Magic examines the hidden powers of mind and nature, written by Schele de Vere. Putnam published the book at New York in 1873. A line from Horace stands at the head, promising light from smoke. The preface lays out the author's case for taking wonders seriously.

Humans, he argues, are meant to master the world the senses show. Yet reports persist of laws and events beyond those senses. Such reports, he says, must not be mocked or waved aside. The task is to sift the true grain from the mass of rubbish. Sorting and classing the claims comes next. The book then treats dreams, second sight, and kindred wonders of the age. De Vere writes as a scholar of language turned student of the unseen.
39257-socialism-utopian-and-scientific:
Socialism: Utopian and Scientific is a political work by Frederick Engels. Edward Aveling translated it into English. Charles Kerr and Company published this edition in Chicago. A special introduction by the author opens the book. Engels explains that the little book began as part of a larger whole. It grew out of his work against Doctor Duhring, about 1875. The Kerr edition was sold at twenty five cents.

The title promises a contrast at the heart of the argument. Utopian socialism is set against a scientific kind. The work became a standard short statement of Marxist thought. Its low priced pamphlet form aimed at wide working class reading. A picture of labour ornaments the title pages. Readers meet Engels's own account of how the piece began.
39300-the-psychology-of-arithmetic:
The Psychology of Arithmetic is a book on the mind in sums by Edward Thorndike of a great teach school of New York. It was first put out in nineteen twenty two. The host print is a late print of the same year set. A note from that school, of the spring of nineteen twenty, stands past the front. The list of parts is a map of the theme.

A lead in treats the mind lore of the school themes at large. Then come the kind of the gifts of sums. The sense of counts, the tongue of sums, the work of tasks, and the thought of sums fill that part. A sum of it and a part on the folk life of sums stand at its end. The next part treats the test of those gifts.
40305-problems-of-the-pacific:
Problems of the Pacific is a survey of world politics by Frank Fox, author of Ramparts of Empire. Williams and Norgate published it in London in 1912, with a map. Its eighteen chapters begin by naming the Pacific the ocean of the future. Russia in the Pacific and the rise of Japan follow, then China and the teeming millions of Asia.

The United States appears as an imperial power, and Great Britain enters the Pacific. The British continent in the Pacific, New Zealand and the smaller colonies, the native races, and Latin America each get a chapter. Canada and the Pacific, the navies and armies of the Pacific, and its treaties come next. The Panama Canal and the industrial position lead to strategic considerations and a last chapter, The Rivals.
40794-essays-in-experimental-logic:
John Dewey gathered his papers on logic in this volume for the University of Chicago Press. Essays in Experimental Logic came out in June 1916 and ran to three printings by 1920. Dewey's note at the front tells where the core pieces first stood.

In 1903 the press had issued Studies in Logical Theory, with work by seven of Dewey's peers and four essays of his own. That book sold out, and the press chief urged a fresh one. Dewey here prints his own essays again, with other studies of like kind. His theme is logic as a working tool: thought tested by what it does, in the Chicago school's famed manner.
40859-ponce-de-leon-the-rise-of-the-arge:
Ponce de Leon is a historical novel of the rise of the Argentine Republic, by an author who signs himself An Estanciero. A note says it was first published in 1878 and long out of print. It has been called the best and most accurate description yet written of the British invasion of the River Plate. This edition appeared at Buenos Aires and London in 1910.

Book one is called The Babyhood of a Great Nation. Its chapters tell of Don Gregorio Lopez and the danger of friendship with an enemy. One shows how a patriot may also be a traitor. The fighting at Perdriel and the day of August 12, 1806 close the book. A second book follows the prowess of the young giant nation.
41713-quips-and-quiddities-a-quintessenc:
An anthology of wit selected by W Davenport Adams. Chatto and Windus issued it in the Mayfair Library at London. The subtitle piles up Q words in play. It promises a quintessence of quirks quaint, quizzical, and quotable. Adams also compiled a dictionary of English literature. Two shillings sixpence bought the limp cloth volume.

The Mayfair Library list in front sets the tone. Mallock, Gilbert, and Brillat-Savarin share its catalogue. Puniana and clerical anecdotes stand among its neighbours. Inside, Adams gathers epigrams, jokes, and sharp sayings from many sources. A Shakespeare tag opens the collection proper. Victorian readers kept such books for railway journeys and after-dinner talk. The humour is quotation, not invention.
41714-the-syndic:
Kornbluth wrote this future-history tale for Science Fiction Adventures in December 1953 and March 1954. Sussman illustrated it for the magazine. An opening note says tales of future utopias have shown many kinds of rule. Kind dictators and pure democracies, from far right to far left, all appear in that note.

The Syndic's easy, half-anarchic society stands alone among them in that note. The tale's frame opens on February 14th, when the Government declared a state of unlimited emergency. The trigger was an aerial bombing that destroyed an armored company on Fort George Hill in New York City. Local Syndic leaders there held a high school, with help from students and neighbors.
41792-theodore-watts-dunton-poet-novelis:
Theodore Watts Dunton, Poet, Novelist, Critic is a critical biography by James Douglas, printed by Hodder and Stoughton in London in 1904, with twenty four illustrations. Portraits and views cluster around the subject's house, the Pines, and its paintings by Rossetti and others.

Twenty eight chapters fill the synopsis. Early chapters treat the renascence of wonder, cowslip country, the critic in the bud, and early glimpses of the gypsies, then East Anglia and London. Chapters on George Borrow, on the acted drama, on Rossetti, and on William Morris follow, with the Examiner and the Athenaeum marking his critical career. Later chapters discuss the great book of wonder, American friends such as Lowell and Bret Harte, Wales, the methods of prose fiction, and a story with two heroines. The renascence of wonder in religion and in humour, and the poem sequence The Coming of Love, close the survey.
42799-the-gay-gnani-of-gingalee-or-disco:
The Gay Gnani of Gingalee, by Florence Huntley, was printed at Chicago in 1908 as volume two of the Harmonic Fiction line. Its second title is Discords of Devolution, a tragical entanglement of modern mysticism and modern science. Huntley had written Harmonics of Evolution.

She gives the book to those wise enough to be foolish at intervals. In her prelude she holds that mother nature sets the core of each person, and native bents persist through school, work, and life. Her own bent was a keen sense of nonsense, second only to her thirst for knowledge and love of truth. She left newspaper work for the School of Natural Science, yet kept her humor. Readers get a romance where occult thought and science clash in jest and earnest.
43369-how-marcus-whitman-saved-oregon-a-:
Oliver W Nixon wrote How Marcus Whitman Saved Oregon, a true tale of pioneer heroism. Nixon had run the Chicago Inter Ocean as president and editor for years. Whitman’s winter ride from Oregon fronts the book in a plate. The set adds sketches of life on plains and peaks.

No full life of Whitman is the aim, Nixon says at the start. Heroism and Christian love of land form his one bright thread. Nixon taught the young folk of old Oregon in eighteen hundred fifty. He heard the Waiilatpui tragedy fresh from those who lived it. He also served as purser on the Lot Whitcomb, a first Oregon steamer. Gray haired men of four states take the book as their gift. Whitman rests in a martyr’s grave with no stone, Nixon laments. These sketches aim to win the dead man his due honour.
4352-laughter-an-essay-on-the-meaning-of:
Henri Bergson, professor at the College de France, wrote this essay on laughter to explain what makes things comic. Translated by Cloudesley Brereton and Fred Rothwell, and revised in detail by Bergson himself, it is the only authorized translation. The essay first appeared as three articles, and Bergson reworked it for book form.

His central idea is that laughter springs from something mechanical encrusted on the living: a person acting like a thing, or a habit tripping up grace. Bergson tests the idea on gestures, words, situations, and character. The essay remains a classic of comic theory, clear enough for general readers and rich enough for students.
43688-wednesday-the-tenth-a-tale-of-the-:
Wednesday the Tenth is a sea tale of the South Pacific by Grant Allen. The novel came out in Boston in the year eighteen ninety. Its first chapter opens on a ship in the lee of an isle. A cry of boat ahoy from the masthead starts the plot in motion.

Eight chapters carry the crew through boat crews, a solved riddle, and island strife. Prints show the landing of Frenchmen and the folk of the isle. Talk in the tale weighs the slave like trade in bound island labour. Heat and risk rise as the crew works on shore in the last acts. Allen was known for plain science books as well as tales of this kind.
44950-plane-and-plank-or-the-mishaps-of-:
Oliver Optic wrote Plane and Plank, or The Mishaps of a Mechanic, the second book of his Upward and Onward series. Lee and Shepard published it at Boston, entered for copyright in 1871 by William T Adams, the author's true name. Fourteen illustrations accompany the tale. Optic dedicated it to his young friend George W Hills. His preface sets the scene: the Missouri River and the city of St Louis. The hero is Phil Farringford.

Phil learns the carpenter's trade in the story. The book sets an inquiring young mechanic, earnest to master his business, against one who feels above his calling and overrates his skill. Phil's father shows the evils of intemperance in his person and history. Christian love and prayer work his reform. The incidents are stirring and some situations surprising, the preface promises.
45164-village-annals-containing-austerus:
Village Annals, containing Austerus and Humanus, a sympathetic tale, was printed at Philadelphia in 1814 with fine engravings. The front picture shows Sir Filmer Hopewell, who opens the tale. Winter grips the land as the tale begins, with frost stopping the streams. Sir Filmer has lost his road in the Dale of Tiviot as the sun goes down.

Two hale youths skim past on skates over the frozen brook. They point him up a hill to a small village and its ale-house, the Lion and Dog. The landlord, a man of sharp features and quick dark eyes, joins his guest by the fire. Over a drink he tells tale after tale of the village and its scenes of distress.
45449-abraham-lincoln-the-practical-myst:
Abraham Lincoln: The Practical Mystic, by Francis Grierson, came out in New York and London in 1918. Grierson had written on mysticism and the war in earlier books. He calls Lincoln the greatest of practical mystics, and says the forces that ruled his life matter now more than ever.

The short parts treat the divine will, a mystical awakening, and the logic of the supernatural. Others look at Lincoln going into the silence, his wit, his face, and the great debate. Grierson draws on Herndon's account of Lincoln and on dreams and forebodings. He sets the freeing of black slaves in Lincoln's day beside the plight of Europe in his own. The book ends by looking toward a new era.
46084-the-secret-life-being-the-book-of-:
Short prose pieces fill The Secret Life, subtitled the book of a heretic and issued by John Lane Company with a nineteen hundred six copyright. No single author is named on the title page. The contents list runs to more than fifty brief items. Their titles range over faith, art, death, and daily manners.

Inside, a reader finds pieces on Hamlet and ghosts next to notes on elbows at the table. Other items take up marriage, health, heredity, and the worth of a soul. Two short pieces stage letters between Abelard and Heloise. The tone stays personal and questioning, as the heretic label suggests. Readers who like short reflective essays in plain sequence will find the range wide.
46745-the-action-of-medicines-in-the-sys:
Frederick William Headland, a London surgeon, won a gold medal for this essay on how drugs act in the body. The Medical Society of London gave its Fothergillian medal for 1852 to the work. Lindsay and Blakiston printed it at Philadelphia in 1853.

Headland asks how healing drugs, taken by the stomach, work their effects on the frame. First come the great classes of drugs and past views of their action. Then ten plain claims set out his own view. The first holds that most drugs must enter the blood before they can act at all. Doctors of 1853 got a clear, prized guide to a dark point of their craft.
46764-the-birds-of-washington-volume-1-o:
The Birds of Washington is a two-volume ornithology by William Leon Dawson of Seattle, assisted by John Hooper Bowles of Tacoma. The Occidental Publishing Company issued the first volume in 1909. Only 1250 copies of all editions were printed, and the plates were then destroyed.

The title promises a complete, scientific and popular account of the 372 species of birds found in the state. More than 300 half-tone photographs show birds in life, nests, eggs, and favourite haunts. Allan Brooks supplied forty drawings and a series of colour plates. The original edition was printed only for advance subscribers, and the hosted copy is a numbered one. Dawson had earlier written The Birds of Ohio. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
4763-the-game-of-logic:
Lewis Carroll wrote The Game of Logic as a book for teaching logic, opening with a dedication poem to his child friend. He says he charms in vain, since memory will never again embody departed days, nor let him gaze on his fairy friend. Yet if her face smiled on him a moment, it would send rays of light from heaven across the night, by which to read her spirit.

Diagrams use colours for counters, marking divisions with x and y and their primes. Verses tell of the sun overhead, shining full and red, then gone away, leaving an empty grey sky. Carroll wishes life's long dream to flow gently onward, with gay flowerets down its willowy way, and no sigh or care to vex his little friend. Readers get logic turned into a game, with counters, diagrams, and verses, meant for a child to play.
47825-darkness-and-dawn-or-scenes-in-the:
Frederic W Farrar wrote Darkness and Dawn, or Scenes in the Days of Nero, a tale of old Rome. Longmans, Green, and Company issued this ninth issue in New York in eighteen hundred ninety seven. Farrar first brought the book out in September eighteen hundred ninety one. He held posts at Westminster as archdeacon and canon.

Agrippina broods in lone thought as the tale opens. Her son Nero takes the throne through crime in early chapters. Seneca and his kin show the court’s wise old guard. Prince Britannicus stands in the young heir’s doomed place. A foreign superstition, the new faith, stirs at the tale’s edge. Onesimus, a runaway slave, bears that strand of the plot. Otho’s supper and Vespasian’s farm give Rome’s breadth in turn. Dante’s dawn verse fronts the book as its hopeful sign.
48642-a-servant-of-the-public:
A Servant of the Public, by Anthony Hope, is a novel of business and society. Methuen issued it at London in 1905, first published that year in full. Four plates by Harold Percival illustrate the tale of the Muddock firm. Chapter one joins the rise of a family to the growth of a trade.

Hope notes how common that pairing is among the nation of shopkeepers. Chapters promise a day in the country, ribbons cast off, and a claimant. Renunciation as drama, the licence of virtue, and what is truth follow in turn. The man upstairs, morality smiling, and the play and the part deepen it. The ways divide and other worlds close the twenty four chapters.
48734-les-mise-rables-v-4-5-the-idyll-an:
Victor Hugo wrote Les Misérables, and this Boston printing of 1887 holds the fourth part, The Idyll and the Epic, in the authorized translation by Sir Lascelles Wraxall. Its full head names the Rue Plumet idyll and the Rue St Denis epic. The first book, Some Pages of History, treats Louis Philippe and cracks in the foundation. Enjolras and his lieutenants close that book. The second book is Éponine, with the lark's field and crimes hatched in prisons.

The house of the Rue Plumet fills the third book, with Jean Valjean as a national guard. Little Gavroche has the sixth book, and slang the seventh, with its origin and roots. Enchantments and desolations fill the eighth: bright light, the giddiness of perfect bliss, and the beginning of the shadow. The fifth of June, 1832, has the tenth book to itself, from the surface of the question to its bottom.
48879-chapters-on-the-history-of-the-sou:
Stuart Daggett wrote chapters on the history of the Southern Pacific railroad. The Ronald Press Company issued the work in New York in 1922. Daggett taught railway economics at the University of California at Berkeley. Twenty-four chapters run from the project's start to final remarks.

Land grants, state aid, and building firms fill the early parts. Rates, politics, water rivalry, and the Thurman Act crowd the later chapters. Portraits show Judah, Stanford, Crocker, Hopkins, and Huntington at their pages. Students gain a dense, sourced history of a great western road and its power.
48955-the-ocean-wireless-boys-on-the-atl:
Wilbur Lawton wrote a boys' tale of a wireless lad at sea. The book came out in New York in 1914. Charles Wrenn drew its plates. Lawton wrote sets on boy flyers and on dreadnought boys. Jack seeks a job in the first part of the tale.

Jack's home, Captain Toby, and a turned-down prize come next. His first post at the key and the ropes of ship life fill it. A storm, a wreck in sight, and a talk on wireless build thrill. Oil on wild seas and a rescue test his pluck in full. Jack breaks rules in a late part with a brave aim. Sea boys get Lawton's brisk pace.
4939-chopin-the-man-and-his-music:
James Huneker's Chopin: The Man and His Music studies the composer through his works. The nocturnes hold melancholy mysteries. The ballades work as faery dramas. The polonaises sound as heroic hymns of battle. The mazurkas dance as dances of the soul. A closing chapter crowns him Chopin the Conqueror.

Huneker opens with Poland and youthful ideals. He notes that Chopin's violence was psychic, a travailing of the spirit, while adventure stayed missing from his daily life. The tragedy, he argues, was within. Readers get criticism that listens as much as it judges, useful for anyone who wants to hear Chopin's music with fuller understanding.
49462-lord-tedric:
Lord Tedric is a science fantasy story by Edward Smith, illustrated by Lawrence. A head note explains its time track premise in teasing form. Small events may result in ultimate catastrophe centuries later, it says. On Time Track Number One that result was fixed and grim. On Time Track Number Two one little event could avert it. Skandos One removed the clothing from the Lady Rhoann in public. 

The text proper opens with Skandos and his chronoviagraph. It shows civilization destroying itself in one hundred eighty seven years. He goes back to the key point and the key figure in time. Tedric is a Lomarrian ironmaster who lived and died a commoner. He fanatically detested human sacrifice but could do nothing. Skandos teaches him to make one batch of super steel. Time then forks between two tracks of history.
49651-tedric:
Tedric is a science fiction story by Smith, illustrated by Allen St John and printed in a magazine in 1953. A note at the front places its hero in battle with a god of Lomarr who demands sacrifice. Tedric is aided by a strange new god of his own, named Llosir. The blurb calls the tale a story of science and swashbuckling adventure.

The opening pages stage a talk among men who can see across time. A prime physicist points to a critical point in the whole existence of mankind. He argues that men should be fed, not bled, to make them strong. Virgins, he says, should not be sacrificed to gods that exist only in fancy. From that claim the story moves into Tedric's world of swords and altars.
4982-a-rock-in-the-baltic:
Robert Barr's Rock in the Baltic opens in the public room of the Sixth National Bank at Bar Harbor, Maine, where Lieutenant Alan Drummond of H.M.S. Consternation waits to change crisp Bank of England notes into American currency. A lady customer passes without noticing his courtesy or his conspicuous presence, and the lieutenant notices her in return.

That small slight begins a romance and adventure stretching between Britain, America, and the Baltic world of the title. Barr writes with a newspaperman's eye for character and place. Readers get a light, clever novel of naval officers, bank notes, and misunderstandings that grow into something larger.
50226-serge-prokofieff-and-his-orchestra:
Louis Biancolli wrote Serge Prokofieff and His Orchestral Music. The Philharmonic-Symphony Society of New York holds its 1953 copyright. The book went to the society's radio members. Biancolli also wrote The Analytical Concert Guide. A portrait of the composer fronts the text. The composer states his own creed early on.

Three lines mark his work, Prokofieff says. A classical line starts with Beethoven sonatas at his mother's hands. It shows in the Classical Symphony and the gavottes. A second line seeks new sounds and strong feeling. The Scythian Suite and The Gambler show that strain. A toccata-like motor drive forms the third. A concert guide like this helps radio listeners follow a modern master's works with his own map in hand.
50404-parlour-magic:
Parlour Magic, a little manual of amusing phenomena for family recreation, was printed at Philadelphia in 1838 in a revised and improved form. The book is respectfully given to the lovers of home. To furnish the ingenious youth with the means of relieving the tediousness of a long winter's evening is the first object, the preface says.

It enables him to provide for a party of juvenile friends an instructive as well as recreative entertainment, without recourse to vulgar modes of killing time. It qualifies the hero of his little circle to divert and astonish his friends, and at the same time to improve himself.
