The boy whose wonder was excited by the scientific lecturer, or the illusions of the ventriloquist, will here find many of these mysteries unveiled. Plain directions strip the tricks of technical language. Science plays at home here.
50423-zachariah-chandler-an-outline-sket:
Zachariah Chandler is a sketch of the life and public services of a Michigan senator. The Detroit Post and Tribune produced the book, and its company published it at Detroit in 1880. James Blaine of Maine supplies an opening letter. A verse from Tennyson stands as the motto.

The preface owns that a newspaper staff wrote the life as a joint work. The facts came from research and from friends of the dead senator. The book is written, it says, from warm political sympathy. Chandler's people in Michigan receive the dedication. Sources include Greeley's history of the war and Wilson's rise and fall of the slave power. The sketch traces a dry goods merchant turned party boss and war senator. It appeared within a year of his death.
50461-herman-melville-mariner-and-mystic:
Raymond Weaver writes a pioneer's life in Herman Melville, Mariner and Mystic, printed in New York with copyright in 1921. Doran made the book. A portrait of Melville, engraved on wood from a photograph, fronts the volume, with his signature.

Weaver owns his debts in front. Carl Van Doren's enthusiasm and scholarship instigated the study, he says. The novelist's granddaughter gave him access to all the surviving records: manuscripts, letters, journals, and books with Melville's own notes. Her vivid interest and keen sympathy earn his highest praise. Most of the letters to Hawthorne in the volume are quoted from a life of Hawthorne by his son Julian, a note adds.
51443-claudian-volume-1-of-2-with-an-eng:
Claudian was the last great poet of pagan Rome. This first volume of the Loeb Classical Library edition gives his larger poems, with an English translation by Maurice Platnauer on the facing pages. Harvard University Press and Heinemann printed the edition in 1922, and it was reprinted in 1963. The contents open with the panegyric on the consuls Probinus and Olybrius and the two books against Rufinus.

There follow the War Against Gildo, the books against Eutropius, and the wedding verses and marriage poem for the Emperor Honorius and Maria. Panegyrics on the consulships of Honorius and of Manlius Theodorus come next. The volume ends with the first book on Stilicho's consulship. Platnauer's introduction and the manuscript notes show the Loeb method at its most scholarly: text, translation, and apparatus together.
51444-claudian-volume-2-of-2-with-an-eng:
Claudian, volume two, is the Loeb Classical Library edition of the Latin poet Claudian, with an English rendering by Maurice Platnauer. Heinemann of London and Putnam's of New York published it in 1922. Latin text and English stand together, in the Loeb manner. The contents open with book two of the poem On Stilicho's Consulship.

Also here are the praise poem on the sixth consulship of the Emperor Honorius, dated 404, and The Gothic War. A set of shorter poems follows. The volume closes with The Rape of Proserpine in three books, plus an index of poems and an index of proper names. Volume one is a separate Gutenberg file.
52510-prince-and-heretic:
Prince and Heretic is a historical novel of the Dutch revolt by Marjorie Bowen, first published in London by Methuen in 1914. Its prince is William of Orange, leader of the Netherlands against Spain. The contents divide between the Netherlanders and the Holy Inquisition.

An alchemist opens the tale, and the Saint Bartholomew wedding follows soon after. Louis of Nassau, Margaret of Parma, and Cardinal Granvelle take their chapters. The rhetoric play and the grandees fill the Brussels court scenes. In the second part the edicts, the petition, and the banquet build toward revolt. The coming of Alva, Philip's avenger, closes the movement. Bowen was a mistress of the historical romance, and this novel gives the Dutch struggle her full treatment of colour, cruelty, and conscience.
53113-myths-and-tales-from-the-white-mou:
Pliny Earle Goddard sets down tribal lore in Myths and Tales from the White Mountain Apache, printed in New York in 1919. The piece is volume 24, part 2, of the papers of the American Museum of Natural History. The tales are free renderings of texts told in the tongue of the White Mountain Apache.

The texts themselves, with word for word renderings, follow as part 4 of the volume, a first note says. They were taken down in the winter of 1910, under a grant for studies in the Southwest. The creation myth, got from Noze, differs in key turns from the San Carlos versions, Goddard notes. Most tales came from the father of Frank Crockett, the man who rendered speech on the spot. Some are sacred in kind.
54008-technic-and-practice-of-chiropract:
Joy Loban, a teacher of anatomy and practice at the Universal Chiropractic College, wrote a full manual of his craft, issued at Davenport, Iowa, in 1915. This is the second, larger form of the book. Loban had taught before at the Palmer School, the first school of the field.

Early parts teach how to feel the spine by hand, trace nerves, and find slipped bones called subluxations. A long part gives thirty two moves for setting bones right, with notes on which moves suit which case. Later parts deal with the cause of disease, diet, poisons, office gear, exams, and the limits of the method. Students get both theory and daily work rules.
54407-gleanings-of-a-mystic-a-series-of-:
Gleanings of a Mystic is a series of essays on practical mysticism by Max Heindel. The Rosicrucian Fellowship issued it in an edition from its headquarters at Mount Ecclesia, Oceanside, California. Copyright was held by Augusta Foss Heindel in 1922. Its twenty-four essays present the fellowship's teaching.

Paired essays open on initiation, what it is and is not, and on the sacrament of communion. Essays follow on baptism, marriage, the unpardonable sin, and the immaculate conception. Others treat the coming Christ and the coming age, and meat and drink as factors in evolution. More take up white and black magic, sound and soul growth, the cosmic meaning of Easter, and the mystery of the Rose Cross. Closing essays give reasons for being a Rosicrucian and the fellowship's object, and a catalogue ends the volume.
55168-fossils-a-story-of-the-rocks-and-t:
Harvey Markman's Fossils, a story of the rocks and their record of prehistoric life, is Popular Series number three of the Denver Museum of Natural History. Markman was the museum's curator of geology and paleontology; this third edition was reprinted October 1, 1954. The contents move from fossilization and geological time through the ages: before the reptiles, the age of reptiles with its dinosaurs, the age of mammals, and the age of man.

Chapters treat prehistoric horses, mastodons and mammoths, and the Rancho La Brea fossil pits. The illustrations include a time chart, dinosaur tracks, molar tooth structures, and work on a dinosaur skeleton. Markman writes for the lay visitor's wholesome curiosity: what happened, how it happened, and how we know. Alfred Bailey edited the series, and Mary Chilton Gray designed the cover and murals.
55503-horrors-and-atrocities-of-the-grea:
Horrors and Atrocities of the Great War is a popular account of the First World War by Logan Marshall, copyrighted in 1915. Its full title promises the desolation of Belgium, the sacking of Louvain, and the shelling of defenceless cities. Special chapters come from Sir Gilbert Parker, Vance Thompson, and Philip Gibbs, a war correspondent.

The first and longest part concerns the sinking of the Lusitania. Chapters tell of the heroes of the ship, the stories of survivors, and the verdict of a British jury. Later parts print the German defence and the American protest. The book is wartime writing at full heat, meant to fix blame and stir feeling while the war still raged.
55718-the-land-of-enchantment-from-pike-:
Lilian Whiting wrote The Land of Enchantment, a book of the West put out at Boston in 1909. Rights run from 1906, and photos fill the book. Its span runs from Pike Peak to the far sea in the west. A plate shows the Bright Angel Trail in the Grand Canyon of Arizona.

Whiting gives the book to the name of Major John Wesley Powell, the great scout of that land. Powell ran the full length of the great chasm, she says, at risk and with grit. His work for the true survey of the West sped the growth of the land. His plea for water for dry lands showed wise sight far in front of his age. Thanks in front name rail men and an artist of Santa Fe who eased her choice of plates. The book reads the West as a place of awe, light, and scale.
55799-lassen-trails-a-brief-guide-to-the:
Stephen Matteson, a former seasonal naturalist in the park, wrote this brief guide to the trails of Lassen Volcanic National Park. His wife Dorothy drew the pictures. The Loomis Museum Association held the 1963 copyright, and the book was made with the National Park Service; this copy is the third printing, from 1970.

A short opening gives tips for beginners on using the trails. Then come 34 numbered walks. They climb Lassen Peak, cross to Bumpass Hell and the Sulphur Works hot springs, and circle lakes with names like Cluster, Twin, and Horseshoe. Other routes reach the Cinder Cone, Devil's Kitchen, and Boiling Springs Lake. A park map sits at the center. Hikers get distances and routes for the whole volcanic park in one small book.
5619-essays-on-mankind-and-political-ari:
William Petty wrote the Essays on Mankind and Political Arithmetic, introduced here with a life of the author. Born on May 26, 1623, son of a clothier at Romsey in Hampshire, Petty studied at Romsey Grammar School and then at Caen in Normandy. There he supported himself by small trade while learning French and advancing in Greek, Latin, mathematics, and much else belonging to his large idea of a liberal education.

After a short Navy place, he went abroad again at twenty, and later became famous for applying numbers to population, trade, and government. Readers get early political arithmetic: essays that count people, houses, and wealth to guide policy. It remains a founding text of economics and statistics.
56906-fe-nelon-the-mystic:
James Mudge wrote a life of Fenelon for the Men of the Kingdom series, printed at Cincinnati and New York in 1906. Mudge had written The Saintly Calling and The Best of Browning. The book is given to his dear wife, a wise mother, a faithful missionary in India, and a worker in many churches. There have been many lives of Fenelon, he begins.

Four came out in the eighteenth century, and two large ones as lately as 1901, he notes. Some were written in cold, supercilious disparagement by people with no experience to qualify them to understand their subject. But the attempt to pull Fenelon down from his pedestal cannot succeed, Mudge holds. So long as his own writings remain, his fame is secure. The French archbishop's quiet mysticism gets a warm defence.
57077-the-old-and-the-new-magic:
The Old and the New Magic is a work on stage magic by Henry Ridgely Evans. It came out in Chicago in 1906 from the Open Court Publishing Company, with pictures. A portrait of Robert-Houdin stands at its front. A sketch of the author states that Evans was a journalist, author, and librarian, born in Baltimore on 7 November 1861.

The sketch traces his stock through his mother to the old colonial families of Maryland: Ridgely, Dorsey, and Worthington kin are named in its first lines. A quote from Goethe in German stands on the title page, a vow to give himself to magic. The book is a study of the art of magic in its old and new forms, by a man whose life the front matter sets out in brief.
5724-a-book-of-operas-their-histories-th:
Henry Edward Krehbiel guides readers through great operas in A Book of Operas, covering their histories, plots, and music. Chapters take up The Barber of Seville and The Marriage of Figaro. They also treat The Magic Flute, Don Giovanni, Fidelio, and Faust. Mefistofele, La Traviata, Aida, Tannhauser, Tristan and Isolde, and Parsifal follow, among others. Each chapter tells the story first, then explains the music.

Readers new to opera gain a friendly companion for the opera house, while seasoned listeners get history and context for familiar works. Krehbiel writes clearly, without assuming technical knowledge, and he treats plot and score as partners. The book remains a useful introduction for anyone who wants to enjoy opera with understanding rather than puzzlement.
57545-letter-on-corpulence-addressed-to-:
Letter on Corpulence, by William Banting, is a short tract addressed to the public. This fifth edition, with remarks by Harvey, was printed in New York in 1865. Banting gives the letter to the public from a plain wish to do good.

Of all the parasites that plague mankind, he writes, none is more distressing than obesity. He had just come out of a long trial of that affliction himself. His change, he says, might be called miraculous if it had not come by the most simple common sense means. Doctors and the public alike, he holds, grasp the disease poorly. The letter tells what he ate and avoided, and how the weight fell. His name later became a byword for dieting of this kind.
57645-fresh-every-hour-detailing-the-adv:
Fresh Every Hour is John Peter Toohey's comic novel, copyrighted in 1922 by Boni and Liveright of New York. Its full title details the adventures, comic and pathetic, of Jimmy Martin, purveyor of publicity. Jimmy is credited with sublime nerve, whimsical imagination, colossal impudence, and the heart of a child.

Jimmy works as press agent at Jollyland, a big summer amusement park near New York. Through the third week of the season his heart behaves like a dependable organ, with one old flutter on record from a cigar counter in New Haven. Then Lolita Murphy comes within his ken. At the sight of her, and soon at the mere thought of her, his heart puts on palpitations fit for the trap drummer of a jazz band. The novel milks the courtship of a publicity man undone by his own heart.
57671-evolution-social-and-organic:
Arthur M Lewis lectures on the history and meaning of the idea of change through time. Charles H Kerr and Company issued the third edition at Chicago in 1908. The book holds the first ten lectures of a winter course. They were given at the Garrick Theater, where the hall drew crowds too big for its seats.

Ten chapters run from Thales to Linnaeus, Lamarck, Darwin and his natural selection, Weismann on heredity, and De Vries on mutation. Later lectures take up Kropotkin and mutual aid, answer Haeckel, and then turn to Spencer, with his social organism and his strong stress on the single man. Lewis ties each stage of science to a socialist reading of it, and his book shows how a party writer used Darwin to argue that society also changes by law.
5770-the-rover-boys-in-the-jungle-or-sti:
Winfield sends the Rover Boys to Africa in The Rover Boys in the Jungle, subtitled Stirring Adventures in Africa. The story opens back at Putnam Hall, where Dick, Tom, and Sam Rover greet the academy as a second home, preferring it even to the farm of Uncle Randolph and Aunt Martha. From schoolboy cheer, the plot moves toward jungle travel, danger, and the brothers' loyalty under pressure.

Readers get classic boys' series adventure: three brothers, a far place, and scrapes that test courage and teamwork. The jungle setting adds wild animals, strange lands, and rescue to the school-story formula. Young readers who enjoy vintage adventure will find brisk chapters and earnest heroes, with the Rover brothers' bond carrying the tale through every peril.
58454-joseph-rogers-m-d-reminiscences-of:
Reminiscences of a Workhouse Medical Officer is Joseph Rogers's memoir of his work among the poor, printed in London in 1889. Rogers died before the printing was done. Professor Thorold Rogers edited the book and saw it through the press. The preface tells the weight of that loss plainly.

Rogers wrote under a mortal disease whose end he clearly foresaw. He would not leave life without a record of the evils he had grappled with. He set down the obstacles in his path and the changes he strove to win. Coming to London, he took up the labour of his life: reform of the medical relief given to the indigent poor. His peers granted that he had earned much of the credit for those reforms. The book is a reformer's brief from inside the workhouse walls.
59155-pueblo-bonito-chaco-culture-nation:
Pueblo Bonito is an official guide booklet for a great ruin in New Mexico. It serves visitors to what is now Chaco Culture National Historic Park. The Bonito Trail, a third of a mile long, is keyed to its numbered paragraphs. Walkers are asked to stay on the trail and off the ruin walls.

Chaco Canyon was made a national monument by proclamation in 1907. Edgar Hewett, of the Museum of New Mexico, had pressed for that protection. Pueblo Bonito, the pretty village, has borne its name since about 1840. Excavation began in 1896 under Wetherill and George Pepper of New York. The Hyde brothers of that city financed four seasons of the work. Two hundred rooms were cleaned out in those first campaigns.
59321-kutnar-son-of-pic:
Kutnar, Son of Pic is a tale of the first men of the caves. George Langford wrote it and drew its plates with his own hand. It came out in New York in the year 1921 as a set's part two. A shot at the front shows the man with the tusk of a great beast.

Kutnar is the son of Pic, the man who first made tools of war. His folk live in the cave of the hills in the north of Spain. Men clad in skins, with clubs and spears, watch a band climb the slope. A great beast stuck in the mire and its guard fill the first plate. Wolves, cave beasts, and a cub of the cave lion crowd the tale. Langford builds a whole world of the first age for the young.
595-the-sisters-tragedy-with-other-poems:
Thomas Bailey Aldrich tells of two sisters who loved one man in the title poem of this volume, set in 1670. Aglae, a widow, and Muriel, her unmarried sister, grieve together in a turret room, each unveiling a hidden love for the dead man. Other poems follow: Tennyson, a shipman's tale, monodies, interludes, and pastorals.

Aldrich writes in polished, musical verse, keen on form and feeling. His lyrics balance grief with grace, never spilling into excess. The book serves as a fine sample of late Victorian American verse, where a small tragedy carries a large, quiet ache.
59527-children-of-the-arctic:
The Snow Baby and her mother wrote this book, and Stokes published it at New York in 1903. The Snow Baby is Marie Ahnighito Peary, born in the Arctic, and her mother the explorer's wife. Ahnighito is home from the Snowland, at her Grossmamma's house, with too much to tell and do and learn for a visit. The next summer her father sails in the great ship, and she and mother stay behind.

Father says she must go to school, and promises to tell Santa Claus to bring a sister. The summer passes on a farm: bunnies to pet, chickens to feed, cows to drive to pasture, and butter to churn. Kindergarten follows, and after Christmas the sister arrives, with a letter from Dad in the far north. The book is a childhood lived in two worlds, half among the fur-clad friends of the Snowland and half in a farmhouse.
59624-the-chicago-massacre-of-1812-with-:
The Chicago Massacre of 1812 is a work of history by Joseph Kirkland. It came out in Chicago in 1893 from the Dibble Publishing Company, with pictures and papers of the time. Kirkland was the author of The Story of Chicago and of tales set in Illinois. In his preface he sets out a view of how the past is best told.

History, Kirkland says, is not a snap-shot. Events take place, and the true record of them comes at a distance behind. At times the first report is too full, and time must sift it to split chaff from grain. That has been the case, he says, with each great modern battle. The book takes the clash at Chicago in 1812 as its theme and works to that rule of care.
59684-life-and-adventure-in-the-south-pa:
Life and Adventure in the South Pacific, by a Roving Printer, is a whaling narrative published by Harper at New York in 1861. Its preface makes no claim to literary merit. Two young men, led to join the whale fisheries, spent five years in the work. From their log books and their memories they compiled a plain, unvarnished narrative of that time.

The book tells of places few have visited, and of an employment of which little is generally known. Its contents run from the boats and whaling gear to the first whale and the cry of there she blows. Lowering the boats, a fisherman's luck, and the Cape Verde Islands fill early chapters. The authors aim above all to make the reader a companion of the traveller. Such whaling tales fed the public's hunger for the South Seas. This one has the salt of the log book in it.
60227-three-sailor-boys-or-adrift-in-the:
Verney Lovett Cameron, a naval commander and explorer, wrote this sea story, published by Nelson in 1902. Three boys of the clipper barque Golden Fleece are sent off in an open boat to turn turtle during a long calm.

Sam Hawse tells the tale. Tom Arbor spots a red sun setting in a bank of black cloud and warns they may never fetch the ship again. They row hard, but the storm is coming. The contents promise a coral island, fish-curing, pursuit by cannibals, captivity, and a dive for liberty. Cameron had crossed Africa and knew the sea at first hand. Boys get a brisk castaway yarn from a man who had lived wilder things.
60280-a-london-mosaic:
George sketches the city in A London Mosaic, printed in New York with copyright in 1921. Stokes made the book, with pictures by Philippe Forbes Robertson. George had writ the novels Caliban and Blind Alley, and a shelf of kindred prose. Hyde Park fronts the volume as a plate.

Nine chapters tile the city. A prelude leads to playgrounds and the friendly bowl. Wanderers, soups and stews, and a search for vice vary the walk. The Poor and Stones ground the tour in street fact. Cafe Royal closes the set in style. Plates show the Regent Canal at Maida Hill and the Cumberland Hay Market. It is a mosaic of London life, piece by bright piece.
60744-the-footprints-of-time-and-a-compl:
The Footprints of Time is a citizens' manual by Charles Bancroft, published by R T Root of Burlington, Iowa, in 1875. Its full title promises a complete analysis of the American system of government. A concise history of the colonies and the United States stands in chronological order.

Facts and statistics are drawn from official sources, the title page says. A portrait of George Washington fronts the book. Bancroft's preface takes its motto from the creed of popular government. The highest government, he holds, is of the people, by the people, and for the people. He traces the footprints of time through all history first. Then comes the close analysis of the American structure. Executive, legislative, and judicial divisions are examined in turn. Each part's powers, relations, and working are explained.
61412-the-course-of-logic:
The Course of Logic is a tale of vast beast minds by Lester del Rey. It first ran in a fiction magazine in September of nineteen sixty three. A tag line says one small slip, quite plain, brought dire loss. A male silth plods at speed, three hundred tons of bulk in stride.

The beast tears up rare trees to wolf them down as it plods on. Warm blood runs in its vast frame for all its lizard like looks. In its bulk rides Arnek, a two pound net of nerve and mind. He sulks at the firm logic of his mate, who won their last clash. Odd minds in vast tools drive the wry tale of the far wilds.
61683-the-description-and-use-of-the-glo:
The Description and Use of the Globes and the Orrery, by Joseph Harris, teacher of the mathematics, reached an eleventh edition in London in 1773. An account of the solar system comes first, by way of introduction. A front plate shows the great orrery, four feet across, made by Thomas Wright, mathematical instrument-maker to the king, for the Royal Academy at Portsmouth.

An advertisement boasts of Wright's long practice in large orreries. His machines show the motions of all the planets and their moons, and the true motion of Saturn's ring. Named buyers include the king at Kensington, the Duke of Argyll, and schools of note. Harris teaches the buyer to use globe and orrery: finding places, hours, seasons, and the motions of the heavens, in plain steps for home study.
62658-big-bend-national-park-land-of-dra:
Big Bend National Park, Land of Dramatic Contrasts and Scenic Grandeur, is a park guide with story and photography by Ray Scott. National Park Concessions published the book, with copyright in 1950. A list of national parks inside runs from Acadia in Maine to the Virgin Islands. Big Bend of Texas stands in that proud company.

The great bend of the Rio Grande gives the park its name and shape. Desert, canyon, and mountain meet in that far corner of Texas. Scott tells the tale of the land and shows it in photographs. Such concession guides sold at park lodges to motor travellers. They mixed geology, history, and views in a handy form. This one sells the drama of the border desert in word and picture.
63778-poetry-of-the-anti-jacobin-compris:
The Poetry of the Anti-Jacobin collects the political satires of a famous Tory magazine. Edmonds edited this third edition with explanatory notes. Putnam issued it in New York in 1890. Six illustrations by Gillray enliven it. The poets were statesmen of Pitt's circle. Canning, Frere, and Pitt himself stand on the title page.

An editor's preface marvels at the poems' survival. Ninety years have not dimmed their interest. Liberal critics like Byron praised their wit. The verses lashed the Whig leaders without mercy. A glance at events of 1797 and 1798 frames them. Pitt's ministry warred with republican France. Public opinion split into two great parties. The notes explain each squib's occasion for modern readers.
63938-medicine-in-the-middle-ages-extrac:
Medicine in the Middle Ages draws extracts from a French history by Edmond Dupouy. Minor translated the pieces, which ran in a Cincinnati medical journal across the winter of 1888 and 1889. The Lancet Press reprinted them at Cincinnati in 1889. Four essays treat the doctors, the plagues, the demon madness, and the literature of the age.

Dupouy opens with the fall of Roman learning in the fourth century. Greek medicine held on at Alexandria, he writes, then passed to the Arabs. Schools at Baghdad, Damascus, and Cordova kept the old texts alive. Rhazes, Avicenna, and Averroes head his roll of Arab masters. A ban on cutting bodies, he notes, held back their surgery. The extracts served doctors curious about their craft's dark centuries.
64314-beyond-the-x-ecliptic:
Fox Holden wrote a tale of deep space called Beyond the X Ecliptic, first run in Planet Stories in November 1953. Earth has lain dry and dying for more than five hundred years, its folk bored, hopeless, and set to dig their own graves. Then, with no clear cause, rain, snow, green grass, and a lit sun come back at once.

In the year 3024 a pilot named Cragin speaks to a hall of men of science. He is the one man who flew past the Barrier, past the X Ecliptic, to a machine planet ruled by beings called the Owners. His plain tale, he warns, may hold few of the hard facts they crave.
6560-deductive-logic:
St. George Stock, of Pembroke College, Oxford, sets out the logic taught in the Oxford schools of his day, with clearness and steady order as his stated aims. His preface tells how one reader urged him to drop the whole plan, while another urged him to cut new matter; he kept the plan and cut the excess. The result aims to match older books in scope, not to break from them for show.

Terms, claims, and proofs are laid out step by step, with Greek letters marked in plain text for the reader's ease. Stock keeps new ideas few, and each one is tied to a line of teaching already in use. For a student of old-style logic, the book offers a firm, plain guide to sound thought.
66187-beyond-the-great-south-wall-the-se:
Frank Savile wrote Beyond the Great South Wall, the secret of the Antarctic, printed in New York in 1901. Savile had written The Blessing of Esau and John Ship, Mariner. Plates painted by Robert Mason go with the tale. Contents run to nineteen chapters. A great low of spirits opens the book. The tale of a chance likeness follows.

The witness of Sir John Dorinecourte and what Baines knew come next. Professor Lessauton's view, and we sail south, lead on. A light in the darkness, before the gale, and the leaping of the wall bring the party behind the barrier. A glacier cave and what lay in it, and the great god Cay, fill the middle. The temple and the lair of Cay stand late. The first chapter opens on a London summer day, with Gerry and the teller sunk in club chairs.
66346-the-lighter-classics-in-music-a-co:
The Lighter Classics in Music, by David Ewen, is a guide to famed music in a lighter vein. Arco printed the book in New York in 1961. The cover promises masterworks by one hundred and eighty-seven composers, treated one by one.

The entries run in name order from Joseph Achron to the end of the alphabet. Bach, Beethoven, Bellini, Berlioz, and Bernstein each get a few pages. Chopin takes a longer span, and Gershwin longer still, at nine pages by the contents. Duke Ellington stands among the opera and concert names, a sign of the book's wide net. Each entry gives the man's life in brief and picks out the works a casual listener would know. The book suits browsers who want the story behind tunes they hum.
66463-don-t-panic:
Don Panic is a science fiction story by Geoff St Reynard, taken from Imagination Stories of Science and Fantasy for November 1954. A blurb says January 9, 1955, began like any normal day on Earth. Then suddenly the planet tossed in a death agony, for the Green Men had landed.

The narrator says that despite mixed reports, the Air Force believed in the flying saucers. The scares began in 1947, and as a responsible agency the Air Force had to start inquiries. At times it let out some facts with care. Then came hysteria, and it would hurry to debunk the whole business as mass hallucinations and crackpot theories. When the public had its balance back, it let out bits of truth once more. Space tale fans get a fifties saucer scare with a twist.
66683-the-story-of-the-battle-hymn-of-th:
Florence Howe Hall wrote The Story of the Battle Hymn of the Republic in 1916. Harper and Brothers published the book in New York and London. Hall was the daughter of Julia Ward Howe, the hymn's author. A last photograph of her mother fronts the volume.

Chapters open with the anti-slavery prelude to the Civil War. The crime against Kansas follows. Then Howe visits the Army of the Potomac, and the hymn is born. The army takes the song up, chapter five reports. Later chapters list great occasions where it has been sung. They tell how the author recited it herself. Tributes and her lesser war poems fill the closing chapters. The full text of the hymn is printed for the reader.
66702-wireless-telegraphy-and-telephony-:
Alfred P Morgan wrote Wireless Telegraphy and Telephony Simply Explained, a practical treatise issued in New York by The Norman W Henley Publishing Company in nineteen sixteen. Copyrights of nineteen twelve and nineteen fifteen stand in the book. Morgan edited the mechanical and electrical pages of The Boy Magazine and had written Wireless Telegraph Construction for Amateurs. He gave the book to Nikola Tesla, whose work he calls the basis of all modern wireless sending.

Early chapters treat the ether, electrical waves, and how waves are sent and caught. Aerial systems and earth connections get full care. Later chapters treat sending gear, receiving gear, and tuning and coupling. Morgan writes in clear prose with many plates for boys and keen home workers. The book shows radio in its spark and crystal age, before the broadcast boom.
66738-nick-carter-stories-no-133-march-2:
Street and Smith issued this Nick Carter weekly at New York on March 27, 1915. Number 133 of the Nick Carter Stories sold for five cents a copy, the masthead states. A year's subscription cost $2.50, postage free, in the terms printed at the front for mail readers.

Won by Magic is the tale promised by the number's bold cover title. Nick Carter, the clean-cut detective of a thousand dime adventures, faces a case of seeming sorcery in it. Such weeklies poured from the presses for decades, and number 133 keeps the formula of disguises, clues and fist fights at full speed.
67515-the-glamour-of-the-arctic:
The Glamour of the Arctic, by A Conan Doyle, tells of the whale men of Peterhead. Most of them, Doyle notes, have not seen corn in the fields since boyhood. They sail at the end of February, prior to the first shoots, and come home in September to stubble.

The trade is old and proud, once shared by Basques, Dutch, and men of Hull and Liverpool. Scoresby was the last great English chief of it. Now the Greenland whale has learned the craft of its own catch. It swims under floes to cut the rope, and keeps deep in the ice. Ships now seek new seas in the far south. Sea readers get a keen sketch of a brave trade in its last days.
67736-the-chemical-constituents-of-piper:
Alice A Ball presented a thesis for the degree of Master of Science at the College of Hawaii in June nineteen fifteen. Its subject is the chemical constituents of Piper methysticum, the active principle of the ava root. The committee chair approved it in May nineteen fifteen. Thirteen sections fill the work, from historical to conclusion.

Method of extraction and method of separation of the resins follow the history. Various metallic salts of the resinous acids come next. The total resins, the barium acid, and its oxidation products fill the middle. The iron acids and alcohol radicals follow. Methysticin and methysticinic acid get their own section. Among the customs of the South Pacific islanders, the most noted is the drinking of ava, or kava, her history opens. Chemistry readers get early kava research by a pioneering Hawaiian chemist.
67899-the-motor-rangers-on-blue-water-or:
The Motor Rangers on Blue Water is a boys' adventure novel by Marvin West. Its other title is The Secret of the Derelict. Hurst and Company published it in New York in 1911. West also wrote other Motor Rangers books, including The Lost Mine. The contents list twenty four chapters of sea adventure. Colonel Morello charters a schooner in the second chapter. The boys are run down and adrift in the Pacific soon after.

Later chapters bring a mysterious craft and a face that terrified. The Island Queen's secret and an attack by Marquesans follow. Nat's skyrocket artillery appears near the close of the book. The story opens on a steep trail above Santa Inez. A party of horsemen rides in single file toward the mission town. The frontispiece shows a terrific shock aboard ship. The series mixes motor age heroes with old sea peril.
67944-a-boy-s-eye-view-of-the-arctic:
Kennett Longley Rawson, cabin boy of the Bowdoin, wrote a boy's eye view of the Arctic, printed at New York in 1926 with an introduction by Commander Donald MacMillan. Rawson's portrait of June 1925 fronts the book. The book is given to his mother, bravest of them all. Photographs by the author and others illustrate it.

Here endeth the lesson opens the chapters, then under weigh. The Bowdoin and her crew sailed from Wiscasset, Maine, on June 20, 1925, a picture caption says. John Jaynes as engineer, Robinson as mate, Rawson as cabin boy, and a short wave radio expert stand in the crew list. A boy ships with MacMillan's expedition to Greenland and Baffin waters. He writes dogs, ice, Eskimos, and shipboard work as a schoolboy saw them, fresh and plain.
68163-an-outline-of-humor-being-a-true-c:
An Outline of Humor, edited by Carolyn Wells, is an anthology of comic writing published by G P Putnam's Sons in 1923. Wells, who also edited The Book of Humorous Verse and A Nonsense Anthology, arranges the pieces as a chronicle of humour from prehistoric ages to the twentieth century.

A long list of permissions shows the range: Mark Twain's Jumping Frog story, limericks and The Two Old Bachelors from Edward Lear, and verses by Holmes, Lowell, Bret Harte, and John Hay. Publishers also granted pieces by Ben King, Sam Walter Foss, Arthur Guiterman, and Lewis Carroll. The dedication honours Doctor Huber Gray Buehler. Books of this sort let households sample centuries of wit in one volume.
68532-little-hickory-or-ragged-rob-s-you:
Little Hickory, or Ragged Rob's Young Republic, by Victor St Clair, came out in New York in 1901. It formed number four of the Bound to Win Library. Street and Smith published the dime tale. Chapter one is called The Bootblack and the Deacon. A country man, fresh in the city, feels lost among the crowds. Ragged Rob, a bootblack boy, cries his trade at his elbow for half a dime.

Rob's face is smeared with blacking, but his blue eyes twinkle. His clothes and cool air mark him as a street boy who fears no one. Fellow bootblacks jeer that the countryman will use up his stock. The tale promises city wits, boy loyalty, and a republic of street lads. Dialect talk fills the pages.
68662-elements-of-arithmetic:
Elements of Arithmetic is a textbook by Augustus De Morgan, professor of mathematics in University College, London. The copy shown is the seventeenth thousand, a sign of long classroom use. De Morgan heads the book with mottos from Melanchthon and Condillac. The Condillac motto insists that we learn not by routine but by our own reflection, and by giving a reason for what we do.

The preface notes that this edition is enlarged by eleven new appendixes. They treat matters the advanced student most needs to know. The first appendix, on computation, and the sixth, on decimal money, are singled out for every student's close attention. They should be read and practised as carefully as any part of the book. De Morgan's arithmetic thus teaches the rules of number together with the habit of understanding them, rather than drilling routine alone.
69246-broken-music:
Broken Music, a novel by Phyllis Bottome, was printed in Great Britain and published in Boston and New York in 1914. Bottome wrote The Imperfect Gift and The Common Chord. She dedicates the book to the memory of the Siegfried Idyll. A preface says the French life in the book rests on a friend's knowledge, whose name she may not give.

The tale opens as a doctor and a priest compare notes: a lady has sent for both to the castle. Neither would have gone to see Jean's aunt uninvited, above all not for lunch. The priest, who loves mysteries ready-made, answers with care. Bottome promises that her figures are not true, yet belong to a system of parallel cases that runs beside the truth.
69272-life-and-literature-in-the-roman-r:
Life and Literature in the Roman Republic is a set of lectures by Tenney Frank, first copyrighted in 1930. It began as volume seven of the Sather Classical Lectures at California. A 1957 California press printing, the first paper bound edition, is the source here. Contents open with social forces as the ground of Roman writing.

Early tragedy and epic, Greek comedy on the Roman stage, and Terence follow in order. Prose of the statesmen, republican historiography with Livy, and Cicero fill the middle lectures. Lucretius and his readers close the course of eight talks in the volume. Scholars and students gain a social history of Latin letters in one sweep.
6952-by-pike-and-dyke-a-tale-of-the-rise:
G A Henty tells how Holland and Zeeland won the right to worship in their own way and shook off the yoke of Spain. His preface calls the struggle unmatched in history for unequal odds, stubborn defense, and long contest. On one side stood the greatest power of the time, driven by a ruthless bigot bent on forcing his faith or wiping out the people. On the other stood fishermen, sailors, and farmers, split into small towns with little bond between them.

They stood only on defense, trusting the justice of their cause, their stout hearts, and their noble prince. Henty writes for lads, and the tale follows pike and dyke warfare through siege and sea fight. It is the first phase of the Dutch revolt, closing before the English aid his later volume tells.
69637-on-a-lark-to-the-planets-a-sequel-:
On a Lark to the Planets is a children's fantasy by Frances Trego Montgomery, printed at Akron, Ohio, by the Saalfield Publishing Company in 1904. It is a sequel to The Wonderful Electric Elephant. Montgomery also wrote the Billy Whiskers books. The pictures are by Winifred Elrod. The book is lovingly dedicated to Juliet Marie Breitung. Its frontispiece shows white pigeons heralding the approach of Venus.

Harold and Ione, the Prince and the little Princess sleep peacefully aboard. It is midnight by the clock, but the boundless space around them is lit by myriads of twinkling stars. The young travellers watch until they fall asleep from exhaustion. Then, with a quick jerk, the balloon comes to a dead halt.
6973-the-boy-aviators-polar-dash-or-faci:
Captain Wilbur Lawton, pen name of John Henry Goldfrap, sends his boy aviators toward the South Pole in the sixth book of their series. The contents open with a polar ship and a mysterious robbery, then off for the South Pole, a message from the air, and a tragedy of the skies. A strange collision, drift on a floating island, flames, and a queer accident test the crew in turn.

The professor is kidnapped, a battle fills the air, and the boys go adrift, meet the ship of Olaf the Viking, and end marooned on an ice floe. Lawton keeps the series pace brisk, with flight, ice, and peril at every turn. The book is a boys adventure of polar daring told from the cockpit.
69971-the-swiss-republic:
Boyd Winchester, late United States minister at Bern, wrote this account of Switzerland, printed by J B Lippincott of Philadelphia in 1891. He gives the book to Henry Watterson of Louisville, in token of a long friendship. The preface, dated Louisville, 1890, says the book rests on four years of notes made during his service, with print in view from the start.

Winchester makes no try at full history in order. He seizes the chief features of the land, its rule, and its people by hints and short views. Chapters on government, national and cantonal, use comparison with American practice. Swiss history and American trials both enter the argument. The close praises six hundred years of a small, free federal republic.
70132-mezzotints-in-modern-music:
Mezzotints in Modern Music gathers James Huneker's essays on the great composers of his day. Charles Scribner's Sons published this fourth edition in New York in 1912. The copyright dates to 1899. Huneker inscribes the book affectionately to Henry Edward Krehbiel. The title page names the subjects: Brahms, Tschaikowsky, Chopin, Richard Strauss, Liszt, and Wagner.

The first essay, The Music of the Future, opens with a death. The death of Johannes Brahms in 1897 removed, Huneker writes, the last of the immortals. Bulow ranked Brahms with Bach and Beethoven. Schumann lavished praise and prophecy on him. Huneker marvels at the slow, patient fertility of the output. Four symphonies, concertos, chamber works, and the German Requiem fill the list. Later essays treat Strauss with Nietzsche, the greater Chopin, and a Liszt etude. A note on Wagner closes the volume.
70203-the-story-of-chamber-music:
The Story of Chamber Music is a guide to small scale music by N Kilburn. The author led church choirs and bands in the north of England. The book stands in a set that tells the tale of each branch of music. Prints dress the text, and the book came out in nineteen hundred and four.

Kilburn notes at the start that one great French hand wrote near none of it. Small group works for home and hall form the field of the whole book. Kin books in the set treat song rites, signs, and the great organ. Plain talk aims the guide at keen fans, not just trained hands. The tale runs from old court rooms to the new string bands.
7098-tales-of-the-enchanted-islands-of-t:
Thomas Wentworth Higginson gathers tales of the enchanted islands of the Atlantic, inscribed to General Sir George Wentworth Higginson in token of kindred and old family friendship. His preface notes Hawthorne's Wonder Book treated Greek myths, yet no one had used the wondrous tales gathered for a thousand years about Atlantic islands. Those hazy legends belong to the mythical period of American history, though earlier historians disdained them.

George Bancroft even prided himself that American annals began bare and literal, but Higginson argues no national history lacks its misty shore. The legends unite both sides of the Atlantic and form part of the common heritage of English speaking peoples. The book rescues phantom isles, saints, and sailors from scholarly neglect.
7108-a-trip-to-scarborough-and-the-criti:
A Trip to Scarborough, a comedy acted at Drury Lane Theatre in 1777, shares this volume with The Critic. The dramatis personae name Lord Foppington, Sir Tunbelly Clumsy, Colonel Townly, Loveless, and Tom Fashion, with La Varole, Lory, Probe, and Mendlegs among the men. Amanda, Berinthia, Miss Hoyden, Missus Coupler, and Nurse lead the women, with sempstress, postilion, maid, and servants behind them.

The scene lies in Scarborough and its neighborhood, and a prologue spoken by Mister King notes how all things change, from Whitechapel to Hyde Park, in state, stage, trade, taste, and passion. Sheridan's comedy of fops, fortune hunters, and seaside manners follows, paired with his famous burlesque on the theater itself.
71345-the-orchestra-and-orchestral-music:
Henderson, author of What Is Good Music, wrote this guide for the Music-Lover's Library, published by Scribner in 1902 and dedicated to the Philharmonic Society of New York. He begins from a fine definition: the modern orchestra is a musical instrument upon which a performer, known as a conductor, plays. The book's five parts take the reader through how the orchestra is constituted, how it is used, and how it is directed.

The first parts sort the families of instruments, the bowed strings, the wood wind, the brass, and the battery, and teach the reading of a score. The last parts give the history: from Peri to Handel, from Haydn to Wagner, and the growth of orchestral music from Bach to Richard Strauss. Portraits of Beethoven, Nikisch, Berlioz, and other masters face the text.
73175-static:
Wallace West wrote this tale of a radio set carried into the African bush. Charles Markley takes his set to darkest Africa, the head note says. The native folk take the box for a god, and Markley's life hangs in the tale's balance.

Water slaps the hull of the Niger packet Lagarto as the tale opens. Close at hand the jungle waves ghostly arms in the moonlight. A native girl learns the truth of the set, the note adds: it is no god, but a man's tool. Just as Markley's life stands in dire risk, a turn changes the look of things. Wireless, then a fresh marvel, meets old Africa in this pulp tale of awe and risk.
73984-sinking-of-the-titanic:
Sinking of the Titanic is a memorial edition on the great ocean disaster of 1912. Jay Henry Mowbray compiled the book, issued by the Minter Company at Harrisburg. The title page promises graphic accounts of hundreds swept beneath the waves.

The stories, it says, were told by eye witnesses of the horror. Photographs of the scenes fill the volume in great number. A preface quotes Sir Humphrey Gilbert: we are as near heaven by sea as by land. The men of the Titanic, Mowbray writes, faced death with high hearts. They gave the last full measure of devotion so that women and children might live. The ship, vaunted as unsinkable, made the wreck the worst that ever befell a vessel, he argues. Accounts of other great disasters are added at the end.
75176-henry-goes-prehistoric:
Tuttle wrote this Western tale of Tonto City and its sheriff, Henry Harrison Conroy. A headline promises that the sheriff could expect anything to come out of the night in Wild Horse Valley, even an idea. Judge Van Treece opens the story in a rage in his office.

Van Treece throws his beloved, dog-eared copy of Shakespeare across the room in his anger. The book flutters to the floor like a wounded duck, and he does not look at it. Conroy, barely five feet seven in his high-heel boots, picks it up calmly, while the tall, skinny judge glares at nobody in particular.
75337-an-address-to-highlanders-respecti:
Archibald Farquharson addressed this plea to Highlanders in 1868, printing it at Edinburgh with sellers in Glasgow, Oban, Inverness, and Stornoway. His title promises to show the superiority of native Gaelic, and of broad Scotch, over artificial English for the family, the social circle, and lyric poetry. A prefatory letter begs the gentlemen of the press to plead his cause.

Farquharson argues that children should first be taught to read their mother tongue, the words they heard from their mother's lips and their playmates. Judgment would then aid memory instead of leaving the child groping in the dark of an unknown language. Only after Gaelic reading is secure should English begin, with every English word translated back into Gaelic as it is read. Farquharson, who had lately written on the Highland Clearances, signs himself a lover of his country.
75524-the-roving-critic:
The Roving Critic, by Carl Van Doren, was published by Alfred Knopf in New York in March 1923. The essays, sketches, and reviews are reprinted from the Atlantic Monthly, the Literary Review, the Nation, and the Texas Review. Ten parts group them, from Toward a Creed to In the Open.

Three of Our Conquerors treats the poetical cult of Lincoln and Whitman in his crises. A eulogium on Howells, dated May 1920, stands alone. Nooks and Fringes gathers Mocha Dick, folk lore in Kentucky, Paul Bunyan going west, and the worst American book. A Casual Shelf reviews books in short compass. Poets' Corner asks whether the immigrant strain is a tap root or a melting pot. The opening essay seeks a fourth dimension in criticism. Criticism, Van Doren notes, ordinarily asks of literature one of three questions.
75585-flecker-s-magic:
Flecker's Magic is a novel by Norman Matson, printed at New York by Boni and Liveright in 1926. Its hero, Spike Flecker, is a young man who means to be a great painter. The book opens in Paris, in a cold drizzle after days of rain. Puddles stand gray under a morose sky.

Flecker peers into the Café of the Lilacs, where a fat man laughs in the warmth. Madame at her high desk gives him a cheerful smile over her coffee. Cold and sad, he returns a sober nod and will not go in to be comfortable. He chooses a chair on the wet pavement instead, the iron table like ice to his hands. Nobody, the story adds, would buy his pictures. Matson writes the artist's Paris of garrets and pride.
75730-the-war-and-our-financial-fabric:
The War and Our Financial Fabric, by Walter Wall, came out in 1915. Chapman and Hall published the study in London. Wall was a fellow of the Royal Statistical Society. British Railway Finance stands among his earlier books. Twenty three chapters and appendices make the volume. What is market money is the first question asked. The currency of custom and credit and confidence follow. Sound banking and the superstructure of wealth come next. The loanable fund, its changes, and the central reserve fill the middle. A theoretic line of safety is drawn late. Frozen wealth and conclusions close the argument. Chapter one opens on the naming of money itself.

Economists' definitions clash past reconciling, Wall writes. The man in the street thinks the matter simple. Pounds, shillings, and pence are money to him, and nothing more need be said.
76286-elfin-music:
Elfin Music is a gathering of English fairy poetry, picked and set in order by Arthur Edward Waite, printed in London in 1888. William Sharp shaped the Canterbury Poets line. A quote from the Ettrick Shepherd heads the book, on the mystic lore of fairy tales.

Waite long opening traces the rise of the romantic in modern verse and the source of the word fairy. He treats the fays of old French tales, Oberon, and the lore of Gothic and Celtic lands. Poems follow from Edgar Allan Poe, Felicia Hemans, and Edmund Spenser. Shakespeare gives Queen Mab and a lullaby for Titania, and Ben Jonson gives Queen Mab as well. Verse fans get the whole fairy line of English song in one small book.
76966-the-phantom-public:
The Phantom Public, a book on democracy and public opinion by Walter Lippmann, was published at New York in 1925. Lippmann dedicated it to the judge Learned Hand. It opens with two hard sayings. Hamilton in 1787 called the voice of the people no true voice of God, and Lord Grey warned that government by public opinion supposes a public ready to decide each question.

The chapters begin with the disenchanted man and the unattainable ideal. Lippmann pictures the citizen as a deaf spectator in the back row, swept along by great drifts of events. Rules, taxes, and wars remind him that public life moves without his grasp. The book argues that the ruling public of democratic theory is a phantom. It became a classic of political thought, still read for its cold eye on voters and the press.
77011-the-organisation-of-thought-educat:
The Organisation of Thought, educational and scientific, gathers addresses by Whitehead, then professor of applied mathematics at the Imperial College in London. Williams and Norgate published it in 1917. Its first chapter, The Aims of Education, was his presidential address to the Mathematical Association in January 1916. It pleads for reform in how schools teach.

Other pieces treat technical education and its ties to science and letters. One address, given in war time at a London polytechnic, speaks to training under the strain of 1917. The mathematical curriculum and the place of mathematics in early teaching follow. The title essay was his presidential address to a section of the British Association at Newcastle in 1916. Whitehead argues for living knowledge over inert ideas, a theme that made his education writings famous. The book shows a great thinker turning to the classroom.
77673-agar-halfi-the-mystic:
Roland Filkin wrote a novel of an Eastern mystic and the Englishman he serves. William Rider and Son issued Agar Halfi the Mystic in London in 1915. Twenty-seven chapters run from a prologue in camp to a close among the stars. Constance Alletson, a lady's glove, and a dog named Hector stir the plot.

Hugo Alexis Brentwood camps by a stream at a mountain's foot at sunset. His servant Halfi reads his master's silence with half-closed eyes. Brentwood, once a rising student of mind, had turned to Eastern occult lore. Readers gain a tale of strange power, love, and East ruling West.
77782-black-magic:
Black Magic, a tale of the rise and fall of Antichrist, is a novel by Marjorie Bowen of 1909. Alston Rivers published the book in London from Brooke Street, Holborn, that year. Contents divide the tale into two parts, The Nun and The Pope, for the reader. Part one follows a young clerk, Theirry, among students, spells, and a witch in its chapters.

Sunshine, The Students, The Experiment, and The Departure open the first part in order. The Snaring of Jacobea and The Snaring of Theirry mark the tightening of the plot there. Part two moves to Rome, with a cardinal, a confession, an empress, and the Pope himself in its heads. Bowen, writing at twenty three, made her name with this rich, dark tale of medieval sorcery. Its Antichrist rises through the Church he means to ruin, in a pageant of courts and covens.
77893-hot-music:
Vic Whitman's crime novel opens in radio station KYK, where a famous dance band is setting up below and Officer Dave Cates is broadcasting above. Cates is the police announcer, and his plain words are code. To the listening details they report that there have been no more developments in the Van Goss jewelry robbery. Headquarters, they add, plans to put more men on the case. Cates, listed as an officer only for this work, is a verbal messenger boy, and he is tired of it.

He dreams of action, of the reward that would bring him nearer a white, green-shuttered bungalow and Anabelle Talbot, the dancer who listens in before going to the Salon Quintesse. Then a wealthy young woman bursts into the telephone room with Leo Archer, the band leader, in tow. The case Cates craved has come to him over the air.
78238-leaves-from-the-notebook-of-a-tame:
Reinhold Niebuhr, then a young Detroit pastor, kept this notebook of his ministry's inner life. Willett, Clark printed it at Chicago in 1929. Niebuhr gave it to his friends and fellow workers at Bethel Evangelical Church in Detroit.

The publishers note that Niebuhr shrank from sending the book out. It might read as proud blame of others, he feared. They answer that he is a rare man who sees more fault in himself than in those round him. What is proud blame, they ask, with Hocking's help. Leaves from a notebook, plain and sharp, show a preacher weighing his own soul and his age's church with the same hard scale.
78384-a-geographical-and-commercial-view:
James McQueen wrote A Geographical and Commercial View of Northern Central Africa, published at Edinburgh in 1821. The book promises a particular account of the course and termination of the great river Niger in the Atlantic Ocean. A map drawn by McQueen in 1820, showing the Niger and the Gir with their tributary streams, opens the volume.

In his preface McQueen tells how the question claimed him. When Mungo Park returned from his first journey, McQueen lived in Grenada in the West Indies. Mandingo men under his charge knew the Joliba by name, and a Hausa man said he had rowed Park across the Niger. McQueen collected every account he could find. His book argues, from such testimony, where the mysterious river must end, years before the question was settled by travel.
79613-woman-in-music:
George Upton, author of The Standard Operas, wrote Woman in Music, first issued in 1880 and brought out again at Chicago in 1886 in a revised and much enlarged form. A fire had destroyed the plates of the first edition and cut its run short. Upton says he wrote the book in spare hours and drew its facts from a long list of sound sources on music.

The enlarged edition widens the field and adds fresh tales of composers whose success owed much to the help or sway of women. Upton aimed the work at music students first, but he hoped the wider public would find it of worth as well. The dedication is to his wife, named as a steadfast comrade and helper.
8144-acetylene-the-principles-of-its-gen:
F. H. Leeds and W. J. Atkinson Butterfield wrote this practical handbook on acetylene, in a second edition revised and enlarged. Leeds, long technical editor of the journal Acetylene, and Butterfield, author of The Chemistry of Gas Manufacture. Explain the physical and chemical phenomena of generating acetylene from calcium carbide and water, and its production, purification, and treatment for light, heat, and power.

The book served engineers and gas workers at a time when acetylene lit homes, bicycles, and workshops before electricity spread. Its chapters move from chemistry to plant and safety, with the clarity of a working manual. For historians of technology, it captures an energy revolution in mid-career, and the science that made a brilliant new light possible.
9306-aesthetic-as-science-of-expression-:
Benedetto Croce, the Italian philosopher, wrote this aesthetic theory, translated by Douglas Ainslie in 1909. Croce dedicates it to his parents Pasquale and Luisa Sipari, and to his sister Maria. His theory holds that intuition and expression are one: to see clearly is already to express, apart from intellect, concepts, and mere sensation.

Chapters treat intuition and art, with a historical summary shortened by the author's consent. Croce argues against splitting feeling from form, and against treating art as mere craft. The book remains a landmark of modern aesthetics, demanding yet lucid, and central to Croce's fame.
a-book-of-operas-their-histories-their-p:
A Book of Operas, by Henry Edward Krehbiel, gives the histories, plots, and music of the standard repertory in sixteen chapters. Krehbiel, the leading American music critic of his day, opens with Rossini's Barber of Seville. His first chapter even reaches back to the Garcia troupe's first American performances of Italian opera in New York.

From Figaro and The Magic Flute the book moves through Don Giovanni, Fidelio, and three treatments of Faust, including Berlioz and Boito. Verdi follows with La Traviata and Aida, then Weber's Freischutz opens the German half. Wagner dominates the close: Tannhauser, Tristan, Parsifal, the Meistersinger, and Lohengrin. Each chapter tells how the opera was made, what happens in it, and where its great tunes and scenes sit, with famous singers weighed along the way.
a-rock-in-the-baltic:
Robert Barr's A Rock in the Baltic, dated 1906, opens at a bank in Bar Harbor, Maine. Lieutenant Alan Drummond of H.M.S. Consternation waits to change his Bank of England notes. A plainly dressed girl enters with anxiety on her face and a cheque in her trembling hand. The cashier's long scrutiny tells Drummond that great issues depend on the moment.

The girl is a Russian princess in flight, and the cheque is her lifeline. Drummond follows her affair into a plot of nihilists, a Baltic island fortress, and a prison rock. Barr, a Scots-Canadian magazinist, writes brisk imperial adventure. Spies, disguises, and a rescue at sea keep his pages turning. The rock of the title is a czarist Alcatraz in northern waters. Romance and revolution share the helm, in the manner of the best Edwardian thrillers.
a-romance-of-the-republic: Lydia Maria Child opens this novel in a New Orleans counting house, where Mr Royal greets young Alfred King as warmly as he once greeted Alfred's father. The book is inscribed to the parents of Colonel Robert Gould Shaw, steadfast friends of freedom and equal rights. It is a romance of the republic in years when those rights were denied. Its first part follows Alfred from that familiar greeting into a wider American story.
a-trip-to-scarborough-and-the-critic:
Richard Brinsley Sheridan wrote both comedies in the hosted volume. A Trip to Scarborough, first acted at Drury Lane in 1777 as the printed cast list records, sends the fashionable Lord Foppington, young Tom Fashion. the hoydenish Miss Hoyden through a round of visits, debts, and marriage schemes in a spa town.

The Critic, printed after it, turns on the theatre itself, mocking playwrights, rehearsals, and stage heroics. Together the pair show Sheridan's range: one play laughs at manners and money in company, the other at the vanities of the stage that performed it. The dialogue is quick, the plots run on disguise and misunderstanding, and the jokes still land because the targets have not changed.
a-voyage-round-the-world-volume-i-includ: James Holman, of the Royal Navy and the Royal Society, voyages round the world in this first volume, covering travels from 1827 to 1832. The advertisement plans four volumes in regular succession, each complete in itself, forming a consecutive series of the author's voyages. This volume contains Madeira, Teneriffe, St Jago, Sierra Leone, Cape Coast, Accra, Fernando Po, Bonny and Calabar, and other rivers in the Bight of Biafra.
acetylene-the-principles-of-its-generati: Frank Henley Leeds and Atkinson Butterfield write Acetylene, a handy guide to making and using it for light, heat, and power, in a second edition made larger. The book treats making acetylene from calcium carbide and water. Its burning in bright and glow lamps comes next, with use plain, in squeezed tanks, thinned, and for making other gases burn brighter. Its aim is to weigh this light source against other lights.
aesthetic-as-science-of-expression-and-g: Benedetto Croce sets out his theory of art as expression, arguing that aesthetic activity is a form of knowledge distinct from logic and science. Translated from the Italian by Douglas Ainslie, the book links beauty to language itself, treating expression as the ground of both art and speech. Dense but systematic, it remains a key statement of early twentieth-century philosophy of art.
amusing-trial-in-which-a-yankee-lawyer-r: An anonymous New York pamphlet stages an amusing trial in which a Yankee lawyer renders a just verdict. The short piece turns courtroom talk into comedy, with the shrewd Yankee outwitting his foes by plain sense and quick wit. It survives as a small example of early American popular humour about law and lawyers.
britannica-1911-acrostic:
Acrostic is a verse puzzle built on first letters. The initial letters of the lines, read in order, form words. Greeks of the Alexandrine period loved the device. Latin writers used it from Ennius onward. Play arguments were written as acrostics on titles. One famous set of verses is ascribed to a sibyl. Its initials spell Jesus Christ, Son of God, Saviour. Those initials themselves form the Greek word for fish.

Fashion kept the form alive for centuries. Medieval monks and German poets used it. Boccaccio and other Renaissance poets indulged in it. Sir John Davies wrote twenty-six acrostic hymns for Elizabeth. Critics have always rated acrostics low, though. Butler and Addison mocked their makers. Double acrostics hide words in final letters too.
britannica-1911-alaric:
Alaric is a life article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about the Gothic conqueror who first stood as a victor in the city of Rome. Born about 370 on an island at the mouth of the Danube, Alaric came of the noble house of the Balthi and belonged to the western Goths, the Visigoths. In 394 he served as a general of Gothic irregulars under the emperor Theodosius in the campaign that crushed the usurper Eugenius.

The article pauses on the system that bred his rise. The empire, its own people crushed by tax and unable to fill the ranks, hired barbarian troops under barbarian chiefs. At the battle of the Frigidus, near the passes of the Julian Alps, Alaric likely learned how weak Italy's north east defences were. Alaric hoped for one of the great war ministries and, denied it, took the step his grumbling countrymen longed for.
britannica-1911-arsenic:
Arsenic is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a chemical element. Its symbol is As and its atomic weight is given as 75. The element was known to the ancients in its sulfides. Aristotle gave those sulfides a Greek name. Theophrastus also names them in his writings. The oxide called white arsenic was known to Greek alchemists. One of them gained it by roasting arsenic sulfide.

Later alchemists used arsenic minerals for a set purpose. They used them to give copper a white colour. Albertus Magnus first said arsenic held a metal-like stuff. Later writers called it a semi-metal or bastard metal. In 1733 Brandt showed white arsenic was its calx. After the fall of the phlogiston theory, views settled. White arsenic was agreed to be an oxide of the element. The entry thus traces a long path of trial and error.
britannica-1911-authentic: Authentic means genuine, as opposed to counterfeit. It can also mean true or original. The word comes from a Greek term for one who does a thing himself. Music uses the word technically as well. There it names one class of the ecclesiastical modes, the church scales of early music. Law uses it too. The title Authentics was applied to Justinian's Novels, the later laws issued by that Roman emperor.
britannica-1911-balderic:
Balderic is the name attached to a chronicle of the bishops of Cambrai, written in the 11th century. The work, called Gesta episcoporum Cambracensium, was long credited to Balderic, archbishop of Noyon. The 1911 Britannica entry says the true author now seems to have been an unnamed canon of Cambrai.

The chronicle matters for the history of northern France in the 11th century. It was first printed in 1615. The best edition named here is the one in the Monumenta Germaniae Historica, with an introduction by L. C. Bethmann. A volume of the Histoire littéraire de la France is also cited for readers.
britannica-1911-baldric:
Baldric is an old word for a belt worn over one shoulder. It runs across the body on a slant and passes under the other arm. The 1911 Britannica entry traces the word from Old French baudrei and Old German balderich, and links it to the English word belt.

Such a belt could be worn just for show. More often it served a use: to carry a sword, a bugle, or some other gear that hung at the wearer's side. The entry is a short one, giving the word's origin, its doubtful roots, and the way the strap was worn.
britannica-1911-bastiat-frederic:
Frédéric Bastiat (1801–1850), a French economist born at Bayonne, the son of a merchant, is the subject of a long 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica biography. He disliked the counting-house routine of his uncle's firm and retired in 1825 to a property at Mugron, farming and studying. Local office followed: justice of the peace in 1831 and member of the department council in 1832. Pamphlets on taxation affecting his district began his writing career in print.

England's example turned Bastiat to free trade. Reading about the Anti-Corn-Law League, he studied it for two years. In 1844 he argued that French and English tariffs both harmed their countries. His Sophismes Économiques made his name. In Paris he met Cobden and Bright, helped found a French free-trade association in 1846, and edited its weekly paper. After the 1848 revolution, though ill and losing his voice, he fought socialism in the Assembly and in rapid essays.
britannica-1911-berard-joseph-frederic:
Joseph Frédéric Bérard (1789–1828) was a French physician and philosopher born at Montpellier. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica follows his training at that town's medical school and his work in Paris on a dictionary of medical science. His 1819 book on the medical doctrine of the Montpellier school is called a key to the Vitalistic school's ideas.

In 1823 he took a chair of medicine at Paris, then a chair of hygiene at Montpellier, but his health broke under the work. His chief book, on the links between body and mind, also came in 1823. He held that inner sense shows us a thinking, willing self, a soul apart from the body. Beside it stands a vital force that runs the frame and shapes the ground for the soul's powers. The article finds his thought midway between two schools and lacking in fresh ideas.
britannica-1911-biquadratic:
Biquadratic is a mathematics word built from the Latin bi-, twice, and quadratus, squared. The biquadratic power of a quantity is its fourth power. Its biquadratic root is its fourth root in turn. A biquadratic equation is one where the unknown's highest power is the fourth. The 1911 Britannica entry states those three senses in as many lines. It sends readers to the articles on Algebra and Equations for working rules.

The entry is a short cross-reference note, not a treatment in itself. No example equation or solution method is given in its space. What it fixes is the naming: twice-squared means square upon square. That gives the fourth power, and the equation class that stops there. Readers who need methods are pointed onward by the entry itself. The term and its uses are the whole content here.
britannica-1911-brachycephalic:
Brachycephalic means short-headed, and the term was invented by Andreas Retzius for skulls whose width nearly matches their length. The rule is a ratio: take the length as 100, and a skull is brachycephalic if its width passes 80. The Mongolian head is given as the type of the class.

Most heads of civilised races, the entry says, fall on the short-headed side. A brachycephalic people is thought to have lived in Europe before the Celts came. Peoples named as strongly short-headed include the Indo-Chinese, Savoyards, Croatians, Bavarians, Lapps, Burmese, Armenians, and Peruvians. Readers who want the measuring method are sent to the article on craniometry at the close.
britannica-1911-carnatic:
Carnatic is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a region of southern India between the Eastern Ghats and the Coromandel coast, in the presidency of Madras. The entry explains the name first: Bishop Caldwell derived it from words meaning “black country,” a fit label for the black cotton soil of the southern Deccan plateau. It then shows how Muslim conquerors and later the British each shifted the name's meaning, until it covered only the lowland coast and dropped out of official use.

The region as Europeans knew it ran about 600 miles along the eastern coast, from the Guntur circar south to Cape Comorin, in widths of 50 to 100 miles. The entry divides it into Southern, Central, and Northern parts and treats it as a region of great historical weight. Readers get a clear case of a place name changing its ground as rulers changed.
britannica-1911-casaubon-florence-estien:
Florence Estienne Méric Casaubon (1599–1671) is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on an English classical scholar, the son of Isaac Casaubon. He was born at Geneva and joined his father in England while still young. He finished his schooling at Eton and Oxford, taking his degree in 1618. His defence of his father against Catholic attackers in 1621 won him the favour of James I and a prebend at Canterbury.

Méric also cleared his father's name against impostors who had published a work on the origin of idolatry under it. During the Civil War he lived in retirement. Cromwell asked him to write an impartial history of the times, but he refused to own Cromwell's authority and declined the task. He also refused a post from Queen Christina of Sweden. After the Restoration he regained his benefice and spent his last years on literary work at Canterbury.
britannica-1911-catholic:
Catholic is a word from the Greek for general or universal, and this 1911 Britannica entry traces how the church took it up. The church adopted the term in the second century to mark Christendom as a whole, set against single churches. With it went the thought that the faith had been spread over the whole earth by the apostles. Only what was found everywhere in the church, it held, could be true.

In time the term filled with dogmatic and political weight. Applied to the church, it came to mean a universal body with authority and orthodoxy, set over against Gnostic and other sects. The entry cites the canon of Vincent of Lerins, from the year 434, with its test of what has been believed everywhere, always, and by all.
britannica-1911-caustic:
Caustic is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a word from the Greek for burning, applied in surgery, mathematics, and optics. In surgery, caustics are substances used to destroy living tissue and check organic poisons, as in bites, malignant disease, and gangrene. The entry lists silver nitrate, the caustic alkalis, zinc chloride, an acid solution of mercuric nitrate, and pure carbolic acid.

In mathematics, the caustic surfaces of a surface are the envelopes of its normals, the paths of its centres of main curvature. In optics, a caustic is the envelope of light rays after reflection or refraction, called a catacaustic in the first case and a diacaustic in the second. Such bright curves can be seen when light falls on a polished steel watch spring laid on a table. The study of these curves, being pure geometry, drew the mathematicians of the seventeenth century onward.
britannica-1911-cerdic:
Cerdic, founder of the West Saxon realm in Britain, is the subject of a short old past entry in the 1911 Britannica. He is called a lord who landed in Hampshire in four ninety five with his son Cynric. Britons met them at the shore in arms. Wins in five oh eight and five nineteen gave him ground. In that last year he took the name of king. A loss at Badbury checked his west push for a time.

His last deed in the text was the taking of the Isle of Wight. That win may have been made for Jutish friends, the note says. All kings of England save a short list are said to spring from his line. Sources named run from the Saxon Chronicle to Bede and Gildas.
britannica-1911-chic:
Chic is a French word, perhaps a shortened form of chicane or taken from the German Schick, meaning tact or skill. In French artistic slang it names a work of art with brilliant but shallow skill in technique. Such a work is made without reference to a model or to study of nature. The entry traces French use of the word back to the reign of Louis XIV.

In that early use, chic denoted a lawyer who was master of chicane, a man skilled in legal quibbling. General use has since shifted the sense toward dress, speech and manner. Now the word connotes smartness, the entry says, in those outward things. The path from a term for hollow technical flair to a word for smart looks is the whole subject here.
britannica-1911-chilperic:
Chilperic is the name of two Frankish kings, and the entry treats them in turn across two centuries. Chilperic I, who died in 584, was a son of Clotaire I and tried at his father's death in 561 to seize the whole kingdom. His brothers forced a division, and Soissons and nearby towns fell to his share. His marriage to Galswintha, sister of Brunhilda, ended with her found strangled in her bed.

Days later Chilperic married Fredegond, his former concubine, and long bloody wars with his brother Sigebert followed from the murder. Gregory of Tours called him the Nero and Herod of his time for his taxes, church seizures and sold bishoprics. He was stabbed at Chelles while returning from the chase. Chilperic II, who died in 720, became king of Neustria in 715 as a tool of Ragenfrid, until Charles Martel overthrew that mayor and set him over the whole kingdom.
britannica-1911-chromatic:
Chromatic is a Greek word meaning coloured, and this 1911 Britannica entry follows its uses in science and in music. In science it lives chiefly in the phrase chromatic aberration, a fault of lenses treated under its own heading. In Greek music the chromatic was one of three kinds of tetrachord, beside the diatonic and the enharmonic. The Greek word, like the Latin color, was also used for ornaments and grace notes.

The chromatic kind, open to three shifts of its notes, counted as the most coloured of the three. To Greek ears chromatic music sounded sweet and plaintive. From a likeness to those old scales, the term now marks any run of notes outside the plain scale, written with sharps or flats. A chromatic scale is a run of semitones, most often written with sharps going up and flats coming down.
britannica-1911-clay-frederic:
Frederic Clay, an English composer who lived from 1838 to 1889, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in Paris, he was the son of James Clay, a famed whist player and writer on that game. He studied music in Paris and at Leipzig under noted teachers. Save for a few songs and two cantatas, all his works were written for the stage.

Clay first came before the public with the opera Court and Cottage at Covent Garden in 1862. Constance, Ages Ago, and Princess Toto are named among his many later stage works. The last two, with words by Gilbert, are called his most tuneful and most pleasing scores. His cantata Lalla Rookh of 1877 held his best known song, I Will Sing Thee Songs of Araby.
