Most of his operas, the text notes, had long been forgotten by 1911.
britannica-1911-climacteric:
Climacteric, from a Greek word for the rung or step of a ladder, is a critical period in human life, the entry explains. In a medical sense it names the period known as the change of life, marked in women by the menopause. That medical use is the head sense given here. Certain ages, especially multiples of seven or nine, have been superstitiously regarded as particularly critical in a person's span.

The sixty-third and the eighty-first years have been called the grand climacteric, singled out above other ages in that belief. No medical detail beyond the menopause is offered in this short notice. The word is also used generally, beyond the body altogether. Any turning point in the history of a nation, a career or the like can bear the name, the entry closes by saying.
britannica-1911-colic:
Colic is a medical term for sudden sharp pain in the belly, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica notes how loosely it is used. The word comes from the Greek term for the large intestine. Physicians outside England use it for any cramping pain of the abdomen. In England the use is narrower, the entry says.

In English practice, colic is tied to pain from set organs. Those organs are the kidney, the ureter, the gall bladder, the bile ducts, and the intestine. So doctors speak of renal, biliary, and intestinal colic. A trend among physicians narrows the term still further. In that view, colic is pain from the squeezing of the muscular walls of a hollow organ. The squeezing counts when the passage of the organ has become partly blocked.
britannica-1911-conduction-electric:
Electric conduction is the trait by which all parts of a body come to one electric level on their own. That holds when no electric force acts on the body. Its reverse trait is resistivity. That trait lets a gap of level stand between parts of a body in a circuit. The body must touch a steady source of force for that gap to show.

All matter holds some power to conduct, great or small. For ease of study the entry splits matter into five classes. Metal conductors stand first, then non-metal conductors. Dielectric and electrolytic conductors follow. Gaseous conductors close the list. No sharp line parts one class from the next. The split is thus a tool of convenience, not a law of nature. Most of the long entry then treats each class in its own turn.
britannica-1911-dalmatic:
Dalmatic is a term entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It explains a church robe worn by deacons in the western church. A close twin robe is worn by the rank just below them. In most lands both robes now take the form of a cloak with a head hole.

The entry marks the twin stripes that run from shoulder to hem as the chief trim. Fringes, bands, and shoulder tassels are listed as lesser trim. The robe began as a loose tunic with wide sleeves in the Roman world. Its name points to the land where the cut first came from. In Italy the robe keeps true sleeves and a tunic shape to this day.
britannica-1911-daniell-john-frederic:
John Frederic Daniell (1790–1845) was an English chemist and physicist born in London on 12 March 1790. In 1831 he became the first professor of chemistry at the newly founded King's College, London. His name lives in the Daniell cell of 1836, long used for telegraph work. He also invented the dew-point hygrometer that bears his name. A register pyrometer and a water-barometer in the hall of the Royal Society were likewise his.

Daniell devised a way to make lighting gas from turpentine and resin, used for a time in New York. His books include Meteorological Essays of 1823 and an essay on artificial climate in hothouses. His Introduction to the Study of Chemical Philosophy appeared in 1839. He joined the Royal Society in 1813 and served as its foreign secretary from 1839. He died suddenly of apoplexy on 13 March 1845, at a meeting of the society's council in London.
britannica-1911-erichsen-sir-john-eric:
Erichsen, Sir John Eric, Baronet (1818–1896), was a British surgeon born on 19 July 1818 at Copenhagen, the son of Eric Erichsen of a well-known Danish family. He studied medicine at University College, London, and at Paris. In his early career he gave himself to physiology, lecturing on general anatomy and physiology at University College hospital. 

In 1848 Erichsen became assistant surgeon at University College hospital, and in 1850 full surgeon and professor of surgery, his lectures and clinical teaching much admired. His Science and Art of Surgery of 1853 went through many editions. He rose to be president of the College of Surgeons in 1880, and from 1879 to 1881 he headed the Royal Medical and Chirurgical Society. He was made a baronet in 1895, having served some years as surgeon-extraordinary to Queen Victoria. The entry calls his reputation world-wide and counts him among the makers of modern surgery.
britannica-1911-exotic:
Exotic, from the Greek exōtikos, foreign, means of foreign origin or belonging to another country. The entry notes the word's narrower modern sense: something not native to a place. It is applied mostly to plants brought in from foreign countries that have not become acclimatized. Used figuratively, it suggests something rare, delicate or extravagant.

The notice runs to a few lines only. It gives the Greek root, the general meaning and the restricted botanical one. No examples of plants or places are named. The figurative shade is added at the end without illustration. As a vocabulary entry it simply fixes the term for use elsewhere in the volume. Nothing in it reaches beyond definition.
britannica-1911-fustic: Fustic, also called yellow wood or old fustic, is a dye-stuff made from the wood of Chlorophora tinctoria, a large tree of the West Indies and tropical America. The wood reaches market in blocks, brown outside and brownish-yellow within, and is sometimes used for inlaid work. Young fustic, or Zante fustic, comes instead from Rhus cotinus, the smoke tree of southern Europe and Asia, and its colouring matter is the substance fisetin.
britannica-1911-glagolitic: Glagolitic is an early Slavonic alphabet. The 1911 Britannica entry is very short, and it gives the word three senses. First, the alphabet itself. Second, the liturgy written in that alphabet. Third, by extension, the people among whom both have survived: the Dalmatians and the Roman Catholic Montenegrins. The entry adds that this survival rests on a special licence of the Pope. For the table of the letters themselves, readers are sent to the article on the Slavs.
britannica-1911-halevy-ludovic:
Ludovic Halévy (1834–1908) was a French author born in Paris. His father Léon tried almost every branch of literature. His uncle Fromental was the famous opera composer. The stage thus surrounded Ludovic from childhood. At eighteen he joined the French administration. His last post served the Corps Législatif under Morny. Writing success let him retire in 1865.

He had met the composer Offenbach ten years earlier. Small stage pieces followed under a pseudonym. Orphée aux enfers, written with Hector Crémieux, made his name. Its run was unprecedented. In 1860 chance paired him with Henri Meilhac. That partnership became one of the French stage's great teams. Their collected theatre fills eight volumes. Halévy also wrote novels, ending with Kari Kari in 1892. He died in Paris on 8 May 1908.
britannica-1911-hieratic: Hieratic, from Greek words for priestly or sacred, is a term applied above all to a style of ancient Egyptian writing. That style is a simplified cursive form of hieroglyphic, made for quicker everyday use than the carved signs. The name itself was first given by Champollion. The whole entry is a brief definition of three lines, and it sits inside a larger hosted file that also holds the end of the Hierarchy article and the entry on Hierax.
britannica-1911-hunneric:
Hunneric was king of the Vandals, who died in the year four eighty-four. He was a son of the great king of that folk. As a youth he was sent to Italy as a pledge when his father made a pact with the ruler at Rome. Back at Carthage he wed a Goth kings child.

When that wife was thought to plot to kill his father with sap, she was marred and sent back to her folk. He took the throne past his fathers death in four seventy-seven. Like his father he held the Arian faith. His reign is marked most by harsh work past the true church.
britannica-1911-le-play-pierre-guillaume:
Pierre Guillaume Frederic Le Play was a French engineer and economist of note. He lived from eighteen o six to eighteen eighty two. His life entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at La Riviere Saint Sauveur, the son of a customs officer, he studied engineering.

Le Play trained at the Ecole Polytechnique and joined the state mines service. In eighteen forty he became chief engineer and teacher of metallurgy work. For near twenty five years he toured Europe in his free seasons. He gathered vast facts on the lives of working class families there. His book of thirty six family budget studies won the Montyon prize.
britannica-1911-meter-electric:
Electric meters measure the electric energy or amount sold to the public. Their device entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Public supply for light and power needs such measure to set fair bills. Meters split by supply type, by record style, and by working rule.

The deepest split is between energy meters and quantity meters in use. Energy meters, called watt hour meters, track what is truly sold here. Quantity meters, called ampere hour meters, assume a steady supply pressure rate. Most meters in use fall under five heads by their build type. They are liquid, motor, clock, stepped record, and induction meter kinds.
britannica-1911-motors-electric:
Electric motors, machines that turn electric power into motion, are explained in a technical entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. In base terms a motor is a generator run in reverse. Both rest on stresses between two magnetic fields that can move against each other. No change of energy is perfect, so some power is always lost.

Losses come from heat in wires, from drag in bearings and brushes, and from eddy currents. In large new machines the entry puts total loss at five or six per cent. Torque, the turning force, comes from the pull between the field and the current in the armature. The entry then splits motors into two broad kinds. One kind runs on direct current, the other on alternating current. Subtypes by winding and feed are listed for each kind.
britannica-1911-mull-fabric:
Mull is the subject of a 1911 Britannica entry on a word with three chief senses. The first sense is a soft plain muslin cloth of light build. England ships much of it to India for sale there. Some grades serve for summer dresses in the home trade too. The name is a short form of the Hindu word mulmul.

The second sense is stuff ground down to powder or small bits. A Scots snuff box is called a mull from its grinding wheel. The third sense is a Scots word for a point of land. Mull of Galloway and Mull of Kintyre are the named cases. That sense comes from a Gaelic word for a bare hill brow.
britannica-1911-panama-republic:
Panama is a republic of Central America given a long article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It fills the Isthmus of Panama, the neck of land between the two American continents. The Caribbean Sea bounds it on the north, Colombia on the east, the Gulf of Panama on the south, and Costa Rica on the west. It was once a part of Colombia.

Its area is set at from thirty-one to thirty-four thousand square miles. Its greatest length is four hundred and thirty miles, and its greatest width is one hundred and eighteen. Its land frontier is short, but its coasts are long, near five hundred miles on the Caribbean and more than seven hundred on the Pacific. The article maps the bays of the north coast, among them Almirante Bay and the lagoon of Chiriqui, with their isles and good anchorages.
britannica-1911-passaic:
Passaic, a city in New Jersey, fills a fast growth place entry in the 1911 Britannica. It sits at the head of boat reach on the Passaic River, south of Paterson. Two rail lines serve the town from east and west. Its folk count leapt to fifty four thousand seven hundred seventy three in nineteen ten. Near half of its folk were born in lands abroad.

East Passaic is a flat of mills fed by river and canal power. West Passaic is a home zone on hills with wide views. Cloth of wool and cotton made half the worth of its goods in nineteen oh five. Gum goods and wire goods add weight to that list. Dutch folk first set the town down in sixteen seventy nine.
britannica-1911-picnic:
Picnic is a form of party in which guests join a trip to a spot where a meal is eaten in the open air. The 1911 Britannica article marks what made a true picnic in the first half of the nineteenth century. Each guest had to bring a share of the food. At the start of that century a Picnic Society met in London. Its members supped at the Pantheon in Oxford Street. Lots were drawn to fix what part of the meal each one would supply.

The French form of the word is said to date from 1692. Its root is in doubt. The word may be a mere rhyming coinage, the article says. Or it may come from French words for pick and for a small coin. That doubt closes the short entry, which is as much word lore as party lore.
britannica-1911-power-transmission-hydra:
Hydraulic power transmission sends force through water held under high pressure. Its methods entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Bramah first proposed a broad system of such power in eighteen o two. Lord Armstrong set up a hydraulic crane at Newcastle in eighteen forty six.

Town water mains gave low and uneven pressure for the crane work. The accumulator, made in eighteen fifty, let firms use far higher pressure. A public supply began at Hull in eighteen seventy seven, then in London. A full system needs a central plant, mains, and machines that use pressure. Public systems must also track how much power each user takes.
britannica-1911-power-transmission-pneum:
Pneumatic power transmission means pressing air at one point and piping it to motors elsewhere. A 1911 Britannica technical entry opens by noting that every wind and sail shows the same idea in nature. The modern use is strict: air is squeezed, sent through tubes, and made to do work. Denis Papin made the first known trial, using a water wheel for power.

He sent pressed air through tubes to a distance for use at the far end. About 1800 George Medhurst took patents in England for like schemes in transport. He built a self moving carriage driven by stored pressed air as well. William Mann patented a compound air compressor in England in 1829.
britannica-1911-rubric: A rubric, in its first sense, is red earth or ochre used for colour. The word comes from a Latin term for red, by way of French. From that sense it passed to words written or printed in red letters, such as chapter headings. The term then passed to the passages so marked. Most of all it names the rules for how divine service is to be held, set in red in service books.
britannica-1911-sabellic:
Sabellic is a term for old tongues of central Italy, treated in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Mommsen first used the word for speech that was not Oscan and not Umbrian. Later study split most of that ground into more exact groups with their own names. What is left is a small set of eight or nine stone texts from the east coast.

Those texts are held to be the oldest of their kind on Italian soil. Their script is not yet read with sureness, and no full sense can be made of them. One odd trait is that the lines run back and forth and turn as they go. The longest text, from Grecchio, is kept at Naples and is thought to be a grave text.
britannica-1911-syndic:
What a syndic is takes up a term study in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word comes from Greek roots for one who helps in a court of law. It names an officer of state with powers that shift by land. It also names a chosen agent of a school, a guild, or a firm. The core sense in both uses is a delegate who acts for a body.

In Italy the sindaco heads a commune, much like a mayor. Paris guilds and the great school there had agents called syndics. At Cambridge the senate hands set tasks to boards of its own members. Those boards are syndicates, and their members are the syndics. Old French and Latin uses fill out the tale.
britannica-1911-tepic:
Tepic was a territory of Mexico on the Pacific coast. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives it 11,275 square miles of land. Its people numbered 150,098 in 1900. The live cone of Ceboruco rises in the west. Slopes and valleys wear dense woods. The low ground is rich and fit for crops of warm lands. Rain is heavy, and the air is hot, damp, and prone to fever.

The Santiago is the chief river of the territory. The Mezquital runs second in size. Coast farms yield sugar, cotton, tobacco, maize, and coffee. Fine woods and healing plants grow there too. Rich mines draw much work in the hills. The town of Tepic, the capital, held 15,488 people. It sits on a plateau near 3,000 feet up. The territory was cut from Jalisco in 1889. Its warlike folk were put under direct rule from the capital.
britannica-1911-traffic:
Traffic, in its proper sense, is the passing of goods between persons, towns, or countries. That is, it is commerce or trade in the plain sense. In current use the word is applied to goods and people in motion together. It covers vehicles and vessels passing to and fro on streets and roads. It also covers movement by sea, river, canal, and rail.

The origin of the word is obscure, the entry states at some length. Like forms occur in French, Italian, and Spanish tongues of the time. A use of a kindred Latin form is quoted from a treaty of thirteen eighty. That treaty was made between Milan and Venice in that year. Other guesses tie the word to sea crossing, to pouring wine, or to a coin. None of those guesses is held to be settled fact.
britannica-1911-triangle-music:
Triangle, in music, is a steel percussion tool of no fixed pitch. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica describes how it is made and played. It is a steel rod bent into a three sided shape. One corner stays open and slightly curved.

The tool hangs from a loop while in use. A player strikes it with a steel stick that has a wood handle. Fast blows at each end in turn make a roll effect. Loud and soft grades come from the force of the blow. Its tone is clear and ringing, the entry says. Small triangles sound best of all the sizes. Beethoven, Mozart, and Weber all wrote parts for it. Scores place it with the bass drum or on its own staff.
britannica-1911-tulle-fabric: Tulle is the subject of a short 1911 Britannica entry on a fine silk net fabric. In England the word is kept to a fine bobbin-net of silk. Such net is used for veils, scarves, and hat trim work. It also serves as trim on dresses. French use of the word is wider than English use. In France it means all machine-made lace built on that net. The word comes from the town of Tulle in France.
britannica-1911-turmeric:
Turmeric is the root of a plant of south Asia, treated in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The plant lives for years and belongs to the same order as ginger. Its root has been used since old times as a spice and as a dye. In Europe it serves chiefly as a dye, and as part of curry powder.

The root is cleaned and dried in an oven before sale. Trade sorts it by place, such as Madras, Bengal, and Java. Round bulbs come from the core of the root, and long fingers from its side shoots. The deep orange color comes from a part named curcumin. Paper dyed with the root turns reddish brown when an alkali touches it. That quirk has made turmeric a handy test for alkalinity since 1815.
by-pike-and-dyke-a-tale-of-the-rise-of-t:
G. A. Henty's By Pike and Dyke tells the rise of the Dutch Republic for boys. Henty calls the Dutch struggle unequal, obstinately maintained and long contested, as Holland and Zeeland fought for freedom to worship as they chose.

On one side stood the greatest power of the time, driven by a ruthless bigot bent on forcing his religion on the Netherlands or exterminating its people. On the other stood fishermen, sailors and farmers, broken into small communities, defended by stout hearts, a gallant prince and the sea itself as ally. Henty's hero fights through this dramatic contest, and young readers of historical adventure will find pike, dyke and siege vividly told.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-acrostic:
An acrostic, from Greek akros stichos, is a poem whose initial or final letters, syllables, or words form certain words or sentences. Epicharmus gets credit for its invention. Lactantius and Eusebius attribute the most remarkable example to the Erythraean sibyl. Its initial letters form Iesous Christos Theou houios soter, Jesus Christ, Son of God, Saviour, with cross in parentheses.

Without the doubtful parenthesis, those words yield the minor acrostic Ichthys, fish, the Lord's mystical symbol. The acrostic was supposedly quite popular among early Christians. Broadly, the name covers alphabetical or abecedarian poems, where successive verses begin with successive letters, as in Psalms 110, 111, and 118, Proverbs 31, and Lamentations. The entry points to Hebrew poetry and parallelism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-andras-meduli:
Andras Medulic, a Croatian painter and engraver, was born at Sibenik in Dalmatia in 1522 and died at Venice in 1582. Italians call him Medola, Medula, or Schiavone. Poor, he studied as a boy the pictures and woodwork in his town's churches, sketching from memory all he had seen. His father took him to Venice, to his godfather Rocco, a painter of little merit. Medulic worked from morning to evening for food and clothing.

He learned by studying and copying Parmigiano and Titian, gaining grace, lightness of touch, and animation of colour. Pietro Aretino, the Divine, welcomed and taught him. His works include the Baptism of Jesus for the Ruzzini. For the Pellegrini he painted Jesus at Emmaus and Pilate Washing his Hands. For the Gussoni he painted Saint Cecilia. He also painted Saint John scenes for the Priuli and the Descent of the Holy Ghost for the Foscarini.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apostolic-syn:
An apostolic syndic is a layman acting in the name and by authority of the Holy See, administers in civil law the goods and money alms meant for Franciscan convents. He thus provides for the brothers' needs. The rule of St. Francis forbade the Friars Minor, the Franciscans, to own property, either as a body or as individuals. At first literal observance was feasible, but as the order grew into a vast world body, countless difficulties arose and a fierce dispute over poverty lasted for centuries.

To guard the letter and spirit of complete renunciation, popes took ownership of all goods given to the friars onto themselves by a legal fiction. Friars thus counted legally as mere users, while the syndic handled the property in the pope's name. The entry explains how a vow of poverty survived inside a great organization through a lay trustee.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-authentic:
Authentic is a term this short entry uses in two distinct senses, and it warns readers not to blur them. In the first sense, a book or document is authentic when its contents carry a special authority, so that the work itself is called authentic. The entry points to the article on the Vulgate, the Latin Bible, for the full account of that first sense.

In the second sense, authentic simply means genuine: a work really comes from the author to whom it is ascribed. The articles on the single books of Sacred Scripture illustrate that second sense case by case. The whole entry is a signpost, sorting the two uses and sending readers to the fuller treatments elsewhere.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-balderic:
Balderic, or Baudry, was Bishop of Dol in France and a chronicler, born about 1050, who died in 1130. After brilliant study at Angers, he entered Bourgueil Abbey in Anjou and became abbot in 1079. In 1107 Pascal II gave him the pallium as Bishop of Dol. He attended the councils of his day, traveled several times to Rome, and left an account of an England journey.

He worked hard to reform monastic discipline and spent his last years in retirement. His most valuable work is the four-book History of Jerusalem, an account of the First Crusade. It rests in part on eyewitness testimony and went to Abbot Peter of Maillesais, a crusader, for correction. His other works include poems on England's conquest and Philip I's reign, lives of saints, and a letter on Breton manners.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-canon-in-musi:
In music a canon is the strictest of all contrapuntal forms. It repeats a given melody in its exact notes and rhythm by one or more voices. The voices enter not at once, but in turn, at a half, whole, or two measures' distance, on any interval. The word first named the law by which voices were to imitate the leading melody, since the imitations were not written out in notes.

The canon reached its greatest growth in the Netherlands School of 1450 to 1550. The Roman or Palestrina School gave it its fullest use, making it the vehicle of the highest ideals. Its calm regularity suited it above all to the finales of Mass settings, though Palestrina also built whole Masses, all five numbers, on the canon form.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-catholic:
Catholic comes from the Greek katholikos, built from katholou, meaning throughout the whole, or universal. In Greek classics and early Christian writers it carried a plain, non-church sense. Justin Martyr wrote of the catholic resurrection, and Irenaeus of the four catholic winds. Modern English would say general and principal instead. The word stood against the partial and the particular.

The phrase Catholic Church first appears in Ignatius of Antioch's letter to the Smyrnaeans, written about 110. There he wrote that where the bishop appears, the people should be present, just as where Jesus is, there is the universal Church. The article traces how the word's meaning shifted and was debated, and how it came to mark the Church at large rather than one local community.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charlemagne-a:
No civil ruler before or since matched Charlemagne's care for church music across his empire. His father Pepin had cared for the Church's song, but Charles acted with wider knowledge and a more thorough plan. His guiding rule on liturgy, as on all else, was conformity with Rome. Tradition says he brought his own chapel singers to Rome to learn at the fountainhead. In 774 he asked Pope Adrian I for two papal singers: Theodore went to Metz and Benedict to the singing school at Soissons.

Ekkehart IV, a tenth-century chronicler of St. Gall, reports two more singers from the same pope. Peter reached Metz, while Romanus, delayed at St. Gall by sickness, was allowed to stay there. The emperor's agents everywhere saw that his music orders were obeyed. He made liturgical music flourish across his vast domain and laid foundations for musical culture that remain potent today.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-choir-in-musi:
An entry on the choir in music, the body of singers charged with the musical parts of Church services. The Talmud attests the careful order of the Temple choir. The first Christians, worshipping with the Jews, used psalm singing with solo and congregational refrain, then, from the fourth century, alternating-chorus psalmody. Through the plainchant period, the choir's music split between solo and chorus chants, and after Constantine's conversion, lector schools trained boys in song.

Most famous was the Roman schola cantorum of Saint Gregory, whose boys came largely from orphanages and whose alumni included many seventh-century popes. Metz and Saint Gall followed in the eighth century, and after the musical staff arrived about 1100, they declined. Part music gradually replaced unison song. When Gregory the Eleventh returned from Avignon in 1377, he joined his choir to the schola cantorum as the College of Pontifical Chaplains, a more lay body.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-church-music:
A long entry on church music, the music used by order or approval of church authority in divine service to glorify God and edify the faithful. True religious music is exalted prayer, an expression of feeling in song, instruments, and action arranged by authority. Pagans, Jews, and Christians alike joined prayer, song, and instruments in public worship, forming an organic whole in which music serves on solemn occasions under proper regulation.

Church music shares melody, harmony, rhythm, tempo, dynamics, and tone colour with secular music, but all must fit the liturgical action, the words of prayer, and the devotion of hearts. When music stays an auxiliary and incentive to worship rather than a mere ornament, it lends ceremony its greatest splendour. When it asserts independence, it distracts. Fitting music lifts minds above everyday thoughts into a joyful mood fixed on sacred words.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cleric:
A cleric is a person legitimately received into the clergy's ranks. Clergy in the strict sense means the whole ecclesiastical hierarchy. For that he must have received at least the tonsure. By divine right the clergy form an order or state essentially distinct from the laity. Christ committed preaching, sacraments, and government of the flocks not to the faithful in general but to defined persons, the Apostles and seventy-two Disciples. The Keys serve as symbol of authority.

Clergy and laity were distinguished in New Testament times: Paul says the Holy Ghost placed bishops to rule the Church. Presbyters are continually distinguished from laity in the Pauline Epistles. The word comes from Greek kleros, a lot. Its restricted sense appears by the third century in Tertullian, Origen, and Clement of Alexandria. The Roman Pontifical calls clerics those whose lot is the Lord himself.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-commissary-ap:
William Fanning's entry defines a commissary Apostolic from the Latin Commissarius Apostolicus. A commissary is one who gains power from a lawful superior to judge a cause or gather facts about it. When the pope names such a delegate, he is called a commissary Apostolic. The Holy See's use of such delegates runs very ancient. Celestine I, early in the fifth century, sent Saint Cyril of Alexandria to judge Nestorius in the pope's name.

English history gives another famed case: Cardinals Wolsey and Campeggio heard Henry VIII's divorce case as papal representatives. Some Apostolic commissions stand permanently, such as the Roman congregations. A commissary's judgments and acts may be appealed to the pope himself. Custom now favors choosing commissaries from the place where they must inquire, judge, or carry out a mandate. Fanning thus sketches a tool of papal government, from single cases to standing offices.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cosmati-mosai:
Cosmati mosaic, a style of inlaid ornamental stonework, entered European decoration in the twelfth century through Laurentius of Anagni. Trained by Greek masters, he broke from Byzantine habit and set squares, circles, and parallelograms of dark marble, porphyry, and serpentine into pale marble grounds, framed by carved mouldings and bands.

His son Jacobus, sculptor, mosaic-worker, and architect, carried the craft forward, and four generations of the family followed it. Their pavements, ambos, screens, and cloisters still appear in Roman churches such as Santa Maria in Cosmedin and Santa Maria Maggiore, at Subiaco, Civita Castellana, and even Westminster Abbey.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dalmatic:
A liturgical entry defines the dalmatic, the outer vestment of the deacon at Mass, solemn processions, and benedictions, except those of penitential character such as Advent and Lent. Regarded from earliest times as a festal garment, bishops also wear it under the chasuble at solemn pontifical Mass. Priests need a special papal privilege to wear it.

At Rome and through Italy it is a knee-length robe with wide sleeves, closed in front and open at the sides. Outside Italy the sleeves are slit to form a scapular-like mantle. Two vertical stripes run from shoulder to hem, joined by cross-stripes. History traces it from Pope Sylvester I through mosaics at Ravenna and Rome to its Dalmatian secular origin, and a section covers its use in England.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dialectic:
A philosophy entry on dialectic, from the Greek for the art of converse, discussion, and dispute. At first it meant inquiry by dialogue, the question-and-answer method of Socrates and Plato. Since reasoning runs deeper than speech, the word then came to mean the art of inference itself, in effect logic. Aristotle praised Zeno as its master for his attacks on motion.

Widened again, dialectic named the whole science of reality, near to metaphysics, and its schools divide sharply. Plato sets ideas apart from sense. Aristotle and the Scholastics embody them in sense data. Kant traces the formal element of knowledge to the mind, and Hegel builds a monistic system from Kant. Theology used Aristotelian logic for natural truth, while the Church warns readers, with Colossians, against being cheated by philosophy and vain deceit.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-glagolitic:
Glagolitic, or Glagolitsa, is an ancient alphabet of the Slavic languages, named from the Slavonic glagol, a word, and glagolati, to speak. It is called in Russian bukvitsa, and its letters are the signs which spoke. A Catholic Encyclopedia article traces an alphabet that survives as a church script in Dalmatia and southern Croatia.

The order of its letters nearly matches the Cyrillic, but the letters themselves look nothing alike, except possibly in one or two cases. Some of the earliest Slavic manuscripts are written in Glagolitic. While Cyrillic held Bulgaria, Russia, and Galicia, the Roman alphabet drove Glagolitic out among the Bohemians, Slovenians, Moravians, and part of the Croatians. Yet the Adriatic Slavs kept the privilege of Mass and offices in their own tongue.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-godric:
Godric is the name of two Abbots of Croyland, both unlucky under Danish and royal exactions. Godric I, abbot from 870 to 941, succeeded Theodore, slain by the Danes, and was elected unanimously despite his reluctance. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows two abbacies worn down by seizure, ransom, and poverty.

Under Godric I, King Beorred seized monastery lands. His successor Ceowulf demanded a thousand pounds, reducing Croyland so low that at Godric's death only five monks remained. Godric II, abbot from 1005 to 1018, faced Ethelred's exactions, Danish ravages, and Sweyn's two ransoms in three months, until Cnut's accession in 1017 brought peace and some relief.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jan-milic:
Pre-Hussite reform preacher Jan Milic was born at Kromeriz in Moravia and died at Avignon on 29 June 1374. From 1358 to 1360 he served as registrar, and from 1360 to 1362 as corrector, at Emperor Charles IV's chancery. In 1363 he became priest and canon, probably also archdeacon, at Prague. Toward that year's end he renounced all dignities, began a life of extreme austerity, and fearlessly denounced clergy and laity vices.

At least once daily he preached at St Nicholas, later at St Egidius in Prague, in Latin for clergy and Czech for laity. After Conrad of Waldhausen's death in 1369, he preached daily at the cathedral in German. In spring 1367 he went to Rome, where the Inquisition imprisoned him because he had declared Antichrist had arrived. During imprisonment he wrote his Libellus de Antichristo, which he submitted to Pope Urban V. The entry presents a reformer before Hus.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jesuit-apolog:
Jesuit Apologetic answers the flood of charges laid against the Society of Jesus, exceptional for frequency and fierceness. Many claims, like blame for the Franco-Prussian War, the Dreyfus affair, the Panama scandal, or assassinations of popes and princes, are too absurd to merit notice. Yet cultured readers still credit them.

The entry refuses sweeping denial and injured tone as misplaced. Jesuits are fallible men, not angels, and nearly a hundred Jesuit writings reached the Roman Index. Against over one hundred twenty thousand Jesuit authors, that share is small, and no censure was of the graver kind. Judged by fair measure, the Society's faults prove human limits, not the vast conspiracies charged against it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-lucic:
John Lucic, or Lucius, was the Croatian historian called the father of Croatian history. Born early in the seventeenth century at Trojir in Dalmatia to an ancient noble family, he studied law at Padua and Rome. He took a doctorate in both laws and returned to Trojir in 1633, where he discovered the manuscript of the Cena Trimalchionis, later published at Padua in 1664.

At Trojir he began the researches into his native country's history that filled the rest of his life. Returning to Rome in 1654, he won the friendship of cardinals and supplied Ughelli with Croatian material for Italia Sacra. He presided over Rome's Illyrian congregation of Saint Jerome from 1663. He published his six books On the Kingdom of Dalmatia and Croatia at Venice in 1673, with Dalmatian inscriptions and notes, dying at Rome in 1679.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-logic:
Logic is the science and art of steering the mind toward clear thought, sound judgment, and valid inference. Its Greek root, logos, means reason, and Aristotle, its founder, called it analytic, while later writers settled on logic as the set name.

Some two hundred definitions have been offered, and the entry samples the chief ones. Port Royal logic of 1662 calls it the art of using reason well, a tag judged too narrow. Hegel, at the other extreme, made it the science of the pure idea, swallowing all reality. Between those poles the survey sorts formal rules, mental acts, and the limits of what reason can claim.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicolas-eymer:
Dominican inquisitor Nicolas Eymeric of Gerona policed doctrine in fourteenth-century Aragon with a zeal that made enemies. Born around 1320, he joined the Dominicans in 1334 and became grand inquisitor of Aragon in 1357 after his predecessor rose to cardinal.

Removed in 1360 to calm tempers, he returned to the office by 1366 and wrote tracts against Raymond Lully and other suspect teachings. His Directorium Inquisitorum later became a standard handbook, and he died at Gerona in 1399. His Directorium Inquisitorum, printed at Barcelona in 1503 and Rome in 1578, became the standard handbook. Opposition to his zeal ran so high that even his supporters could not keep him in office.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-passion-music:
Passion music traces how the Passion story, once merely read in Holy Week, became solemn chant. When that shift happened is not yet settled. By the eighth century the Mass deacon, in alb, declaimed the Passion before the altar on a fixed tone. Christ's words used the Gospel tone of inflections and cadences. One voice first carried the whole, until the twelfth century split it three ways.

Priest, or celebrant, took Christ's words, deacon took the Evangelist, or chronicler, and subdeacon took the crowd, or turba, with other speakers. Their pitches, interplay, and phrasing survive and can be heard in Holy Week in nearly any city church, though priests now sing all three parts. Later pages follow the chant into polyphony, oratorio, and Bach, and the rules that still govern its singing.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-de-jar:
Pierre de Jarric was a French Jesuit missionary writer, born at Toulouse in 1566. He entered the Society in December 1582 and taught philosophy and moral theology at Bordeaux for many years. His wish to join the missions unfulfilled, he served them with his pen, producing the Histoire des choses plus mémorables advenues tant ez Indes orientales, with parts about 1610 and in 1614.

The history pictures Jesuit missionary enterprise to 1610, chiefly in Portuguese spheres, with valuable data on colonial history, geography, and ethnography from Spanish and Portuguese reports and Guzman's and Guerreiro's histories. Dedicating the second part to Louis XIII, Jarric aimed to stir the French king toward efforts like Spain's and Portugal's. Frequently reprinted, notably in Martinez's Latin translation of 1615 to 1616, it remains useful. He died at Saintes on 2 March 1617.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-preacher-apos:
The preacher apostolic is a dignitary of the papal household. Paul IV set the post on a regular footing in 1555,. The change irked some prelates, since the preacher had to speak plain truths ere the papal court and mind them of their duties. Ere 1555, regular clergy, above all Franciscans, had at times preached ere the Roman court.

Later holders include Alonso Salmerón, companion of St Ignatius, and Francis Toleto, who held the post through seven pontificates. Marzatti, Cassini, and Barberini, Minor Capuchins, also held it, and Toleto, Marzatti, and Cassini rose to the cardinalate. By a Brief of 2 March 1753 to Father Michael Angelo Franceschi, Benedict XIV gave the dignity forever to the Capuchin Order,. Two late holders stand out: Lewis Micara of Frascati, later Rome's Cardinal Vicar, and Lewis of Trent, picked to preach at the Vatican Council's first session.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-prefect-apost:
Prefect apostolic, from Latin praefectus, one put over a thing, is the Holy See's way of ruling lands with no resident bishop dioceses. In recent centuries the Holy See has ruled such lands through prefects apostolic or vicars apostolic, and the lands are called prefectures apostolic and vicariates apostolic. The course is taken when local facts, such as hostile civil powers, leave doubt whether a bishop's see could stand for good.

A mere prefecture supposes the Church has grown but little there. Fuller growth leads to a vicariate apostolic, the middle stage between prefecture and diocese. A prefect apostolic ranks below a vicar, holds narrower powers, and as a rule lacks the bishop's stamp, which a vicar commonly bears. His work is to steer the mission in his care: setting missionaries, framing rules for sound management. He also holds rare faculties for cases else reserved to higher hands.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-prefecture-ap:
This entry lists prefectures apostolic raised or changed while the earlier volumes of the work were in print. Bar-el-Gazal was split from the Sudan's Vicariate Apostolic and made a prefecture on 30 May 1913, under the Sons of the Sacred Heart. Its bounds run north on the 10° north latitude, then along the Bar-el-Arab, Bar-el-Gazal, Bar-el-Gebel, and Lobat rivers.

Betafo was cut from Central Madagascar by a Decree of 15 May 1913, under the Missionary Fathers of La Salette. Korogo in equatorial Africa rose on 17 November 1911, when the Ivory Coast prefecture split in two, the north part forming Korogo under the Lyons Society of the African Missions. Pierre-Marie Kernivinen was named first prefect apostolic on 16 January 1912. The Mariana and Caroline prefectures were suppressed in 1911, save Guam, forming a new vicariate.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-prothonotary-:
The prothonotary apostolic belongs to the highest college of prelates in the Roman Curia, and the title also goes to honorary prelates on whom the pope bestows it with special privileges. This encyclopedia entry traces the office back to the seven regional notaries of ancient Rome, who grew into the supreme palace notaries of the papal chancery as the papal administration expanded. In the Middle Ages these officials stood so high that they often rose straight from the office to the cardinalate.

Sixtus the Fifth raised their number to twelve, but their weight faded until the office had nearly vanished by the French Revolution. Gregory the Sixteenth restored the college of real prothonotaries in 1838 with seven members. The entry sorts the four classes of the office, real and honorary, and notes that their privileges, dress and insignia were fixed in detail by a Motu Proprio, a pope's personal decree.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ptolemy-the-g:
Ptolemy the Gnostic, a second-century heretic and personal disciple of Valentinus, was probably still living about 180. This encyclopedia entry admits that almost nothing else certain is known of his life. Harnack's guess that he matches a Ptolemy mentioned by Saint Justin remains unproved. With Heracleon, Ptolemy led the Italian or Western school of Valentinian Gnosticism, and his writings survive only in fragments.

Two pieces remain. One is a fragment of a scriptural commentary, preserved by Irenaeus in his work Against Heresies. The other is a letter to Flora, a Christian lady, preserved by Epiphanius. Flora had asked where the Law of the Old Testament came from, and Ptolemy answered that it cannot simply be ascribed to the Supreme God. His system then builds a wild reading of John's Gospel prologue, finding there the first Ogdoad, a group of eight divine beings, of the higher world called the pleroma.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-roman-catholi:
Roman Catholic is a composite term whose history this entry traces, arguing that Catholic alone is the proper name. English speakers unwilling to admit the claims of the One True Church styled its members Roman Catholics in official documents. Anglicans commonly picture the whole Church as three branches, Roman, Anglo, and Greek.

The Oxford English Dictionary traces the composite term to the early seventeenth century. Use in the Spanish Match negotiations of 1618-24 helped fix it as a non-controversial legal term. Its earliest quoted instance is Sandys in 1605; Day contrasted Roman Catholiques and true Catholiques in 1615. The dictionary account is substantially right but incomplete: the term is older. Around 1580, English Catholics defended attendance at Protestant services under recusant fines. Persons, writing as Howlet, published reasons for refusing church, answered by the Puritan Wiburn's Checke, which uses Roman Catholic repeatedly.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-savaric:
Savaric, bishop of Bath and Glastonbury and cousin of Emperor Henry VI, died at Rome in 1205. Archdeacon of Canterbury in 1175 and of Northampton in 1180, he was elected bishop of Bath in 1191 while abroad with crusaders, and ordained priest at Rome the next year. His entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows a bold plan to join abbey and see.

Celestine III agreed to annex Glastonbury Abbey to Bath, making Savaric joint bishop of both. The monks objected and appealed to Rome, but lost in 1196. Though Savaric had been a hostage at Mainz for Richard I's ransom, the freed king backed the monks, and only in 1199, after a forcible entry, was Savaric enthroned in the abbey. A second appeal to Innocent III failed, and in 1202 he was again declared abbot, becoming a generous benefactor.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-aldric:
St. Aldric was bishop of Le Mans under Louis the Pious, born about 800 and dead at Le Mans on 7 January 856. This entry follows a youth raised at the courts of Charlemagne at Aachen and of his son Louis, esteemed by both monarchs. At twenty-one he withdrew to Metz and became a priest, only for Louis to recall him as guide of his conscience.

Nine years after ordination he became bishop of Le Mans, famed for exalted virtue and for civic spirit. He built aqueducts and churches, restored monasteries, and ransomed captives. In the civil wars after Louis's death, loyalty to Charles the Bald cost him his see and drove him to Rome, until Gregory IV restored him. The entry closes with his work as deputy of the Council of Aachen.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-dominic:
Dominic founded the Order of Preachers, the Dominicans, and this long entry traces a Castilian canon who became one of the Church's great organizers. Born at Calaroga about 1170 to Felix Guzman and Joanna of Aza, he served as sub-prior and then prior of the reformed chapter at Osma. Passing through Toulouse in 1203, he saw the ruin worked by the Albigensian heresy. The Catholic Encyclopedia article of 1913 follows him to his death on 6 August 1221.

From that shock grew his plan: a band trained to preach true doctrine and root out error. Bishop Foulques of Toulouse gave the group a fixed home at Fanjeaux, and in 1215 set it up as a diocesan congregation. Dominic dreamed bigger, of a world order carrying its message everywhere. The entry shows that dream taking shape, house by house, through preaching, study, and sheer persistence.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-dubric:
Dubric ranks among the greatest of Welsh saints, yet his life reaches us only through a book written five centuries after his death. Bishop and confessor, he died in 612 and is pictured holding two crosiers for his rule over Caerleon and Llandaff. The Catholic Encyclopedia article of 1913 treats the life of about 1133, written for the moving of his relics, as tradition rather than history.

That account makes him son of Eurddil, daughter of a prince of Ergyng, born at Madley on the Wye. A child prodigy, he grew into a scholar famed across Britain and founded a college at Henllan. The entry lets readers enjoy the story while knowing its limits: genuine memories may hide inside, but five hundred years stand between the saint and his biographer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tepic:
Tepic is a Mexican diocese, suffragan of Guadalajara. It covers its federal state of 10,951 square miles, plus a few parishes in western Jalisco, with 171,837 people in 1910. The bishop's city stands 3,146 feet high with 16,805 people. Nuño de Guzman discovered and devastated the land in 1530, treating natives cruelly. Plots and insurrections followed, and to check them some were hanged, others imprisoned, and many tortured for confessions. Despair drove many Indian carriers to hang themselves in groups of ten.

Spanish towns like Tepic and Compostela already stood when services began, thriving after Guadalajara's bishopric in 1548. The mountain Nayarit peoples stayed refractory to civilization and Christianity. Franciscans Caballero and Ramirez failed to penetrate the mountains in 1668, and Father Margil retreated in 1711. Nayarit belonged to Durango from 1620 until its bishop gave the mission onward. The diocese now holds a seminary with 72 students, 23 schools, six colleges with 3,000 pupils, and three Protestant churches.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-dominican:
Eastern half of Hispaniola, the Dominican Republic, is the island nation surveyed here. Also called San Domingo or Santo Domingo, it forms the larger, eastern division of Haiti island, second of the Greater Antilles, some 18,045 square miles. A winding line from Yaqui River's mouth in the north to near Point Beata in the south divides it from Haiti republic in the west.

Atlantic washes its north shore, Caribbean its south, Mona Passage parts it from Porto Rico in the east. Spanish-speaking Dominicans, mostly of mixed African and European descent, contrast with French-speaking, purely African Haitians. Climate varies, San Domingo city enjoys health despite bad sanitation, and church history, schools, and trade fill out the portrait.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-religion-:
Was Shakespeare Catholic? That question drives this cautious entry, which begins with a warning from Milton's case. Protestant authority claimed after Milton's death that he had professed Catholicism, on his brother's supposed testimony, yet the claim proves certainly untrue. Caution must therefore govern Shakespeare too, dead over seventy years before Archdeacon Davies wrote that he died a papist.

Davies, an Anglican clergyman in neighbouring Gloucestershire, had no clear motive to invent the note and may echo local tradition. Independent evidence adds weight: John Shakespeare, the poet's father, left signs of Catholic sympathy. Plays, sonnets, and Stratford records are sifted, but the entry stops short of a verdict, leaving probability, not proof.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tunic:
A vestment shaped like a sack, closed at the top except for a slit to pass over the head. It has sleeves or side slits for the arms. A tunic reaching the feet is called a gown tunic. One without sleeves or with short sleeves is called a colobium, and one leaving the right shoulder free an exomis.

In liturgical language the tunic, or tunicella, is the subdeacon's upper vestment, matching the deacon's dalmatic in form, ornament and use. The bishop puts it on the newly ordained subdeacon with the words about the tunic of joy. Over time it grew shorter, gained side slits, and came to be made regularly of silk.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-vicar-apostol:
A vicar apostolic is a prelate who acts in the pope's place, and the entry distinguishes three uses of the title. In the early Church, popes charged resident bishops, such as the archbishops of Arles for Gaul and Thessalonica for Illyria, with watching over church affairs in a region.

Later the title covered prelates commissioned to administer vacant dioceses, or sees whose bishops were hindered from ruling. With the powers of a vicar capitular and sometimes extraordinary faculties from their brief of appointment. Most commonly it means the bishop sent to govern a missionary region where no regular hierarchy yet exists, holding delegated, not ordinary, power, with no cathedral or chapter of his own.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-vicariate-apo:
This extra article gathers vicariates apostolic erected or changed too recently for the encyclopedia's earlier volumes. It is a list of new missionary districts rather than a single story, running from Bagamoyo and Banguelo in equatorial Africa. Their boundaries were redrawn in 1913, through Basutoland in South Africa, raised from prefecture to vicariate in 1909, to the Ivory Coast, raised in 1911.

Each entry gives the same plain facts a missionary in charge would need: date of erection, the religious order in charge, the first vicar apostolic. The latest returns cover priests, churches, schools, Catholics, and catechumens. Basutoland, for instance, closed 1912 with twenty-three Oblate priests, twenty-one churches and stations, seventeen schools, about ten thousand Catholics and eight hundred catechumens among four hundred thousand people.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-visitors-apos:
Visitors apostolic are officials church lawyers commonly class with papal legates, differing from other apostolic delegates chiefly because their mission is transient and quite short. In ancient times popes generally inspected dioceses through nuncios or delegates, at times sending special visitors even in the early ages, while today nuncios serve a diplomatic rather than visiting role.

Visitors are now deputed for special crises, not at fixed intervals. They inspect the Church's state in the country entrusted to them and report to the Holy See, sometimes with the same attention to detail as a bishop's visitation. They may also visit provinces of a religious order whenever the pope judges it useful or necessary. In every case the pope, through delegates, exercises his supreme and direct rule over every part of the Church. The visitor's exact powers come only from his brief, and his office ends once he has submitted his report.
charles-dickens-and-music:
James T. Lightwood, author of a book on hymn-tunes, published his study of Dickens and music in a first edition of 1912. Tom Pinch at the organ makes the frontispiece. Seven chapters ask what music meant to a novelist who filled his books with songs, singers, and instruments of every kind.

Early chapters sort flutes, organs, and guitars, and odd instruments besides. Church music gets a chapter of its own. Songs and singers take two more. Lightwood explains the Christy Minstrels and the Jim Crow craze along the way. Lists at the back name every song Dickens mentioned, index the instruments and characters, and catalogue music titles founded on his people.
children-s-rights-a-book-of-nursery-logi:
Kate Douglas Wiggin published her essays on children in 1892, calling them a book of nursery logic. A prefatory note admits the papers began as talks to societies for child training. Three essays are by her sister, Nora A. Smith. Wiggin opens by asking her window-washer, Dennis, what he thinks of children's rights. He reckons children take them anyway.

Plays, playthings, and reading get one essay each. What shall children read is the practical question. The kindergarten earns two essays, one tying it to social reform, one to the public school. How shall we govern our children argues for natural penalties over fear. The unruly child leaves the play circle until sympathy returns. Other people's children close the argument.
chopin-the-man-and-his-music:
James Huneker's Chopin: The Man and His Music divides its subject into a life and a survey of the works. Poland and youthful ideals open the first part. Paris in the maelstrom, then England, Scotland, and the grave at Père la Chaise follow. Huneker calls Chopin's violence psychic, a warfare waged inside the soul.

The second part takes the music kind by kind. The studies are titanic experiments; the preludes, moods in miniature. Nocturnes become night and its melancholy mysteries, and the ballades faery dramas. Polonaises sound as heroic hymns of battle, mazurkas as dances of the soul. Huneker writes with a critic's extravagance and a pianist's knowledge. His Chopin is the poet and psychologist of the piano, judged piece by piece with love and no restraint.
composition-rhetoric:
Composition-Rhetoric, by Stratton D. Brooks, is a school textbook dedicated to Marcia Stuart Brooks, whose teaching first showed the authors that composition could become a delight. Part I begins where its theory begins: with ideas. Expression of ideas arising from experience comes first, then ideas furnished by imagination, then ideas acquired through language.

The whole composition, letter writing, and poetry complete the first part. Part II teaches the four forms in turn: description, narration, exposition, and argument. An appendix reviews grammar, figures of speech, and the rhetorical features of the sentence, with lists of synonyms and words for exercise. The text opens frankly: we all enjoy talking, yet writing comes harder, especially on assigned topics in which we are not interested.
dave-darrin-at-vera-cruz-fighting-with-t:
A naval tale for boys by H. Irving Hancock fills Dave Darrin at Vera Cruz. Ensign Dave Darrin and his chum Dan Dalzell are now officers, keen for fight or frolic. Twenty-four chapters carry them to Mexico.

Lieutenant Cantor, a brother officer with an evil eye, makes trouble from the start. Dave disobeys orders in a rescue and waits in fear for his captain's verdict. The captain weighs Dave's report, Cantor's, and the words of Coxswain Riley and Corporal Ross. Sniping at Vera Cruz, a traitor in the service, and a skirmish at the Diligencia fill the action chapters. Hancock wrote the set for boys who dreamed of the fleet.
deductive-logic:
St. George Stock's Deductive Logic is a textbook written to represent the logic taught in the Oxford schools of its day. Stock, of Pembroke College, Oxford, stresses clearness and consistency above novelty, and says plainly that he has kept only a few new points while following received teaching.

The book trains a student to judge whether an argument truly follows from its starting points, the heart of deductive reasoning, which moves from general rules to particular cases. Terms, propositions and the valid forms of argument are set out in order, with the faults that make reasoning fail. Stock writes for beginners who need a steady, teachable account rather than a display of original theory. Students of philosophy or of older university curricula will find it a clear window onto Oxford logic.
doe-osti-1396238-arm-data-oriented-metri:
A software package for testing climate models against ARM data fills this technical report, numbered DOE/SC-ARM-TR-202 and revised in October 2020. C Zhang, S Xie, and C Tao wrote it, all at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory. Support came from the Department of Energy's Office of Science, through its biological and environmental research arm.

The package builds metrics and diagnostics from ARM observations, then scores models with them. One section uses simulations from twenty-three models in the CMIP5 atmospheric-only runs, covering the years 1979 to 2008. Cloud fraction from the Active Remote Sensing of Clouds product is among the data streams tabulated, by site and by month and hour. The report is a user's guide to a named evaluation tool.
doe-osti-17076349-vulnerability-of-power:
Closeout report ORNL/TM-2026/4934, dated September 2026, sums up a grid modernization project on how electromagnetic threats could hurt power plants. DaHan Liao, Yilu Liu, and colleagues from Oak Ridge, Lawrence Livermore, and the University of Tennessee studied pulses from high altitude nuclear bursts, solar storms, and deliberate interference.

Much past work covered transformers and lines, while plant vulnerability lagged. The team estimated equipment exposure with field measurements plus models, and inspected generating sites including a TVA hydropower plant. They also probed newer gear such as solar inverters and distributed units out in the open. Shielding tests and many technical papers came out of the work, which the closeout lists in full.
doe-osti-17120802-m2mt-26la0301031-enabl:
Khanh Dang and Laurent Capolungo of Los Alamos report fiscal 2026 progress on qualifying 3D printed 316H stainless steel for reactor use through simulation, issued 2 October 2026. Printed parts differ from wrought steel, with columnar grains, cell structures, and pores. Qualifying them by testing alone is slow, so a crystal plasticity model stands in for part of the evidence.

Work this year calibrated the model first on printed material measured in the lab, then on solution annealed wrought 316H data. Irradiation microstructure findings fed hardening terms into the model. Point defect and in situ creep calculations followed. Chapters detail dislocation glide and climb, diffusion driven by point defects, and density evolution. Tensile and creep responses are then predicted for unirradiated and irradiated printed steel.
doe-osti-17138815-anomaly-detector-robus:
Benjamin Blakely, Yeni Li, Akshay Dave, and Richard Vilim of Argonne stress test anomaly detectors for reactor plants, in report ANL-26/38 dated September 2026. All work used recorded telemetry from a liquid metal research facility. No attacks were run and no scanning was done: every disturbance was synthesized offline from real data.

Part one runs eleven detectors, from classic statistics to neural networks and causal learners, against eleven disturbance kinds at four severity levels, for 3,080 test cases. Three levels stay inside behavior the plant has shown; the fourth goes beyond it. Part two uses physics consistency relations to tell real equipment wear from faked signals, shown on a pump loop and a cold trap. Part three delivers the telemetry collector and client library.
doe-osti-17152729-documentation-of-monar:
Sijay Huang, Benjamin Liu, John Barber, and a Los Alamos team document MONARCH, a software application for semiconductor device simulation, in a report issued 6 October 2026. The code models PiN diodes, a basic light emitting and sensing structure, under both steady heat and changing temperature. A radiation damage model tracks how defects build up and drain carriers over time.

Chapters cover installation, then each model in turn: recombination paths in the diode, laser diode additions, heat flow coupling, and damage physics down to cluster dynamics and carrier reactions. Test cases walk through a one dimensional diode example, from mesh and variable setup to initial conditions. The document serves as the reference for new users setting up runs.
doe-osti-2572521-maximum-likelihood-esti:
Tutorial note LA-UR-25-27249, by Terry R. Adams of Los Alamos and issued July 21, 2025, teaches the basics of maximum likelihood estimation. The method picks the distribution parameters that make the data actually observed most probable. Adams sets it beside rival approaches such as ordinary least squares regression and the generalized method of moments, then weighs what it does well and where it falls short.

The worked example is a two-parameter gamma distribution. Readers see the likelihood function built, the log-likelihood formed, and the estimates derived step by step. The estimator is then run on sampled data sets so its behavior is visible, not just asserted. Appendices supply the Python code used to draw the samples and to optimize one parameter numerically. The note is written as a compact reference for staff who need the method's logic without a textbook's bulk.
doe-osti-2583544-an-lisis-de-tareas-del-:
Informe técnico NREL/TP-7A40-92776, by Jal Desai and Cory Chovanec, is the Spanish version of the Energy Auditor job task analysis. The auditor is the weatherization program's scout: the person who walks a home, finds where it wastes energy, and prescribes the fix. This text lists the auditor's tasks in full, from safety checks on combustion gear to HVAC review.

Pros on the EA-QCI design panel, with Professional Testing, Inc., vetted and refreshed the Energy Auditor credential and the linked Quality Control Inspector award that this analysis supports. Task analyses are the base texts of certification: exam plans, course outlines, and skill standards all trace back to them. Issuing this one in Spanish serves the bilingual crews who do much of America's weatherization work. Funds came from the Weatherization Assistance Program under its home energy pros project.
doe-osti-2588548-comstock-measure-docume:
Marlena Praprost of the National Renewable Energy Laboratory wrote this measure documentation, NREL/TP-5500-95015, dated September 2025. Inside ComStock, the national commercial building stock model, this measure replaces fossil fuel boilers with electric resistance boilers. It is a simple electrification swap. Its costs and savings hinge on local fuel prices.

The method mirrors the ComStock pattern: a 2018 baseline stock, one measure applied, and an end-use savings shape as the product. That shape is a time-series profile of energy change by end use and fuel, with annual totals. Price assumptions get explicit treatment. Fuel costs are estimated from 2022 Energy Information Administration averages by state. Residential heating oil and propane prices stand in where commercial prices are not published. They are converted to dollars per thousand BTU using standard heat contents. The full dataset is public through the ComStock data lake and viewer, filterable down to a single county.
doe-osti-2589310-ecohydrological-control:
Mariah Carbone of Northern Arizona University led this final report on award DE-SC0021139, covering work from August 2020 to August 2024. The project studied soil breathing in the East River watershed near Crested Butte, Colorado. The central question was how snow and rain water change the carbon dioxide leaving the soil, and which sources produce that gas.

Field stations were placed at four sites along a slope on Snodgrass Mountain, in aspen and spruce-fir forest with different snowpack and water table depths. Sensors tracked carbon dioxide in the soil profile around the clock. Radiocarbon measurements split the surface gas between root respiration and microbes breaking down soil matter. Plant growth and microbe records added context. Results ground a larger follow-on study of mountain watershed carbon.
doe-osti-2589909-catalytic-difunctionali:
A final project summary on award DE-SC0023205, led by Keary Engle at Scripps Research and Will Gutekunst at Georgia Tech, reports a catalytic shortcut from plain hydrocarbons to designer polymers. Nickel catalysts add two groups across cyclic dienes, ring-shaped molecules with two double bonds, in one step. The products are new ring-shaped monomers for a polymerization method called ROMP.

Mechanism studies and catalyst tuning gave a gram-scale route to selective double arylation, and swapping the boron partner widened it to aryl-plus-alkyl products. The aryl-alkyl monomers polymerize faster, thanks to lower strain in the eight-membered ring during reaction. Resulting polymers carry a set sequence and shape, and sulfonated versions were tried as fuel cell membranes. Routes to break the polymers back down to monomers support recycling.
doe-osti-2997855-electrochemical-denitra:
Savannah River National Laboratory year one report SRNL-STI-2025-00233 is dated September 2025. Dylan Rodene, Edelmy Marin Bernardez, Matthew Gordon, and a large team open a three-year project on electrochemical waste treatment for Hanford. The EDCGe system would use electricity to destroy nitrates and organics in high-level waste feed while generating caustic the process needs. Cutting nitrate early eases off-gas worries downstream.

Year one highlights include proof-of-concept denitration in benchtop cells at high voltage and flow cell versions of the same chemistry. Polymer ion-exchange membranes were used in the bench cells, while ceramic sodium-conducting membranes were made by 3D printing and tape casting. A subcontractor assessed engineering-scale versions, and a ruthenium on alumina catalyst was picked as the baseline for off-gas treatment. Flow modeling in ANSYS Fluent, with water and aluminum as the model fluids and solid, supports the cell design.
doe-osti-2997856-fy25-progress-report-sr:
Savannah River National Laboratory fiscal year 2025 progress report is dated 23 September 2025. Stephanie Gamble, Anna D'Entremont, Jason Bakos, and co-authors advance software that spots corrosion and cracks in plutonium storage canisters. The 3013 canisters are inspected by laser microscope and a wide-area 3D measurement system, producing huge image files no human team can scan fully. The work is a joint effort with the University of South Carolina.

Machine learning models read height, color, and grayscale maps from those scans after training on labeled examples. Crack hunting has taken priority over broader corrosion signs such as pitting, at program direction. Scoring uses precision and recall per feature, with crack positive rate naming the share of true cracks found. Better labeling tools were built this year, since labeled data is the bottleneck for every model gain. The surveillance program gains a tireless first reader for its weld inspections.
doe-osti-2999104-ultra-high-bandwidth-ul:
Daniel Dominguez and Katherine Kearney of Sandia describe a new X ray sensor in report SAND2025-12408, printed September 2025. Tests at the Z Machine, Sandia's pulsed power facility, judge weapon parts partly by X ray yield and power. Today's calorimeters read the warmth an X ray burst leaves in a tantalum plate, through a temperature probe. Such probes are cheap but carry errors, and are too slow for the fastest detail.

The replacement is a photonic integrated circuit, a light circuit etched on a chip. Its heart is a Mach-Zehnder interferometer, which splits light and recombines it so small changes shift the signal. Low confinement waveguides carry the light with the reach the design needs. The report works through the maths, the chip layout, and three rounds of fabrication in Sandia's silicon fab. The goal is a sensor with high bandwidth and dynamic range for shock work.
doe-osti-3000175-multiscale-modeling-and:
Mohan Sankaran and Davide Curreli of the University of Illinois wrote this final report for grant DE-SC0023404. It covers September 2022 to August 2024, on the meeting point of plasma and liquid. Cold atmospheric plasma touching water can drive chemistry without catalysts, useful for water treatment, medicine and making chemicals. Yet the border zone, where excited gas species dive into liquid and react, hides most of its steps from direct view.

The team attacked the gap from both sides. Laser diagnostics probed which species the plasma makes and how they cross the interface. Multiscale computer models, spanning the gas, the boundary and the liquid, simulated the non-equilibrium reaction chemistry that follows. Together the two views aim to name the pathways plain instruments miss. The report gathers the models, the measurements and what they jointly reveal about this busy, thin frontier.
doe-osti-3002240-feasibility-assessment-:
Anant Raj, Brandon Schreiber, Pradeep Ramuhalli, and Christian M. Petrie test a damage-finding idea in Oak Ridge report ORNL/TM-2025/4070, dated August 2025. The idea is electrical impedance tomography: inject small currents through a part, measure the voltages, and compute an image of its interior. The parts of interest are graphite components for microreactors, where cracks are hard to spot from outside.

The team modeled the method with finite-element software and open-source tomography tools. They weighed electrode layouts and reconstruction math against the shapes graphite parts actually take. Finding damage without cutting the part open would help operators judge component health during service. The report closes with what the simulations say about sensitivity, and what a bench demonstration would need to prove next.
doe-osti-3004329-nano-and-earth-science-:
Kevin Leung leads a Sandia and university team in report SAND2025-14101, printed September 2025, on recycling electric vehicle batteries. Cobalt supply is tight, and standard recycling smelts or dissolves whole cathodes at high energy cost. The team borrows from nanoscience and earth science instead: peel lithium cobalt oxide cathodes into nanosheets, then swap ions in water.

In the nanosheets, cobalt ions exchange with nickel ions from solution, upcycling the material toward nickel-bearing cathodes. Raman and X-ray spectroscopies, electron microscopy, and diffraction tracked the swap. Heat treatment reassembled the sheets into working cathode material. A companion study found surfaces that prefer nickel over cobalt from mixed solutions, a separation step the supply chain needs. Density functional theory calculations guided both halves of the work.
doe-osti-3005718-non-abelian-quasipartic:
Yuli Lyanda-Geller of Purdue University gives the final report for DOE grant SC0010544, covering work from 2013 to 2024 under two successive titles. The through-line is exotic quantum states: non-Abelian quasiparticles and topological superconductivity, pursued for quantum information science. Such states could store information in a form naturally protected from local noise.

The report summarizes progress on hole systems with spin-3/2 carriers in two dimensions, and on hybrid superconductor-semiconductor structures. Majorana fermions and parafermions, the excitations that make topological computing conceivable, were studied in electron and hole systems alike. Quantum Hall physics served as the breeding ground for much of the theory. The record lists years of invited talks and community uptake of the group's methods. It is a capstone for a long theory program rather than a single experiment.
doe-osti-3009956-elucidating-processes-c:
Final report for DOE award DE-SC0019172, by Kerri Pratt of the University of Michigan, covers Arctic atmospheric aerosol work from September 2018 to August 2025. The gap addressed was stark: almost no single-particle chemistry data across the full Arctic year.

The APUN campaign sampled at Utqiagvik, Alaska from October 28 to December 22, 2018, through the polar night, logging over 500,000 individual particles in six weeks. Delayed sea ice freeze-up let local sea spray, with high cloud-forming potential, dominate the fall air. Aboard the icebreaker Polarstern, the MOSAiC expedition then collected daily particles from November 2019 to October 2020, finding sea salt and marine organics year-round.
doe-osti-3012683-twenty-third-conference:
Hosted by the High Energy Physics group at the University of Cincinnati, this short final report covers the Twenty-third Conference on Flavor Physics and CP Violation, held June 2 to 6, 2025. The conference is a leading meeting in flavor physics, the study of how particle types transform, and CP violation, a matter-antimatter imbalance. Sessions split between the Queen City Club downtown and the university campus.

Attendance drew 56 regular participants and 40 graduate students, with speakers from China, Europe, India, Japan, Canada, and the United States. The program held 37 invited plenary talks and 30 parallel talks, with results from Belle II, LHCb, DUNE, and other major experiments. DOE funds helped rent the facility and cut the graduate student fee to 80 dollars against a regular 400 dollars.
doe-osti-3013461-national-cancer-institu:
Oak Ridge report ORNL/SPR-2025/4243, by Heidi Hanson, Dakotah Maguire, Janet Agbaje, and Chad Melton, dated September 2025, sets out the National Cancer Institute's exposomic linkage protocol. Exposomics studies how lifetime environmental exposures shape disease. To link exposures to cancer patients, researchers first need each person's residential history, where they lived and when.

The protocol builds continuous address timelines from messy records with duplicates, overlaps, and gaps. A residential summary table holds one record per person, with quality flags grading how complete the history is. The current file covers 1,552,264 records from cancer registries in Kentucky, New Jersey, Louisiana, and Iowa. The document also specifies geographic resolution levels and privacy-conscious data fields for later exposure linkage.
doe-osti-3014397-creating-and-interfacin:
James Rondinelli of Northwestern University led this final technical report for award DE-SC0019356. It covers September 2019 to September 2025. Co-investigators sat at the University of Chicago, MIT, and UC Berkeley. The project created designer chemical qubits. These are molecules engineered to hold quantum information and to sense their surroundings. Molecular color centers can be tuned by chemistry atom by atom. Solid-state defects cannot.

One thread modeled Stark shifts and vibrational coupling in molecular color centers. The aim was to predict electric-field response. The forecasts say polar, heteroleptic color centers can reach electric-field sensing on par with diamond NV centers. Complementary measurements identified which structural motifs maximize responsiveness. The team aimed these sensors at strongly correlated materials, two-dimensional magnets, and ferroelectrics. Conventional probes struggle to reach those targets.
doe-osti-3015897-extreme-wave-computatio:
Will Wiley was the National Laboratory of the Rockies technical contact for this January 2026 cooperative research final report, NLR/TP-5700-98141, under agreement CRD-24-24954. Elie Al Shami is also named on the record. The subject is the CETO wave energy converter, a machine that makes electricity from ocean waves. The question was how the machine holds up when extreme waves hit it.

The work used computational fluid dynamics, computer simulation of water flow, checked against model test data supplied by the participant. From those tests the team built a test matrix for the numerical runs. Loads from the fluid simulation then fed a one-way structural analysis, so wave forces could be mapped onto the machine's parts.
