Designers get survival load numbers for a class of storms that test tanks cannot easily reproduce.
doe-osti-3022330-conceptual-design-of-a-:
INL report INL/RPT-25-87433, by Nicolas Woolstenhulme and twelve colleagues, lays out a conceptual design for a water tank critical facility. The site is the planned SPARC complex. SPARC's horizontal split table suits solid-core experiments. But the host building began life as a pool-type research reactor. That makes it a natural home for a second capability: critical experiments with full-size light water reactor fuel bundles standing in water.

The design study reviews historical water tank critical experiments, then develops a critical assembly tank concept the authors judge simple to build and deploy. Supporting systems are considered too. They include receipt and upending of commercial fuel bundles with industry containers, and crane handling into storage racks or the tank. A gamma scanning strategy uses brief low-power runs under 100 watts to map fission product activity rod by rod.
doe-osti-3022559-stellarator-theory-and-:
A Columbia University closeout report by Allen Boozer sums up DOE award DE-FG02-95ER54333 on stellarator theory and non-axisymmetric shaping, for May 2023 to April 2025. In two years the grant produced eleven papers in major refereed journals. The work was done with graduate student Todd Elder. It covered the three-dimensional magnetic geometry that makes stellarators confine plasma without a large internal current.

Topics span divertor concepts and transport theory. Post-award results noted in the report include a paper on microturbulent transport. Such transport is usually assumed intrinsically ambipolar, but the paper argues an important exception. Electrostatic microturbulence generates magnetic perturbations at finite plasma pressure, and turbulent magnetic fields are inherently chaotic, breaking magnetic surfaces. The report is candid that the renewal was not funded and that the work went on during a sabbatical while a funding decision was pending.
doe-osti-3023847-the-poisson-tensor-comp:
Daniel M Dunlavy, Richard B Lehoucq, Carolyn D Mayer, and Arvind Prasadan of Sandia National Laboratories introduce a new statistical estimator in SAND2026-18285R. Counting samples of a multi-variable distribution into histogram bins leaves many bins nearly empty, which makes plain histograms shaky. Their Poisson tensor completion estimator fills those sparse bins by exploiting links between samples.

The key move is to treat histogram bins as a space partitioning of counts from a non-homogeneous Poisson process. A low-rank Poisson tensor decomposition then completes the mean measure over all bins, even those holding few or no samples, and the estimates come out non-negative by construction. For sub-Gaussian distributions, the authors show a substantial gain over standard histogram estimators, resting on the concentration of norm phenomenon.
doe-osti-3028184-variable-effects-of-dis:
William Mikhel James of Los Alamos National Laboratory reviews what dispersed nanoparticles do to triboelectric nanogenerators in LA-UR-26-22715, issued April 6, 2026. These generators harvest energy from contact and motion between two films, an attractive power source for the shrinking wearable devices the paper opens with. Sprinkling nanoparticles into the polymer layers is a popular tuning trick, and the title promises the honest version: the effects vary.

The analysis adapts Maxwell's equations to these systems with an added surface polarization term for the time-varying field the moving triboelectric charges create. Nanoparticles then enter through several channels at once: porosity, surface area, surface charge density, and the field distribution inside the films. Together those set charge generation efficiency and how long the charge is retained, which explains why one filler can help and another hurt.
doe-osti-3029958-technology-maturation-p:
Haiqing Lin of the University at Buffalo wrote this technology maturation plan, dated January 2026 and revised in April, under award DE-FE0032209. It maps the road from lab proof to market for catalytic membrane reactors that make hydrogen from waste biomass. The reactors use carbon molecular sieve hollow fibers to pull hydrogen out during the water-gas shift step. That trick sidesteps the reaction natural ceiling on turning carbon monoxide into carbon dioxide and hydrogen.

Two parts must mature together: the heat-stable membranes and new carbon dioxide tolerant catalysts made by a flame aerosol route. Target feedstocks include municipal solid waste, legacy coal waste, and waste plastics that would otherwise be burned or buried. The plan walks through readiness levels as the National Energy Technology Laboratory defines them for fossil energy work.
doe-osti-3343334-understanding-the-role-:
Deborah Levin of the University of Illinois reports final results under grant DE-SC0021348, covering September 2020 to August 2024, on waves that ride inside ion beams. When electrons are fired into a fast ion beam to neutralize its charge, lone wave packets called electrostatic solitary waves, or electron holes, can form. The team modeled when and why they appear, using their 3D particle-in-cell code CHAOS and checking it against earlier published runs.

The test beam was argon ions at 427 kilometers per second, fed electrons at 2 electronvolts in a full Maxwellian spread. Two shapes were run: a flat 2D case 0.375 centimeters across, and a full 3D case with walls at zero volts. Probe traces at 20 centimeters matched the benchmark, and phase plots show the holes marching along the beam in both shapes.
doe-osti-3346767-prairie-state-generatin:
Richard Dessenberger, Roland Okwen, and Mansour Khosravi of the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign model carbon burial at a power plant in report DOE-UIUC-31892-14, issued May 4, 2026. The Prairie State Generating Company site near Marissa, in Washington County, Illinois, could take 162.5 million tonnes of industrial carbon dioxide over 20 years, at 8.125 million tonnes a year. Target rocks are the St. Peter and Everton sandstones and the Knox Group, capped by Maquoketa Shale.

Data from the Lively Grove number 1 test well anchored two 3-D static models, one per storage stack. Porosity maps for the St. Peter and Everton show values thinning toward the east and southeast. Where core data ran thin, the team assigned a shale porosity of 0.041 and used a Kriging fill method for the Shakopee and Oneota units.
doe-osti-3363586-resstock-measure-docume:
Philip White, Andrew Speake, Rajendra Adhikari, and Anthony Fontanini document a ResStock building stock measure. All four work at the National Laboratory of the Rockies. The report is NLR/TP-5500-94459, dated May 2026. The measure covers electric vehicle adoption with Level 1 charging. ResStock measures are retrofit or adoption packages applied across modeled homes. This one adds home charging from a standard outlet.

The authors draw on survey and census data. The data cover vehicle ownership, driving, and charging behavior. Maps show ownership by building type and income for California microdata areas. Those distributions feed the OpenStudio-HPXML workflow. It models each dwelling unit. Analysts can thus estimate how Level 1 adoption changes household energy use.
doe-osti-3363587-resstock-measure-docume:
Philip White, Andrew Speake, Rajendra Adhikari, and Anthony Fontanini document the Level 2 counterpart to their Level 1 measure. All four work at the National Laboratory of the Rockies. The report is NLR/TP-5500-94460, dated May 2026. Within the ResStock building stock model, this measure assigns electric vehicles to modeled households. The vehicles charge faster at home, on a 240 volt circuit.

As in the companion volume, the team builds input data from outside sources. The data cover ownership, driving behavior, and charging behavior. They break out by building type, tenure, and income. Each modeled home runs through the OpenStudio-HPXML workflow. Analysts can thus compare charging energy demand against the slower Level 1 case, on a consistent basis.
doe-osti-3363588-resstock-measure-docume:
Rajendra Adhikari, Andrew Speake, Philip White, and Anthony Fontanini document a ResStock measure. All four work at the National Laboratory of the Rockies. The report is NLR/TP-5500-94463, dated May 2026. The measure pairs electric vehicle adoption with Level 2 charging and demand flexibility. Flexible charging can shift its draw away from peak hours, which changes what vehicle adoption means for the grid.

Charging and discharging energy are modeled in OpenStudio-HPXML using an EnergyPlus lithium-ion battery model. The Level 2 charger in this measure draws 5.69 kilowatts, reflecting the average output of a 240 volt outlet. Other inputs scale average driving energy and home charging share. Together they shape the size and timing of charging events across the housing stock.
doe-osti-3363807-susy-2025-at-uc-santa-c:
A final technical report from the University of California, Santa Cruz covers SUSY 2025, the 32nd International Conference on Supersymmetry and the Unification of Fundamental Interactions. Wolfgang Altmannshofer and Howard Haber organized the meeting, held August 18 to 23, 2025 at the Santa Cruz Institute for Particle Physics under DOE award DE-SC0025979. The reporting period ran from August 2025 through January 2026.

The conference drew 175 registered participants from universities and research institutes worldwide. Its program held 40 plenary talks plus parallel sessions on Higgs physics, flavor physics, and the Standard Model effective field theory, among other topics. Sessions mixed theory and experiment across particle physics, cosmology, and string theory. The report preserves the schedule and session structure of a long-running meeting series that now reaches well past supersymmetry itself.
doe-osti-3366045-growing-representation-:
University of Tennessee's final report for grant DE-SC0022027, led by Nadia Fomin, covers the NPET fellowship program, which recruited its first cohort in the summer of 2021. The program recruited undergraduates from minority-serving institutions into year-long nuclear physics research in eastern Tennessee, pairing University of Tennessee Knoxville mentors with Oak Ridge National Laboratory. Ten students formed the first cohort, chosen from 18 applicants.

The first summer ran virtually in 2021, weeks after funding arrived, and the virtual format itself drew applicants whose home programs had canceled in-person research. Students presented posters at regional and national meetings, and several entered graduate programs, including PhD programs at Tennessee, Florida International, and Duke. Monthly workshops and close mentoring by scientists, postdocs, and graduate students targeted physics identity and belonging, the program's stated route to retention.
doe-osti-3377000-preliminary-modeling-of:
Idaho National Laboratory report INL/RPT-25-87307, by Dade R. George and Robert F. Kile and dated August 2025, takes a first pass at modeling triply periodic minimal surface structures in the RELAP5-3D thermal hydraulics code. Such lattices are sponge-like metal forms with huge inner surface area. They tempt heat exchanger designers who need compact duty. A one-dimensional system code has no native way to hold their shape, so the team faked it with care.

Two test rigs anchor the work: FLIP and MAGNET. The MAGNET line ran in two forms, one on air and one on helium. The lattice was modeled as a slab, with a surface area multiplier bolted on. That factor credits the true area in play. One test section is a seventy millimeter square pipe, split into three parts. The authors call the work preliminary, a base for closer models.
doe-osti-3377481-cyber-informed-engineer:
A June 2026 guide by Gareth Williams of the National Laboratory of the Rockies brings cyber-informed engineering into strategic planning. The Energy Department's CESER office sponsors the program, run with Idaho National Laboratory. Cyber-informed engineering asks a question at design time: if an attacker bent this system, what breaks? Planners at the top level set the budgets and rules that decide whether that question gets asked.

The guide sorts its prompts by theme. One set covers consequence work: naming high-harm outcomes and the gain from blocking them. Risk prompts ask how teams surface what could go wrong, with mixed experts in the room. Performance prompts split by phase, from concept to project control. Change control gets its stress: how reviews keep pace as systems shift. Each prompt cites the 2023 CIE strategy. Williams writes for leaders who fund and steer projects, not for bench engineers.
doe-osti-3403355-enhancing-300-degree-ce:
Sandia report SAND2026-24593, printed July 2026, works on electronics that must run at 300 degrees Celsius. Andrew A. Wright, Manuel Montano, Joshua Larson, Ken Coombes, Deborah Hagen, and Steven Larson wrote the study. Ceramic circuit boards and new joining methods sit at the center of the work.

Heat caused drift and strain inside key parts as temperatures neared failure points. One part, called HTOP01, shapes the output signal sent to the surface. Its health sets how true that signal stays. Next steps named in the text include better heat control, new die attach materials, and part screening for tough service.
doe-osti-3409827-building-ai-that-works-:
ESnet progress report LBNL-2001772, dated June 2026, describes ORBIT, an AI toolkit for network operations staff. Bin Dong leads a seventeen-author team at the Energy Sciences Network. ORBIT was built to explore agent-based AI ahead of the ESnet 7 upgrade.

Network operators lose time hunting facts across split data sources. ORBIT aims to speed ticket work and give cleaner answers. A gateway guards security with logging, prompt-injection defense, and leak checks. Timing studies tracked the hours operators spend checking ticket context. The report weighs real workflow gains, not AI hype, for a production science network.
doe-osti-3602550-holographic-aerosol-mon:
Report DOE/SC-ARM-26-028, dated August 2026, is an interim account of a holographic monitor test for biological aerosols. Chongai Kuang and Maria Zawadowicz, both at Brookhaven National Laboratory, are the two printed authors. Biological aerosols include bacteria, fungi, viruses, pollen, and spores. They matter for clouds, disease spread, and nutrient cycles, yet their size, shape, and counts are hard to pin down.

The monitor, called HoloCMA, images coarse particles in the air at the Bankhead National Forest site. Its first version sat on the Aerosol Observing System roof and read far lower counts than the site's particle sizer. A second version with active sampling was installed in February 2026. Moves to escape pump vibration, network faults, and severe weather all cut into its run from February to May 2026. A live dashboard shows counts over time and a library of particle images.
essays-on-mankind-and-political-arithmet:
Essays on Mankind and Political Arithmetic collects the writings of William Petty, the seventeenth century thinker who tried to count a nation's people and wealth. Petty, born in 1623 at Romsey in Hampshire, was a clothier's son who studied at Caen, Utrecht, Leyden, Amsterdam, and Paris. The long introduction traces that restless schooling, his work with the philosopher Thomas Hobbes, and an early patent for a copying machine.

Political arithmetic, Petty's own term, means judging policy by numbers: how many people a country holds, what they earn, and what taxes or trade they can bear. His essays apply that counting habit to population growth, cities, and national strength. Readers meet the founding habit of statistics here in plain argument form, written by a man who served Parliament, worked in Ireland, and trusted figures over fine phrases.
evolution-of-the-japanese-social-and-psy:
Gulick's Evolution of the Japanese studies how Japanese society and mind changed in the modern era. Sidney L. Gulick served as a missionary of the American Board in Japan. The contents open with preliminary considerations on Western views of Japan. Japan seemed to break Western theories of national evolution, he notes.

A historical sketch moves from mythology and tradition to authentic history. Old Japan gives way to the transition toward New Japan. Foreign pressure forced centralization, the sketch argues. Gulick stresses the union of Occidental and Oriental civilizations then under way. He compares Japan with India to sharpen the case. The book treats rapid change happening before the reader's eyes. It aims at thoughtful readers of any nation.
five-weeks-in-a-balloon-or-journeys-and-:
Jules Verne wrote Five Weeks in a Balloon, his first famous adventure novel, presented here in William Lackland's English version. Dr Samuel Fergusson plans to cross Africa by balloon, a route no explorer had survived on foot. His friend Dick Kennedy, a blunt Scots hunter, doubts the scheme loudly. Fergusson's servant Joe supplies courage and comic sense.

The balloon Victoria rises from Zanzibar and drifts west across the continent. Storms, thirst, hostile attacks, and a failing gas supply test the three men. They rescue a missionary, cross Lake Victoria's region, and hunt for water in the desert. Verne packs the flight with geography lessons and lists of earlier African explorers. Readers get the founding book of his Voyages Extraordinaires, where science, danger, and wonder share one balloon basket.
for-every-music-lover-a-series-of-practi:
Moore's essays aim to open music to the general listener, not just the trained few. She argues that music, like religion, is meant for all, and traces its origin and function through myth and legend. Portraits of Malibran, Mozart, Brahms, Liszt, Paganini, and Jenny Lind front the chapters.

One essay takes up tempo rubato, the stolen time that bends a melody. Aubertine Woodward Moore traces it from Greek declamation through Gregorian chant and recitative to Chopin. Chopin, she writes, held his left hand steady as a conductor while the right hand swayed the tune. The volume appeared in 1902 as a companion to her earlier musical book.
fun-and-frolic:
Fun and Frolic is a profusely illustrated miscellany for children, edited by E. T. Roe. Poems and short tales fill its pages. It opens with Grandmother's Chair, a verse portrait of an old woman knitting by the fire. She waits, in the poem, to join her husband and children in heaven. Other pieces turn to school, home, and adventure. One tale follows Ned, orphaned by yellow fever in New Orleans at fifteen. He works his way by ship to San Francisco and reaches his uncle in the California diggings.

The mix is typical of its century: sentiment, moral lessons, and lively incident. Illustrations crowd the text throughout.
gascoyne-the-sandal-wood-trader-a-tale-o:
R. M. Ballantyne sends young readers to the South Pacific in this sea tale of the sandal-wood trade. A schooner captain named Gascoyne trades among the islands, where missionaries, sailors, and island peoples meet. Chapters promise battles, fires, rescues, and chases at sea. Henry, a young officer, and his widowed mother hold the home side of the story.

Suspicion hangs over Gascoyne: is he an honest trader or Durward the pirate? Proof seems to damn him, yet those who know him best doubt it. A pastor's household, a captured boy, and the girl Poopy drive the action toward a bold escape. Ballantyne mixes storms, fights, and faith into a brisk tale of the old Pacific trade.
germany-the-next-republic:
Carl W. Ackerman, an American newsman, wrote Germany, The Next Republic? in 1917, while the United States and Germany were at war. He says the title states the goal he thinks the Allies must hold: lasting peace will come only when Germany is a republic. While the Kaiser, his generals, and the old leaders rule, he argues, the world will face the same terror as in this war.

Ackerman reports on the Reichstag's moves toward reform, led by men such as Scheidemann, and on how the German people bear the war. He holds that the people will not throw off their rulers until those rulers are beaten and disgraced. The book is wartime argument, not neutral history, and its value lies in showing how Americans were urged to think about Germany's future.
giles-an-address-on-the-need-for-medical:
Arthur Edward Giles, a London doctor, gave this address to the Manchester Medico-Chirurgical Society on January 12, 1927. It was reprinted from the Lancet that same month. Giles argues that doctors are asked about birth control by married patients, yet medical schools teach them almost nothing on the subject. The result, he says, is that sound advice is hard to get.

Giles then reviews the methods in plain order. He treats abstinence as fair for a time but not for long, and weighs the so-called safe period, which he notes is never fully safe. He judges other methods by their fairness to the wife and their real effect. The address is short, frank, and clinical. It shows a senior doctor pressing his profession to face a topic it had long left in silence.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-ClassificationU:
File 105-82555 was the FBI's headquarters file on Lee Harvey Oswald, and this memorandum of October 22, 1964, belongs to it. By then the Warren Report had been public for a month, and the Bureau's Oswald paperwork was still growing.

The archive's filing heading for the memo concerns classification, the Bureau's judgments about what in the Oswald record stayed secret and why. Classification fights decided what researchers could see for thirty years, until the Review Board of the 1990s overruled many of them. The single memo is preserved as a page of the main file, from the first year of its long secrecy.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-DomesticIntelli:
Dusko Doder reported for the Washington Post on a scandal closing in on Canadian Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau. Canada's security forces stood accused of bugging, break-ins, and dirty tricks against people at home. Doder framed the affair as Canada's own version of Watergate.

The comparison tells readers how serious the charges were. A democratic government was facing proof that its security services had broken the law in the name of security. The article preserves an American view of that crisis as it broke, when the scale of the abuses was still coming to light.
govdocs-archive_org-the-hypostasis-of-th:
The Hypostasis of the Archons is a Gnostic treatise found at Nag Hammadi in Egypt. Roger Aubrey Bullard's edition gives the Coptic text with translation and commentary, prepared with Martin Krause.

The treatise retells Genesis from the Gnostic side. The archons, proud rulers of the material world, make man, envy his spirit, and send the flood, while a higher God works to save him. Bullard's commentary explains the language and the ideas line by line. For students of early Christianity and Gnosticism, the edition is a cornerstone: text, translation, and guidance in one volume.
history-of-cuba-or-notes-of-a-traveller-:
Maturin M Ballou published this history of Cuba at Boston in 1854. The copy was already in its sixth thousand. Ballou frames the book as a traveller's notes from the tropics. Its subtitle promises a political, historical, and statistical account of the island.

The account runs from Cuba's first discovery to Ballou's own time. He lingers on Havana, its harbor, streets, and open carriages called volantes. Ladies ride hooded against the sun in his street scenes. Sugar, trade, and Spanish rule fill out the picture. American readers of the 1850s got a full, curious portrait of a near island.
in-search-of-the-okapi-a-story-of-advent:
Ernest Glanville wrote In Search of the Okapi as a tale of adventure in Central Africa, published in Chicago in 1904. Dick Compton studies Arabic while Venning watches nature and asks questions. Chapters promise a novel craft, a canoe adrift, and the story of Muata. Lions, wild dogs, and man-eaters threaten the party.

A fight with a gorilla and a night in the reeds raise the danger. In one scene a leopard claws through a shelter as a jackal howls. A secret way and vaults lead toward the rare okapi. The book is a boys' adventure in a wild setting.
laughter-an-essay-on-the-meaning-of-the-:
Henri Bergson wrote Laughter as an essay on the meaning of the comic. Bergson taught at the Collège de France and belonged to the French Institute. Cloudesley Brereton and Fred Rothwell made this authorized English translation.

Bergson himself revised the translation in detail, the preface stresses. He asks why people laugh and what laughter does in society. Comic figures, he argues, often act like stiff machines. That stiffness, seen in a living person, provokes laughter. His short book became a classic text for anyone studying comedy. Later writers on humor still argue with Bergson's machine idea. His examples from stage comedy keep the theory concrete.
laxd-la-saga-translated-from-the-iceland:
Muriel A. C. Press translated Laxdæla Saga from the Icelandic for J. M. Dent in 1899. The saga opens with Ketill Flatnose and his descendants in the ninth century. His sons prepare to leave Norway for Iceland.

Ketill himself sails to Scotland around the year 890. Unn follows to Iceland and divides her land among kin. Weddings, births, and feuds fill the chapters that follow. The saga traces one great family's fortunes across generations. English readers meet Iceland's classic prose tradition in a clear Victorian translation. Feuds over love and honor drive the saga's best-known episodes. Press's version keeps names, dates, and places carefully ordered.
love-and-freindship-sic:
Love and Freindship gathers Jane Austen's early writings, spelled just as she spelled them. Austen wrote these pieces in her teens, long before her famous novels. The title work is a tale in letters, from Laura to Marianne and others. A second unfinished novel in letters, Lesley Castle, follows it here.

Young Austen mocks the weepy novels of her day with wild delight. Her heroines faint, elope, steal, and die of grief in quick order. Every letter piles absurd trouble on absurd trouble. Yet the wit is sharp, and the comic timing already feels masterly. These pages show the future author of Pride and Prejudice learning her art by laughter.
masterman-ready-or-the-wreck-of-the-paci:
Frederick Marryat published Masterman Ready in 1841, for young people. Its full title adds Or, The Wreck of the Pacific. The tale opens in October, in a heavy gale at sea.

The Pacific runs before the wind in the wide Atlantic. Her captain watches the helm while waves lift and drop the ship. A lad of twelve clings to old Ready, the weather worn seaman. Ready calms the boy and tells him how a good ship rides a storm. Ready has sailed such seas for years and trusts the ship. His calm voice is the moral core Marryat built the tale round.
mount-music:
E. Œ. Somerville and Martin Ross published this Irish novel in 1920. The title page names both authors, though the catalog record credits Somerville alone. They were already known for The Real Charlotte and the Irish R.M. stories. The novel opens in a schoolroom, where young Christian Talbot-Lowry defies her bullying brother John.

Christian, nine in years and ninety in spirit, escapes to her father's hound kennels. She will not say she saw what she did not see, whatever the arm-twisting. The Lowry family's world of horses, hounds, and country houses fills the tale. Somerville and Ross write Irish gentry life with comedy and an undertow of loss.
nasa-tm-19630002685-heat-transfer-to-blu:
John O. Reller, Jr. of Ames Research Center wrote this NASA memorandum, TM X-391, in 1960. It studies how heat flows into blunt, round-nosed bodies. Such bodies face the fierce heating of high-speed flight and reentry. A blunt nose spreads heat better than a sharp spike does.

Catalog notes say the work compares heat rates for bodies of revolution. It also weighs how the nose shape changes those heat rates. Designers of capsules and missiles needed such rates to size heat shields. Too much heat in one spot could burn through a hull. Reller's figures fed the blunt-body rule that shaped early American spacecraft.
nasa-tm-19630004028-a-wind-tunnel-invest:
Willard G. Smith of Ames Research Center wrote this NASA memorandum, TM X-398, in February 1961. It reports wind tunnel tests of a reentry vehicle with folding wings. The wings could retract, or fold back, for the plunge through the air. Tests covered speeds below sound and just above it.

A blunt body survives reentry heat best, but it cannot fly well. Fold-out wings promised a craft that could glide and land after entry. Smith's tunnel runs checked stability and forces with wings out. The data weighed a bold trade: more parts and risk, for a runway landing. Such studies fed the long road toward reusable winged spacecraft.
nasa-tm-19640019815-characteristic-featu:
Wilton E. Causey of Marshall Space Flight Center wrote this memorandum, TM X-53108, in August 1964. It studies repeating orbits in the Earth-Moon system. The setting is the restricted three body problem of classic mechanics. In that model, Earth and Moon pull on a much lighter craft.

Causey presents orbits that return to their start state in a rotating frame. He gives each orbit's period and its closest passes by Earth and Moon. Time spent between the two worlds is also listed. The orbits take one to four months per circuit. Each crosses the Earth-Moon line behind the Moon at least once. Such paths later mattered for Moon bases and relays.
nasa-tm-19660009105-magnetic-storms-in-t:
K W Behannon and Norman F Ness at Goddard wrote this October 1965 study of magnetic storms in Earth's magnetic tail. The tail is the long part of Earth's field stretched away from the Sun. It forms where the solar wind meets the geomagnetic field. The authors base their work on detailed measurements of the field at a range of distances, the abstract begins.

Storms in the tail store and release energy that reaches Earth. They disturb communications and can drive strong auroras. Satellite measurements in the tail itself were still new in 1965. Behannon and Ness use them to describe the storm process where it starts, rather than only its effects felt on the ground below.
nasa-tm-19660017356-electron-hydrogen-io:
A Temkin, in Goddard's Laboratory for Theoretical Studies, examined a subtle point in atomic theory in this February 4, 1966, paper. When an electron strikes a hydrogen atom hard enough, it can knock the atom's own electron free. That event is ionization. Temkin checks a wave function form proposed by Peterkop and by Rudge and Seaton for that process.

He finds that their form fails a required boundary condition. Far from the center, the error grows without limit, he shows. Temkin then turns to a zeroth order form from another theory. Threshold behavior, how the chance of ionization starts at the lowest energy, is the paper's second subject for specialists.
nasa-tm-19660021073-a-chain-matrix-analy:
A Goddard analysis dated July 19, 1965, works through a radar antenna problem with chain matrices. The antenna is a monopulse type, which senses aiming error in two planes at once by comparing signal strength. The technique under study scans the antenna's aim point, its boresight, by electronics rather than by motion. Chain matrices are a bookkeeping method that passes a signal through each part of a circuit in turn.

Electronic scanning gives fast, wear-free aiming for tracking antennas. The cost is complex circuitry whose errors must be predicted. A matrix analysis does that prediction in an orderly way. Tracking stations for the space program were the natural users of a dual-plane sensing design studied this carefully.
nasa-tm-19660026808-design-methods-for-m:
F. Edward McLean and Barrett L. Shrout, of NASA's Langley Research Center in Virginia, presented this paper at an Acoustical Society of America meeting in St. Louis in November 1965. Their topic is the sonic boom, the sharp pressure wave a fast airplane drags across the ground below.

The paper reviews theory-based design methods for weakening that boom. The methods shape the airplane itself to cut the pressure field's energy and peak pressure. The authors highlight a chance to reduce overpressure for large, slender airplanes, using their extended near-field behavior. They back the discussion with comparisons between theory and wind-tunnel measurements.
nasa-tm-19670030895-wind-tunnel-investig:
Bernard J. Blaha, Robert A. Wasko, and Donald L. Bresnahan, at the Lewis Research Center in Cleveland, put a small Saturn model in a wind tunnel. The model copied the S-IC boost stage of the Saturn V. Two F-1 engine nozzles were fitted, and cold high-pressure air stood in for the exhaust jet.

The team measured the hinge moments that fight the engines' steering actuators. Base flow deflectors raised those moments, the tests showed. Moments peaked at the lower Mach numbers and eased as speed grew. Running the jet raised the moments compared with jet-off runs. Base pressures were recorded alongside, for the same deflector cases.
nasa-tm-19690007457-mean-gradient-heat-t:
James C. Hill wrote this January 1969 progress report, numbered X-641-69-6, on heat transfer in isotropic turbulence. Isotropic turbulence churns evenly in all directions, with no favored flow. Hill studies a steady fluid with a uniform average temperature gradient across it. The question is how the churning carries heat from warm side to cool.

Three ways of closing the statistical equations are discussed, ending with the direct-interaction approximation. That route needs a hard equation solved for an averaged response function. Hill tried the calculation in ordinary space coordinates first, as practice for harder shear flows. He reports plainly that numerical troubles defeated that attempt. The report closes with suggestions for finishing the work in wave-based coordinates.
nasa-tm-19690010296-an-exploratory-exper:
Separating two parallel lifting stages of a reusable launch vehicle is this thesis's subject. It is a master's thesis in aerospace engineering at the University of Virginia. The two stages fly side by side, then must part cleanly at three and six times the speed of sound. A collision or a tumbling stage at such speeds would end the mission.

Wind tunnel tests with models form the experimental half of the study. A computer program, written by Joseph Gera, tracks the vehicles' motion through the staging maneuver for the analytical half. Chapters describe the tunnel, models, and support gear, then the method of analysis. Experimental and numerical results are compared before the concluding remarks.
nasa-tm-19690011491-preliminary-developm:
Ramon M. Barnes of Lewis Research Center builds a new lab method for checking the makeup of superalloys in this report. The method uses a spark through a liquid layer on a solid sample. Barnes compares it with the standard point-to-plane spark method in air. Two test cobalt-base superalloys served for the checks.

Curves for the alloy parts shifted between the two methods. The liquid-layer method seemed to cut matrix effects for some elements. Close looks at samples and spectra hinted that mixed effects act as one to give that seeming cut. A side method with arc transfer gave true, steady results. The work aids tests of alloys used in hot engine parts.
nasa-tm-19690014794-apollo-saturn-5-flig:
Kennedy Space Center issued the Apollo/Saturn V Flight Safety Plan for vehicle AS-504 on February 22, 1969. Flight safety chief Arthur H. Moore and other program officials approved it. The plan states safety requirements, restrictions, and instrumentation for each launch. It covers the giant rocket from countdown through powered flight to orbit insertion.

Responsibility splits between the Air Force Eastern Test Range and Kennedy Space Center. The range commander sets flight termination requirements and protects life and property beyond the center. The center's director protects people and property inside Kennedy, clears launch danger areas, and owns crew safety. Requirements for destroying an errant vehicle and dispersing its propellant are also described.
nasa-tm-19690018463-cavitation-performan:
Phillip R. Meng and Royce D. Moore of Lewis Research Center evaluated a helical inducer in liquid hydrogen for this report. The 80.6-degree inducer ran at thirty thousand revolutions per minute. Tests covered a range of liquid hydrogen temperatures and flow coefficients, in both cavitating and noncavitating operation.

Net positive suction head needs fell as liquid temperature rose. At fixed temperature, those needs rose rapidly with flow coefficient. At low flow coefficients and higher temperatures, the inducer still produced useful head rise. It did so even with vapor present at its inlet. Such behavior matters for rocket turbopumps, which must keep feeding engines without losing prime in hydrogen service.
nasa-tm-19700019348-control-of-cell-divi:
Clarence D. Cone Jr. gave this presentation at the Twelfth Annual Science Writers Seminar in San Antonio, Texas, in March 1970. The seminar was run by the American Cancer Society. His topic is how the voltage across a cell's surface membrane controls whether that cell divides.

Cone argues that the ion pattern set by that voltage acts as a precise switch on division in body cells. He says the theory was tested and held up in work with mammalian cells. It also links cancer's two main dangers, uncontrolled growth and spreading, to one fault in the cell surface. Cells with strongly negative voltages, like nerve and muscle cells, seldom divide at all.
nasa-tm-19700023780-a-screening-and-sele:
Gerald Halpert of the Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this preprint in April 1970. It gives a screening and selection method for nickel-cadmium cell plates. Such plates sit at the heart of the rechargeable batteries that powered many spacecraft, so matched plates mattered for safe, even power.

Halpert's procedure sorts cell materials before assembly to improve uniformity and reliability across a batch. Screening by weight, he reports, proved a successful way to even out plate capacity. A statistical study of the test results shows a strong link between a plate's weight and its capacity. That link lets builders predict the capacity of every plate in a batch from weight alone.
nasa-tm-19710022873-new-directions-in-ma:
S S Manson of the Lewis Research Center gave this opening lecture at an August 1971 conference in Kyoto, Japan, on the mechanical behavior of materials. It surveys the harsh demands that coming machines would place on materials. His examples were car thermal reactors, jet engines, the space shuttle, and space nuclear power systems. Each project needed metals and plastics beyond the proven state of the art.

Manson showed recent research answering those demands. Topics ranged from new composite materials to powder metallurgy and directional solidification. He covered cold fracture and hot creep and fatigue as well. New test facilities and analysis methods featured throughout. The lecture mapped where materials research had to go next.
nasa-tm-19720016331-the-asee-university-:
This final report, numbered X-752-71-277, covers a summer faculty fellowship program at Goddard Space Flight Center. Its partners were the ASEE, the University of Maryland, and Catholic University. University faculty came to Goddard for about ten weeks at a time. The report marks the completion of the program's sixth year at Goddard.

At Goddard the fellows joined active research projects in their own fields and took part in seminars tied to that research. The stated aims include drawing universities into Goddard's research problems and keeping fellows researching after the summer ends. The program also aimed to stimulate Goddard staff through the exchanges and to build closer university ties. Contents cover administration, participants, the educational program, and the fellows' research reports, which open with studies of the SAS-A satellite.
nasa-tm-19720022697-average-daily-variat:
T L Skillman of NASA analyzed magnetic field readings from the ATS-5 satellite in this August 1972 report, NASA TM X-66004. ATS-5 sat in geostationary orbit, circling with Earth's rotation. Its magnetic field monitor recorded the field hour by hour. Skillman averaged those records to reveal the daily rhythm of the field. The data span two full years, from September 1969 through September 1971. Few studies then held such a complete record.

Hourly averages of each field component were sorted and studied. The sorting used levels of magnetic disturbance, ranked by the Kp index. Quiet days and stormy days show different daily patterns. Separating them shows how the field breathes with the solar wind. The report runs to fifty five pages. Its tables served magnetosphere modelers for years.
philip-winwood-a-sketch-of-the-domestic-: The hosted sample stops at the front matter of Philip Winwood, the publisher's list of Robert Neilson Stephens's works and the start of the full title. No chapter text is visible. The complete title describes a sketch of the domestic history of an American captain in the War of Independence. It covers events between and during 1763 and 1786 in New York and London. It claims to be written by his enemy in war, Herbert Russell, a lieutenant in the Loyalist forces.
podcast-joerogan-TukvVnadRic:
Schoolchildren in Zimbabwe who reported a UFO landing in 1994 are the subject of a segment of the Joe Rogan Experience. At the Ariel School, dozens of young students told the same strange story of a craft and small beings. A Harvard professor later interviewed them on camera.

Rogan retells the case and weighs what makes it hard to shake: the number of witnesses, their agreement, and their calm years later as adults. He asks what else could explain that morning. The segment keeps one of the most debated UFO cases in circulation, told as a story first and a puzzle second.
public-lands-and-agrarian-laws-of-the-ro:
Andrew Stephenson, a professor of history at Wesleyan University, traced Rome's public lands from the earliest times to the founding of the Empire in a study printed at Baltimore in 1891. The work appeared in the Johns Hopkins University Studies in history and political science.

Stephenson follows the growth of private property in land, the swelling of the public domain by conquest, and its slow loss through sale, gifts, and colonies. Since grants of land required laws, the agrarian laws run through the whole story. Readers get a compact history of land, power, and reform in republican Rome.
shakespeare-and-music:
Edward W. Naylor published this study with J. M. Dent in London in 1896. Pictures drawn from the music of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries light up the text. Naylor holds degrees in arts and music, and he writes for readers who know the plays well but the old tunes less.

Songs, dances, and stage music run through Shakespeare's work, from catches and ballads to solemn measures. Naylor traces what those sounds were in Shakespeare's own day and how they worked in performance. The book helps modern readers hear the plays as their first crowds heard them, with period instruments and tunes restored to view.
sketches-of-western-north-carolina-histo:
C. L. Hunter wrote Sketches of Western North Carolina, Historical and Biographical, dated 1877. The book treats the war for freedom in Mecklenburg, Rowan, Lincoln, and nearby counties, with lives of the men who took part. Hunter states that much of the matter had never been printed before, and he adds mixed facts beyond the main war years.

Hunter opens by calling history a teacher that works through true examples. He argues that free states gain much when young men study the past. The war for freedom, in his view, shows weak colonies with no army, navy, or firm rule still standing up to the trained troops of a strong nation.
sonnets-on-sundry-notes-of-music:
Sonnets to Sundry Notes of Music carries William Shakespeare's name. The poems run in numbered sets. The first tells of a lording's daughter. She was the fairest of three sisters. Her fancy turned from her master to an Englishman. Long was the fight doubtful, love with love. One man of the two had to be refused. Art, with arms contending, won the day. The learned man bore the maid away.

The second poem hails a day in May. Love spied a blossom passing fair at play. The wind found passage through its velvet leaves. The lover wished himself the heaven's breath. He longed to blow on those cheeks as air does. His hand, though, has sworn off the flower. It will never pluck it from its thorn. A third piece turns to flocks that feed not.
tales-of-the-enchanted-islands-of-the-at:
Thomas Wentworth Higginson wrote Tales of the Enchanted Islands of the Atlantic to retell old sea legends for new readers. In his preface he notes that Hawthorne had retold Greek myths in his Wonder Book, but no one had done the same for Atlantic island tales.

Higginson argues that early American lore is far from plain or dull, since each trip to the New World crossed a wild sea. He sees islands as places of magic, with height above depth and safe land beside storm. Readers get tales shaped over more than a thousand years, shared by both sides of the Atlantic as a joint birthright.
the-boy-aviators-polar-dash-or-facing-de: Captain Wilbur Lawton wrote The Boy Aviators' Polar Dash, or Facing Death in the Antarctic. A note in the book says Lawton is a pen name for John Henry Goldfrap. It is sixth in his Boy Aviators set. The first chapters are The Polar Ship, A Mysterious Robbery, and Off for the South Pole. Adrift on a Floating Island, Caught in the Flames, A Queer Accident, and The Professor is Kidnapped close the list shown.
the-crater-or-vulcan-s-peak-a-tale-of-th:
J. Fenimore Cooper's The Crater, or Vulcan's Peak, a tale of the Pacific dated 1863, opens with a preface that faces a puzzle head-on. Readers will ask, Cooper says, why geographies and histories never mention the Reef, Rancocus Island, Vulcan's Peak, the Crater, or the other islands his pages describe.

His answer is blunt: the writers of those works most likely never heard of such places. Silence in the geographies, he argues, is weak proof against a spot's existence. Barely three and a half centuries back, those same books held not a syllable about the whole American continent. Less than a century back they began describing New Zealand, New Holland, Tahiti, and Oahu. Even Japan, he notes, gets thin and faulty treatment in the largest of them.
the-eclipse-of-faith-or-a-visit-to-a-rel:
The Eclipse of Faith; or, A Visit to a Religious Sceptic reached a fifth edition at Boston in 1854. Its American preface warns readers to take the book's aim aright. The author, thought to be Henry Rogers of the Edinburgh Review, made no such vast claim. He did not try to answer every charge against Christian faith. He did not try to clear every doubt.

The book stages long talks between a believer and a sceptic friend. Rogers saw faith unsettled in high and low ranks alike, above all on the Bible's authority. His talks test doubt with patience, wit, and learning.
the-game-of-logic:
Lewis Carroll wrote The Game of Logic as a book that teaches reasoning with boards, counters, and play. A diagram of squares and marks stands at the front, with a verse on red and grey counters.

Carroll gives the book to a child friend in a poem that mourns lost days and a fairy friend's smile. The game uses red counters for full truth and grey for none, set on a board ruled by the terms of a claim. Hard rules of logic turn into a board game a child can play. Carroll, who taught math at Oxford, hides strict lessons on how claims join and clash inside jokes and verse.
the-republic:
Plato's dialogue appears in Benjamin Jowett's translation with a long introduction calling it the longest of Plato's works except the Laws and certainly the greatest. The introduction grants nearer approaches to modern metaphysics elsewhere and clearer institutions in the Laws.

No other dialogue, the editor argues, matches its largeness of view, perfection of style, knowledge of the world, dramatic power, irony, humor, and imagery. Life and speculation, politics and philosophy, are interwoven at its center. New readers are thus told to treat the work as the hub around which the other dialogues group themselves.
the-romantic:
May Sinclair published The Romantic in 1920. The novel is arranged in two books. They are named for Charlotte Redhead and John Roden Conway. An epigraph is credited to the saying of the Romantic. It claims every kind and beautiful thing was made so by some cruelty.

The opening follows Charlotte walking a station platform. A large man in tweeds walks beside her. She studies his dignity and heavy swing without looking at him directly. Instead she fixes on the gabled station and bridge girders. She notices the signal post, the rails, and small fields after rain. She even smiles at the clank of her own boots. He hated that sound, the narrative notes.
the-rover-boys-in-the-jungle-or-stirring:
Dated November 10, 1899, Edward Stratemeyer's introduction presents The Rover Boys in the Jungle as the third story of his series. He wrote it under the name Arthur M. Winfield. It is a companion to At School and On the Ocean, though complete in itself.

The scene shifts from Putnam Hall, where Dick, Tom and Sam are cadets, to the wilds of Africa. The lads travel there with their uncle. They seek Anderson Rover, their father, who disappeared many years before. A remarkable message from the sea prompts the journey. Stratemeyer promises stirring adventures and perils in the heart of the continent before the search is resolved.
the-sisters-tragedy-with-other-poems-lyr: Thomas Bailey Aldrich's The Sisters' Tragedy with Other Poems, Lyrical and Dramatic is represented here by its contents list. No poem text follows, beyond a date line of A. D. 1670 under the title poem. The list names The Last Caesar and In Westminster Abbey. Alec Yeaton's Son and a monody on the death of Wendell Phillips appear. Pauline Pavlovna and a pastoral called Corydon also figure. Interludes, an echo-song, and a petition close the list shown.
the-trials-of-the-soldier-s-wife-a-tale-: Alex. St. Clair Abrams published The Trials of the Soldier's Wife at Atlanta in 1864, entering copyright in the Confederate States district court, and calling his tale one of the Second American Revolution. This record shows a transcriber's note, the title page, and the start of a dedication to Colonel John H. Jossey of Macon. The note confesses, on the author's own admission, that the book is filled with many errors, of which only the obvious ones were corrected. The soldier's wife and her trials begin beyond these leaves.
un-doc-international-review-of-criminal-:
Developing a Computer Ethic forms part of the United Nations manual on computer crime, printed in the International Review of Criminal Policy, Nos. 43 and 44. Law alone cannot police the new machines. Older crafts like medicine had centuries to build their codes of conduct. Computing had only decades.

The piece argues for a clear code of right use. Computers now hold wealth that can move at a keystroke. They also carry out acts on their users' behalf. That dual role raises fresh blame questions. Both the firms that run systems and the people who use them need a sense of duty. Teaching should start in primary school and run through college. World guides from 1992 put respect for others' rights at the core.
verses-for-children-and-songs-for-music: Juliana Horatia Ewing wrote Verses for Children and Songs for Music. The Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge issued the book at London. The pages given here hold the title page and a list of the poems, so the verses themselves are not shown. Titles promise garden and nursery scenes. They name The Burial of the Linnet, Master Fritz, and the Willow-Man. Our Garden and Dolly's Lullaby follow. A hero to his hobby-horse, the dolls' wash, and an only child's tea-party close the list.
